title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
text:
0  Preface
Are Islamophobic attitudes more widespread in eastern Germany than in the West? Who holds them, and how are they related to political orientations? To answer such questions with data, you need two things: a clean dataset such as the 2023 German General Social Survey (ALLBUS), and a tool that can analyse it. This book is an introduction to that tool: R for statistical data analysis in the social sciences. It is written for students who are new to R, often with some experience of SPSS, and who are looking for a simple, modern introduction.
You work your way from the first data import through descriptive and inferential statistics to factor analysis and regression. The toolkit is deliberately small: the tidyverse for data manipulation and visualisation, and mariposa, a package developed in Marburg, for statistical analysis. On top of that, you use Quarto to turn your code into a published report.
The methods are intended for social science studies that meet scientific survey standards. You can use the same techniques for data collected without such standards, and survey weighting is included from the start.

title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
section: What you will be able to do after this book
text:
What you will be able to do after this book

Import datasets from SPSS, Stata or Excel and handle labels and missing values.
Transform and recode data and build scales from items.
Carry out univariate, bivariate and multivariate analyses, with and without survey weights.
Compute and interpret correlations, factor analyses, and linear and logistic regressions.
Turn results into publication-ready graphics with ggplot2.
Document an analysis so that it can be reproduced.
Write and check R code with AI assistants without passing on research data.

title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
text:
Overview of the chapters

1RStudio

Install R and RStudio in the right order.
Use the RStudio interface with confidence.
2Quarto and reproducible research

Explain the difference between an R script, R Markdown and Quarto.
Create a .qmd document, render it and export it to HTML/PDF/Word.
3The R programming language

Create and name variables and assign values to them.
Keep your code understandable for your future self with # comments.
4Data import and inspection

Import an SPSS dataset with read_spss(), including all variable and value labels.
Search for variables by name or label with find_var().
5Transforming data and building scales

Create new variables with mutate().
Write conditional logic with case_when(), recode_values() and if_else().
6Visualisation basics

Explain the grammar of graphics approach of ggplot2.
Visualise frequencies, distributions and relationships with the appropriate geom_*() layers.
7Univariate and bivariate analysis

Report the frequency distribution of a variable, weighted and unweighted.
Determine the mean, median, spread, IQR, skewness, kurtosis and standard error.
8Latent structures

Set up and read an inter-item correlation matrix and visualise it as a heatmap with ggplot2.
Understand the KMO measure and Bartlett's test as assumption checks and find them in the efa() output.
9Explanatory models

Run a simple linear regression with one predictor, draw the regression line by hand from the model coefficients in a scatter plot (geom_abline()) and follow the OLS logic (“least squares”).
Run, weight and interpret a multiple linear regression: coefficients, Beta, R², model F.
10Working with AI assistants

Explain why an AI assistant may invent functions and arguments for mariposa.
Write a request that gives context: goal, package versions, documentation, variables and error message.

title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
text:
How to read this book

Read the chapters in order. They build on each other. Chapter 3 assumes the basics from Chapters 1–2, all methods chapters from Chapter 7 onwards assume the data preparation from Chapters 4–5, and Chapters 7–9 use the visualisation basics from Chapter 6 throughout.
Run the code as you read. Keep RStudio open alongside the book and copy the chunks into your Quarto document. Copying and pasting is explicitly encouraged.
Take the exercises seriously. Each chapter ends with four exercises: two reproduction exercises, one transfer exercise and one mini research question without a model solution. If you apply the mini research questions in the methods chapters consistently to a question of your own, you build up a small research project alongside the main ALLBUS study. Try each exercise yourself first.
Get the dataset early. You need ALLBUS 2023 from Chapter 4 onwards; how to get the data is explained under Example dataset.

A short roadmap through the six stages:

title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
text:
Why R?

R is a programming language developed specifically for statistical computing and data visualisation.
R is open source: there are no licence fees, and the add-on packages are free too.
You can analyse and visualise data very flexibly. Small analyses and large pipelines follow the same coding style.
Research organisations, companies and public authorities use R worldwide. R skills are in demand on the job market.
R runs on all common platforms and can be integrated into any IT infrastructure.

title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
text:
Why tidyverse and mariposa?
Instead of a long list of specialised packages, we work with the tidyverse ecosystem and the mariposa package.
Tidyverse. A collection of packages designed to work together (dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, readr, purrr, tibble, stringr, forcats, lubridate) that share a common style for data manipulation and visualisation. Once you have understood the tidyverse, you can read almost any modern R script.
mariposa. A package developed in Marburg (Marburg Initiative for Political and Social Analysis) that provides the methods typical of social science analyses in a consistent syntax close to the tidyverse: data import from SPSS, handling of labels and missing values, descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVA, correlation, factor analysis, regression. The output follows the table layouts of SPSS, so if you are switching from SPSS you will recognise it. The results are checked against reference output from SPSS Statistics 29. The mariposa vignette “SPSS Compatibility” shows which functions have been compared with SPSS and how thoroughly.

title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
text:
Requirements
R (programming language, open source). You can find the current version at cran.r-project.org. This book requires at least R 4.3; R 4.5 or later is recommended so that all functions shown here run without changes.
RStudio as the integrated development environment (IDE). The IDE itself is still called RStudio; the company behind it has been called Posit since 2022. You need the desktop version: posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop. If you prefer not to install anything locally, you can use Posit Cloud (formerly RStudio Cloud) in your browser instead.
Packages. At the start, we install the tidyverse ecosystem and the mariposa package once; we use them throughout the book. Both are available on CRAN, the official R package archive:

install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("mariposa")

This book was rendered with mariposa 0.7.4. To see which version you have, run packageVersion("mariposa"). Older versions (before 0.7.4) give different output in some places or do not yet have some of the arguments.
Load both packages in every R session:

library(tidyverse)
library(mariposa)

Later, patchwork is added for combining plots in Chapter 9, and lavaan and semPlot for confirmatory factor analysis in Chapter 8. Apart from these, the book deliberately uses no other packages.

title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
text:
Example dataset: ALLBUS 2023
Throughout the book we work with the ALLBUS, the German General Social Survey. The examples come from the 2023 wave with 5246 respondents and 579 variables.
How to get the data. You can find the English-language edition of the dataset, “German General Social Survey – ALLBUScompact 2023”, in the GESIS data catalogue under study number ZA8833. You need a free GESIS account; after registering, you can download the SPSS version. Save the file in your project folder as ALLBUS2023.sav.
As the common thread through the methods chapters, we use the question:

Who holds Islamophobic attitudes in Germany in 2023, and how are they related to political orientations and social structure?

The question runs through every chapter:

Chapter 4: Data import and inspection. You import the ALLBUS, find variables with find_var(), declare missing values and create your analysis subset.
Chapter 5: Transforming data and building scales. From six ALLBUS items you build an Islamophobia scale, and alongside it a populism scale, including careful reverse coding, a minimum number of valid answers and POMPS for comparability.
Chapter 6: Visualisation basics. You get to know the grammar of graphics behind ggplot2. You use these tools in the following chapters to illustrate each method.
Chapter 7: Univariate and bivariate analysis. You describe the distribution of the scale, compare East and West, and test the relationship with populism.
Chapter 8: Latent structures. You check the factor structure and reliability of the scales with EFA, Cronbach’s α and a first look at CFA.
Chapter 9: Explanatory models. You ask which characteristics (education, age, region, populism) best explain Islamophobia, using factorial ANOVA and multiple and logistic regression, and present the results as a publication-ready coefficient plot with patchwork.
Chapter 10: Working with AI assistants. You let an assistant help you with further steps of your analysis and check its suggestions. The assistant does not get to see the ALLBUS data.

This way you see how the individual methods combine into a complete analysis.

title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
text:
How the chapters are structured
Every methods chapter follows the same structure: a question is answered in code, and the output is given an interpretation. Large parts of the chapters consist of R code in code chunks:

allbus |> describe(islamophobia, weights = wghtpew)

The result appears directly below, rendered into the book. You can copy the code into your own Quarto document at any time; copying and pasting is explicitly encouraged.
Pipe operator. Throughout the book you will see the native pipe |>. It passes the result of one function on to the next and turns nested code into a readable sequence of steps:

allbus |>
  filter(eastwest == 1) |>
  describe(ls01)

In older code you will often find %>% (from the magrittr package). The two do almost the same thing; Chapter 3 briefly explains the difference.
Boxes. Four kinds of boxes appear throughout the book. Two of them are always open, because you need them at exactly that point:






Tip



SPSS → R. Direct translation help for people switching from SPSS: the SPSS command and its R equivalent.


The second open box warns about mistakes that are easy to make and that you often notice only late:






Warning



Caution. Common pitfalls and stumbling blocks.


The other two contain additional knowledge and are therefore collapsed. You do not need them for the next step in the chapter; clicking the line opens them:






NoteBackground: theory behind a method





Short notes that explain why a method works the way it does, where a scale comes from or what belongs in a methods report.



The notes on shortcuts that mariposa offers are collapsed too:






Importantmariposa tip: more compact solutions





Places where mariposa offers a particularly compact solution.

title: R Workshop – Social Sciences
text:
Further reading
If you want to go deeper:

Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel & Garrett Grolemund, R for Data Science (2nd edition), the standard work on the tidyverse, free online.
Hadley Wickham, Advanced R, for anyone who wants to understand R as a programming language.
mariposa documentation: yannickdiehl.github.io/mariposa, with function reference and vignettes.
Posit, Quarto documentation, the reference for books, reports and coursework written with Quarto (see Chapter 2).

title: 1  RStudio
text:
1.1 What this chapter is about
R itself is only an interpreter: a programming language that takes commands and returns answers. To work with R comfortably, you need an integrated development environment (IDE): an editor, a console, a file browser and a variable inspector in one window. RStudio provides this environment. In SPSS you reach everything through point-and-click dialogs; in RStudio you write your steps as code in a Quarto document. Your steps are then reproducible, you can comment them, and you can keep them under version control.
If you have not yet installed R and RStudio, the first two sections show you how. Then open RStudio and follow the remaining sections in it. By the end, you will be able to find your way around RStudio, install additional packages and create your first project.

title: 1  RStudio
text:
Note



Research journal: Where are you in your mini study? You are just starting. In Chapters 1–3 you set up your tools. From Chapter 4 onwards you load the 2023 German General Social Survey (ALLBUS), from Chapter 5 you build a scale of Islamophobia from six survey items, from Chapter 7 you test hypotheses, and from Chapter 9 you model which social and political characteristics best explain Islamophobia. This is the first stage, in which you set up your workspace.

title: 1  RStudio
section: What you will be able to do after this chapter
text:
What you will be able to do after this chapter

Install R and RStudio in the right order.
Use the RStudio interface with confidence.
Create a project and keep your work organised in it.
Explain the difference between the console and a Quarto document.
Understand what the working directory is and check it with getwd().
Install, activate and update packages, in particular tidyverse and mariposa.
Open the help pages and package vignettes you need.
Use the most important keyboard shortcuts.

title: 1  RStudio
text:
1.2 Installing R
R itself is the engine in the background, the language that runs your commands. RStudio is only the interface. You need to install both: R first, then RStudio. If you do it the other way round, you get the error message “No R installation found” when you first start RStudio.
Go to cran.r-project.org and choose your operating system:

macOS → download the .pkg file for your architecture (Apple Silicon = M1/M2/M3/M4, or Intel) and install it by double-clicking.
Windows → click base, then the download link, and run the .exe file.
Linux → follow the instructions for your distribution on the CRAN page.

R 4.5 or later is recommended. If you already have an older version, that is not a problem; you install the new one alongside it.






NoteBackground: R on the Mac





On Macs with Apple Silicon (M1–M4) you download the arm64 version, on older Intel Macs the x86_64 version. If you do not know which one you have: Apple menu → About This Mac → Chip. To compile packages you also need the Xcode Command Line Tools. They are installed automatically when needed, or you can install them in advance in the Terminal with xcode-select --install.

title: 1  RStudio
text:
1.3 Installing RStudio
Once R is installed, download RStudio from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop. The page detects your operating system and suggests the right version. Install it like any other program.
If you prefer not to install anything locally, you can use Posit Cloud in your browser instead. The account is free, and RStudio runs entirely online.






NoteBackground: RStudio and Posit





The IDE is still called RStudio; the company behind it was renamed Posit in 2022. If you find references to “RStudio Cloud” on the web, the service is now at posit.cloud.

title: 1  RStudio
text:
1.4 The user interface
RStudio’s graphical user interface (GUI) is divided into four panes (Figure 1.1). As long as no document is open, the console takes up the whole left half. The editor at the top left appears as soon as you open a document (Section 1.5.2).





Figure 1.1: The four panes of RStudio. The chunk in the Quarto document 01-first_steps.qmd creates var1. The result appears below the chunk and in the console, and the new object appears in the Environment.









Pane
Contents
What you need it for



1 top left
Editor for Quarto documents (.qmd)
Writing, saving and running code


2 bottom left
Console
Trying out code directly, viewing output


3 top right
Environment, History, Connections, Tutorial
Seeing objects, command history, databases


4 bottom right
Files, Plots, Packages, Help, Viewer
File browser, plots, help, packages



The following sections go through the panes one by one. The green number at the top right of each screenshot shows which pane it comes from. The screenshots come from the German edition, so the example document in them is called 01-erste_schritte.qmd, not 01-first_steps.qmd.

1.4.1 Options for reproducible work
Before you start working with RStudio in earnest, go to Tools → Global Options and turn off two convenience features that do more harm than good in everyday research:


Restore .RData into workspace at startup: untick it.

Save workspace to .RData on exit: set it to Never.

This means you have to load your data and variables again every time you restart. In return, you get a genuinely fresh workspace without invisible leftovers from earlier sessions. This is the basis of reproducible work: your analysis should depend only on what is written in the document.








If you prefer a dark look, you can find colour schemes for the editor and the console under Appearance.

1.4.2 Console
The console is the first place to practise: here you can try out input directly. The > sign is the prompt, and you can use R like a calculator:

2 + 3

[1] 5










What you type in the console, however, is not saved anywhere permanently. As soon as you want to keep an analysis, it belongs in a Quarto document (see Section 1.5.2).

1.4.3 Environment and History
In the Environment tab you find the Global Environment (drop-down menu). This is where R stores all the objects you have created: variables, datasets and functions.








Under History you see all the commands you have run so far. Double-clicking a command copies it back into the console, where you can change it or run it again. In the console, you can also call up the history directly with cmd (macOS) or ctrl (Windows) + ↑.

1.4.4 Files and the working directory with getwd() and setwd()

Under Files you see the file browser for your working directory. This is the folder in which R looks by default when you read or save a file. If you write read_spss("ALLBUS2023.sav"), R looks for the file in exactly this folder. getwd() in the console tells you which folder this currently is:

getwd()
# [1] "/Users/anna/Documents/R-Workshop"

You can set the working directory by hand with setwd("…"). In practice you hardly ever need this if you work with a project (see Section 1.5.1). Whenever you open a project, the working directory is automatically the project folder. This is the basis for portable documents: there are no absolute paths anywhere, and every file path is relative to the project folder.














Warning



Caution: Absolute paths. Never write read_spss("/Users/anna/Documents/...") in your document. As soon as you share it or move it to another computer, the path no longer works. With projects, the relative path is enough: the file name alone will do if the file is in the project folder.


The file name alone is enough because R looks for it in the working directory, and with a project this is the project folder on every computer. The absolute path, on the other hand, points to a folder that exists only on Anna’s computer (Figure 1.2).





Figure 1.2: The project R-Workshop on two computers. With the file name, read_spss() finds the file on both; with the absolute path, only on Anna’s computer.

title: 1  RStudio
text:
1.5 Working with RStudio
The rest of the chapter is practical. Three ideas are central here: the project as a container, the Quarto document as the place where you work, and keyboard shortcuts to speed things up.

1.5.1 Creating a project
Before you work with data, it is worth creating a project. Choose File → New Project → New Directory → New Project to open the dialog, then enter a name and a location.








What a project gives you:

When you open the project (by double-clicking the .Rproj file), RStudio reopens all the files you had open.
You can open as many projects as you like at the same time and switch between them.
The working directory is automatically the project folder, so you no longer have to type full paths.

Move your datasets (for example ALLBUS2023.sav, once you have it) into the project folder, and you can import them directly with read_spss("ALLBUS2023.sav").

1.5.2 Quarto documents: your main working file
A Quarto document is a text file with the extension .qmd. It contains text with code chunks of R code in between. When you run a chunk, the result appears directly below it. Chapter 2 shows how a Quarto document is structured and how it becomes a finished report.
To create a new document, choose File → New File → Quarto Document…. In the dialog, enter a title, leave HTML as the format and untick Use visual markdown editor. You then see the source as it is shown in this book. Delete the example text below the header (everything after the second --- line) and save the document in the project folder with cmd/ctrl + S, for example as 01-first_steps.qmd.






Tip



SPSS → R: Syntax file and Quarto document. The Quarto document plays the role of the SPSS syntax file. You still work in syntax, only in a different language, and the text and results sit right next to the code. Most SPSS workflows can be transferred step by step, often in fewer lines.


A first example: insert a chunk with cmd/ctrl + option/alt + I and write two lines in it. In the document it looks like this:
```{r}
var1 <- 2 + 3
var1
```
Put the cursor in the first line and run it with Run (or cmd/ctrl + Enter), then do the same with the second line. The result appears below the chunk and in the console:

var1 <- 2 + 3
var1

[1] 5


In RStudio, the result appears in a box directly below the chunk:








var1 is now visible in the Environment with the value 5. Chapter 3 explains what exactly a variable is, how you call functions and which data types R knows.






Warning



Caution: Assignment operator. Use <- for assignments, not =. = also works in many cases, but in more complex contexts (function arguments) it leads to subtle bugs. Make <- a habit.


Console or document? Everything you want to keep goes into the Quarto document. You use the console for trying things out, for example for a quick calculation or to find out what an error message means. You also type install.packages() in the console, because you install a package only once per computer. library(), however, belongs in the first chunk of the document, because every new R session needs it again (Section 1.6.2).
In other books and tutorials you will often come across R scripts. An R script is a text file with the extension .R that contains only code, without text or results in between. You run its lines in the same way with cmd/ctrl + Enter; the result then appears only in the console.

1.5.3 Tab completion and the package prefix ::

RStudio offers tab completion. While you type, a drop-down list appears with suggestions for completing your input. From the third character onwards it appears by itself; otherwise you call it up with the Tab key. If you type w_m, for example, RStudio suggests the mariposa functions w_mean(), w_median() and w_modus(), with the help for the highlighted function next to them.








If the cursor is inside the brackets of a function and you press Tab, RStudio lists all its arguments. Function arguments tell a function which data to process and how. In mariposa functions the first argument is usually data, followed by the variables you are interested in and, optionally, weights = wghtpew for weighting.








If two packages share a function name, you can resolve the ambiguity with the package prefix: package::function. After mariposa::, RStudio also shows you all the functions in the package:









1.5.4 Useful keyboard shortcuts
These keyboard shortcuts save you a lot of time in the long run:







Shortcut
Effect
When it is useful




cmd/ctrl + Enter

Run current line
In a chunk



cmd/ctrl + S

Save document
After every change



cmd/ctrl + option/alt + I

Insert new chunk
In a Quarto document



cmd/ctrl + shift + Enter

Run whole chunk
After changes in the chunk



cmd/ctrl + ↑

Show previous commands
In the console



control/ctrl + L

Clear console
When it gets cluttered



cmd/ctrl + shift + C

Comment out line
To switch code off for a moment



cmd/ctrl + shift + A

Reformat code block
To tidy up indented code



option/alt + -

Insert assignment arrow <-

Instead of typing it by hand



cmd/ctrl + shift + M

Insert pipe |>

When writing pipes (see Chapter 3)



For a complete list of all available keyboard shortcuts in RStudio, press option/alt + shift + K.






NoteBackground: |> or %>%?





Since version 2021.09, RStudio has offered the native pipe |> (available from R 4.1). Before that, the magrittr pipe %>% was standard. We use |> throughout this book. Under Tools → Global Options → Code you can choose which operator the shortcut inserts; we recommend the native pipe.

title: 1  RStudio
text:
1.6 Packages
R already comes with a good number of useful functions, known as base R. For many analysis steps, however, they are too abstract, so we use additional packages that extend the set of functions available. In this book we deliberately work only with the tidyverse ecosystem for data manipulation and visualisation and the mariposa package for statistical analysis.
Functions such as read_spss() and w_mean() are contained in a package, in this case mariposa. The tidyverse brings together several packages, such as dplyr and ggplot2, that follow the same rules and that you install together with one command (Figure 1.3).





Figure 1.3: Functions are contained in packages, and packages that belong together form an ecosystem. On the left the tidyverse, on the right mariposa with two of its functions.


You work with a package in two steps:

Install it with install.packages("name"), once per computer. Imagine buying a tool at the hardware shop and putting it on your tool shelf.
Activate it with library(name), once per R session. You take the tool off the shelf and put it on the workbench.

Installing a package without calling library() is like leaving a tool unused on the shelf. Conversely, if you call library(forcats) without having installed the package, you get an error.

1.6.1 Installing with install.packages()

The tidyverse is available on CRAN, the central archive of R packages, and you can install it directly:

install.packages("tidyverse")

This installs the packages dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, readr, purrr, tibble, stringr, forcats and lubridate in one step.
mariposa is also on CRAN, and you install it in the same way:

install.packages("mariposa")

For combining plots in Chapter 9 you also need patchwork:

install.packages("patchwork")







NoteBackground: CRAN and GitHub





R packages are kept in two different places:

CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network) is the official package archive, comparable to an app store. Every package is checked automatically before it is accepted (Does it build on all platforms? Is the documentation complete? Do the tests pass?). Updates are stable but arrive later.
GitHub is the platform for developers. This is where you find the current state of development: the newest functions and the latest bug fixes, but with less checking. Many packages appear there earlier than on CRAN.

In this book you install both packages from CRAN, which is the stable option. If you need the development version of mariposa, you get it from GitHub with the helper package remotes (remotes::install_github("YannickDiehl/mariposa")); you do not need it for this book.




1.6.2 Activating with library()

You need to activate installed packages with library() in every R session:

library(tidyverse)
library(mariposa)
library(patchwork)

After these three lines, all three packages are on the workbench (Figure 1.4). When you close RStudio, they stay installed on the shelf; in the next session you call library() again.





Figure 1.4: install.packages() puts a package on the shelf once per computer; library() puts it on the workbench in every R session.


You can also install and activate packages in the Packages tab (at the bottom right in RStudio). This is good for a quick overview, but for reproducible work, code is the better way. A tick in front of the name shows that the package has been activated with library().









1.6.3 Keeping packages up to date with update.packages() and packageVersion()

You can start updates in the Packages tab or with code:

update.packages(ask = FALSE)     # update all CRAN packages, mariposa included
packageVersion("mariposa")       # which version is installed?







Warning



Caution: Updates in the middle of a project. If you update a package in the middle of a project, the behaviour of your functions may change. Update packages between projects, or record the versions you used with sessionInfo(). This book was rendered with mariposa 0.7.4; with older versions some output differs.



1.6.4 Citing packages with citation() and toBibtex()

If you use mariposa for the calculations in your coursework, cite the package. citation("mariposa") gives you the complete reference including the DOI, and toBibtex(citation("mariposa")) gives it in BibTeX format for your bibliography (see Section 2.9).

title: 1  RStudio
section: 1.7 Finding help with ?, vignette() and browseVignettes()
text:
1.7 Finding help with ?, vignette() and browseVignettes()

Even people who work with R every day cannot remember every function. R therefore gives you a complete function reference in the Help tab. Some entries are hard going at first, but once you are used to them they are the most reliable source.








If you have a particular function in mind, the quickest way is through the console: a question mark in front of the function name is enough. For example, for the mean function from base R:

?mean

The help page opens in the Help tab at the bottom right. It shows a description of the function, its arguments and their default values, and it always ends with examples. You can copy the examples straight into your console.
The default values are listed under Usage: for mean(), the defaults are trim = 0 and na.rm = FALSE (Figure 1.5). The entry for an argument under Arguments explains what it does.





Figure 1.5: Structure of the help page for ?mean. The grey bars stand for text that is left out here.


To list all the functions in a package, open the Packages tab, find the package and click on it. This takes you to the package reference.
Many developers also maintain their own websites for their packages, and these are often the best place to start:


tidyverse.org/packages: an overview of all tidyverse packages with vignettes and function reference.

yannickdiehl.github.io/mariposa: function reference and vignettes on labels, weighting, descriptive statistics, correlation, regression, scale analysis and SPSS compatibility.

A vignette is a longer article on how to use a package, usually with a worked example, and it comes with the package. On the package websites you find the vignettes under Articles. In RStudio you open one with vignette("name"), or list all vignettes of a package with browseVignettes("packagename").
When you search the web for help, Stack Overflow is the main place to go. Add the keyword Stack Overflow to your search query: almost every typical R problem has been answered there before.

title: 1  RStudio
text:
First five steps after installation
If you started this chapter on a fresh computer, here is the checklist to work through before you move on to Chapter 2:

R installed (from cran.r-project.org) and RStudio installed (from posit.co). Order: R first, then RStudio.

Packages installed: install.packages("tidyverse"), install.packages("mariposa"), install.packages("patchwork").

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
text:
2.1 What this chapter is about
Research only counts as science if other people can follow it. If you publish an analysis, you should show every step from the data to the result, so that readers do not have to reconstruct intermediate steps or reformat tables from the output window.
Quarto is a tool that puts this into practice. It combines R code and the written report in a single document: you write your term paper, seminar presentation or bachelor’s thesis together with the code that produces the numbers. Quarto renders this into HTML, PDF or Word. If you change the data or a methodological decision, all the code in the document runs again the next time you render it, and the numbers, tables and graphics are up to date automatically.
This chapter takes you from your first .qmd document to a reproducible project that meets the standards of open science. The book you are reading was built with Quarto, so these pages are themselves an example of what this chapter explains.

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
text:
Note



Research journal: Where are you in your mini study? You set up the IDE in Chapter 1. Now you get to know the format in which you will publish your findings on Islamophobia at the end: a reproducible report that combines code, tables and graphics in one document. When you produce coefficient plots and regression tables from Chapter 9 onwards, you will want to bring them together in a Quarto document instead of copying them into Word.

text:

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
section: 2.2 Why Quarto? From script to report
text:
2.2 Why Quarto? From script to report
If you work in SPSS, you know the routine: you click through the menus, the output appears in a separate window, and you copy tables and graphics into Word, where you format them again. If you later notice that you recoded a variable incorrectly, the whole process starts again.
In Quarto, analysis and report are no longer separate. Both live in the same document:








SPSS workflow
Quarto workflow



Where are the calculations done?
SPSS output window
Code chunk in the .qmd



Where is the text written?
Word
Text in the .qmd



How do tables get into the report?
Word (copy, format by hand)
Quarto (automatically when rendering)


What happens when the data change?
Copy everything again
Render button, done


How does someone else reproduce it?
Hope that the order of clicks is documented

.qmd plus data → identical result



Quarto is the successor to R Markdown. R Markdown was centred on R; Quarto works with several languages (R, Python, Julia, Observable) and unifies the configuration. In this book you use Quarto with R. Everything you know from R Markdown tutorials works in Quarto almost unchanged.






NoteBackground: R Markdown, Quarto, knitr





Internally, Quarto still uses knitr, the R engine that runs code chunks and embeds their results in Markdown. What Quarto adds is the layer above it: a uniform YAML format, a consistent output architecture and support for books (like this one), websites, slides and dashboards. Most examples from R Markdown tutorials work the same way in Quarto.

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
text:
2.3 Markdown: the writing layer
Before you build your first .qmd, here is a short cheat sheet for Markdown, the markup language in which you write the text of a document (everything that is not R code). Markdown is deliberately simple: a few special characters are enough for most formatting.


Markdown
Result



# Heading 1
largest heading


## Heading 2
next smaller heading


**bold**
bold


*italic*
italic


`inline-code`

inline-code (monospace)


- first item
bullet point (with -)


1. first item
numbered list


[Text](https://…)
link


> Quote
indented quotation


blank line
new paragraph



That is all you need for 90% of term papers. Tables, footnotes and images have their own Markdown syntax; the Quarto Markdown reference is the cheat sheet for later.

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
text:
2.4 Your first .qmd

You already created a Quarto document in Section 1.5.2: File → New File → Quarto Document…. In the dialog, you enter a title and an author, choose HTML as the format and click Create. RStudio opens an example document, which you can turn into HTML straight away with the Render button (or cmd/ctrl + shift + K).
A minimal .qmd has exactly three parts:
---
title: "My first report"
author: "Anna Schmidt"
format: html
---

## Introduction

In this report I analyse the ALLBUS 2023.

```{r}
mean(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
```
In the example you can see:


YAML header between the --- lines: metadata and format configuration.
Markdown text: see the cheat sheet above.
Code chunks in triple backticks with {r}: they are run when you render, and their output goes straight into the report.

The rendered result shows your text, the line of code and its output (3), all in one finished HTML file. You can use this workflow for everything from a term paper to a PhD thesis.
Each layer ends up in its own place in the report (Figure 2.1): the YAML header becomes the title and author, the Markdown text becomes the heading and paragraph, and the chunk becomes the line of code with its output [1] 3.





Figure 2.1: The first .qmd from this section and the rendered report. The numbers show what each layer becomes.

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
section: 2.5 The YAML header: the control panel
text:
2.5 The YAML header: the control panel
The YAML header controls how your document behaves. Instead of seeing all the fields at once, you build it up in three stages, from “the minimum that renders” to “a complete term paper”.

2.5.1 Stage 1: Minimal
---
title: "My first report"
author: "Anna Schmidt"
format: html
---
With this, the document renders as HTML. That is all you need to begin with.

2.5.2 Stage 2: Term paper level
---
title: "Islamophobia in Germany 2023"
subtitle: "An analysis based on the ALLBUS"
author: "Anna Schmidt"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    number-sections: true
lang: en
---


toc: true turns on the table of contents, and toc-depth: 3 includes three levels of headings.

number-sections: true numbers the sections automatically (1, 1.1, 1.1.1).

lang: en gives you English labels (for example “Table of contents”; lang: de would give “Inhaltsverzeichnis”).

date: today sets the render date automatically.

2.5.3 Stage 3: Full research report
---
title: "Islamophobia in Germany 2023"
subtitle: "An analysis based on the ALLBUS"
author:
  - "Anna Schmidt"
  - "Boris Müller"
date: today
date-format: "D MMMM YYYY"

format:
  html:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
  pdf:
    documentclass: article
    geometry: margin=2.5cm
  docx: default

bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl

execute:
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false

lang: en
---
New in this stage:

Several author entries as a list (indented, with -).
Several output formats at once: Quarto renders all three in one run.

bibliography points to a BibTeX file (see Section 2.9).

csl selects the citation style (APA, Chicago, …).

execute sets default options for all code chunks: echo: true shows the code, and warning: false / message: false hide R’s warnings and messages.







Warning



Caution: YAML indentation. YAML is sensitive to spaces. Nested fields are indented by two spaces; tabs or inconsistent indentation lead to render errors. If a Quarto render stops with “yaml parsing error”, check the indentation first.

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
text:
2.6 Code chunks in detail
A code chunk has two parts: a header line with options and a code body.
```{r my-chunk, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=6}
mean(mtcars$mpg)
```
The most important options:






Option
Effect



echo
Show the code? (TRUE shows it, FALSE hides it)


eval
Run the code? (FALSE shows the code without running it)


include
Code and output in the document? (FALSE hides both but still runs the code)



warning, message

Show warnings/messages?


fig-cap
Figure caption



fig-width, fig-height

Size of the figure in inches


fig-align

"left", "center", "right"




Figure 2.2 shows the chunk with mean(mtcars$mpg) without an option and with three settings. With eval=FALSE the code appears in the report, but R does not run it; with include=FALSE R runs it, but none of it appears in the report.





Figure 2.2: The same chunk with mean(mtcars$mpg) under four settings: what appears in the report and whether R runs the code.


Which option you need depends on what should appear in the report:


Show code and output. → Default. No option needed.

Show only the output, hide the code. → echo: false (for example graphics in a report).

Show the code but do not run it. → eval: false (for example an illustration that would need someone else’s data).

Hide code and output but still run the code. → include: false (for example a setup chunk that loads packages).

Show code and output but suppress warnings. → warning: false, message: false.

Chunk labels (such as my-chunk above) must be unique within a document. They serve as cache keys and as anchors for cross-references to figures.
Since Quarto appeared, a second way of writing chunk options has become common: the #| style, inside the chunk instead of in the header:
```{r my-chunk}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6

mean(mtcars$mpg)
```
Both ways are allowed. This book uses the header notation ({r my-chunk, echo=TRUE}) because it is more compact. In recent Quarto examples on the web you will more often see the #| style, which is easier to read when there are many options.

2.6.1 Setup chunk
At the start of a document there is usually a setup chunk that loads packages and sets defaults. include=FALSE hides it from readers:
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(mariposa)
allbus <- read_spss("ALLBUS2023.sav") |>
  set_na(-56, -55, -54, -53, -51, -50, -42, -41,
         -33, -32, -15, -11, -10, -9, -8, -7, -6)
```
The call set_na() declares the negative codes of the English edition of the ALLBUS as missing values (see Chapter 4).
All later chunks inherit this state. This is why the chapters of this book do not load tidyverse and mariposa again in every chunk: the setup chunk at the top has already made everything available.
When you render, Quarto starts a new R session in which only base R is loaded. Anything you loaded or imported in the console beforehand does not exist there. The setup chunk is what puts tidyverse and mariposa on the workbench and allbus into the Environment (Figure 2.3).





Figure 2.3: The R session during rendering, before and after the setup chunk.


Stop and think. What happens when you render if the setup chunk has eval=FALSE instead of include=FALSE and a later chunk runs nrow(allbus)?






TipAnswer





```{r setup, eval=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(mariposa)
allbus <- read_spss("ALLBUS2023.sav") |>
  set_na(-56, -55, -54, -53, -51, -50, -42, -41,
         -33, -32, -15, -11, -10, -9, -8, -7, -6)
```

```{r}
nrow(allbus)
```
With eval=FALSE, R skips the setup chunk. The new session stays empty, so neither the packages nor allbus exist. Rendering therefore stops at the second chunk with the message object 'allbus' not found, and no report is produced.

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
section: 2.7 Inline R code: numbers in the text
text:
2.7 Inline R code: numbers in the text
Sometimes you only want to give one number in a sentence, such as the sample size, a mean or a p-value, instead of including a whole table. Quarto lets you do this with inline R code, written in backticks with an r at the start:
The sample contains `r nrow(mtcars)` cars.
Average fuel economy is `r round(mean(mtcars$mpg), 1)` mpg.
When you render, this becomes:

The sample contains 32 cars. Average fuel economy is 20.1 mpg.

Inline code is one of the most important tools for reproducible reports: instead of typing a number by hand, you let R calculate it from the data. If you later filter differently or add a new wave of data, all numbers in the report are updated automatically the next time you render, and none is accidentally left at an old value.
R returns numbers with full machine precision (23.847395). For the text, you therefore round with round() to as many decimal places as readability requires, usually one or two.

kable() is part of knitr and comes with every R Markdown or Quarto installation, so you do not need an additional package. For most term papers this is all you need. If you later need more elaborate tables (column groups, conditional colouring, multi-line headers), the packages gt or flextable are the next step. Neither is among the packages used in this book.

2.8.2 Graphics
Every ggplot2 object that a chunk returns appears as a figure in the report. You control the caption and size with chunk options:
```{r fig-mpg, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Fuel economy by number of cylinders"}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```
The fig.cap option (fig-cap in the #| style) appears as the caption; with number-sections: true the figure is numbered automatically, as “Figure 1.1” or similar. With a chunk label such as fig-mpg you can refer to it in the text with @fig-mpg.

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
text:
2.9 Citations with BibTeX and Zotero
Quarto places citations directly in the text. You need two things: a BibTeX file with your sources and a reference to it in the YAML header.
The BibTeX file references.bib is in the project folder:
@article{Goodman2016,
  author  = {Goodman, Steven N. and Fanelli, Daniele and Ioannidis, John P. A.},
  title   = {What does research reproducibility mean?},
  journal = {Science Translational Medicine},
  year    = {2016},
  volume  = {8},
  number  = {341},
  pages   = {341ps12}
}

@book{Wickham2023,
  author    = {Wickham, Hadley and Çetinkaya-Rundel, Mine and Grolemund, Garrett},
  title     = {R for Data Science},
  edition   = {2},
  year      = {2023},
  publisher = {O'Reilly}
}
The YAML header points to the file:
bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl     # optional: citation style
In the text, you cite with @key:
As @Goodman2016 show, reproducibility can be defined in different ways.
For a detailed discussion, see also [@Wickham2023].
Quarto formats the citations automatically and adds a list of references at the end. In HTML, the list appears in a separate appendix at the end of the page. If your document ends with a heading that has no text below it, such as ## References, this heading becomes the heading of the appendix. If you want the list somewhere else, put an empty block with the ID refs there:
::: {#refs}
:::
@Goodman2016 becomes a citation with the names in the sentence and the year in brackets; [@Wickham2023] becomes a citation entirely in brackets (Figure 2.4). Without a csl line, Quarto uses the Chicago author-date style; with lang: en, English words such as “and” and “2nd ed.” appear in the citations and the list.





Figure 2.4: The two citations from the example after rendering, in the default style and with lang: en.


Most students manage their sources in Zotero. With the plugin Better BibTeX for Zotero you export your library as a .bib file and keep it in sync automatically. In the Quarto visual editor in RStudio you can also look up Zotero sources directly via Insert → Citation.

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
section: 2.10 Open science: reproducibility as the standard
text:
2.10 Open science: reproducibility as the standard
Quarto is also the technical basis of a research practice that has become established since around 2015 under the name open science. There are three concepts you should know.

2.10.1 Reproducibility vs. replicability
Goodman, Fanelli and Ioannidis (2016) distinguish two terms that are often confused in everyday use:


Reproducible = same code + same data → same result. This is the minimum technical requirement. Quarto gives you this for free.

Replicable = same method + new data → similar result. This is the scientific question: can someone else confirm your finding with a new sample?

Reproducibility is a precondition for replicability, but not the other way round. A study can be perfectly reproducible and still remain a one-off result (often with p = .04).

2.10.2 FAIR principles
The FAIR principles describe what makes good research data and good research software:

Findable: can be found through persistent identifiers (for example a DOI).
Accessible: can be retrieved through open, documented protocols.
Interoperable: stored in standardised formats (.csv instead of tricks that only work in .xlsx).
Reusable: can be used again, with sufficient documentation and a clear licence.

For a term paper, one small step is enough: put your code and (if possible) your data on a platform such as OSF and give them an open licence.

2.10.3 Platforms and preregistration


OSF (Open Science Framework): a free platform for research projects. You store code, data and preregistrations there.

Zenodo: assigns persistent DOIs to code releases (often linked to GitHub).

Preregistration: the research question, hypotheses and analysis plan are set down in writing before the data are collected or analysed. This protects against p-hacking and HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known). It is useful for confirmatory studies; exploratory research is labelled as such.







NoteBackground: The replication crisis





The replication crisis in psychology and the empirical social sciences (from 2011, brought to a head by the Open Science Collaboration in 2015) showed that many published findings cannot be reproduced. In some cases the methods were poorly documented; in others, the incentives in research rewarded significant results more than careful methods. Open science, preregistration and reproducible reports (Quarto, R Markdown) are the structural response to this.

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
text:
2.11 Project structure and version control
A well-structured Quarto project typically looks like this:
my-project/
├── R/
│   ├── _common.R             # shared theme and helper functions
│   └── prep.R                # data preparation as a function
├── output/                   # generated tables and graphics
├── ALLBUS2023.sav            # raw data, never edit
├── README.md                 # description of the data source
├── references.bib
├── analysis.qmd              # the main document
└── my-project.Rproj
Three rules that have proved useful:

Treat raw data as read-only. You never write back to ALLBUS2023.sav. Processed data stay in memory (during the analysis) or are saved as a derived file in output/.
Keep code, data and document together. Never use absolute paths (/Users/anna/...): they break as soon as you share the project. In RStudio projects, paths are automatically relative to the project folder.
Shared code goes into R/. If three .qmd files prepare the same data, the code belongs in R/prep.R, and each document loads it with source("R/prep.R").


2.11.1 Version control with Git: where to start
Git is software that saves every state of your project and lets you go back to any of them at any time. For a single term paper you do not need Git. As soon as two people work on the same script, Git becomes indispensable. RStudio has Git built in (the Git tab at the top right).
This book does not cover Git in detail; it would fill a chapter of its own. If you want to get started, the best introductions are Jenny Bryan’s guide Happy Git with R and the GitHub Student Developer Pack (free private repositories).

title: 2  Quarto and reproducible research
text:
2.12 Publishing: HTML, PDF, Word
Which output format is right depends on who will read it:

HTML: for your own website, for GitHub Pages, for interactive reports with links. Renders fastest.
PDF: for coursework submissions and formal reports. Quarto uses LaTeX in the background; install it once:


install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()







Warning



Caution: The first PDF render can take a while. tinytex::install_tinytex() downloads a small LaTeX distribution (about 5–10 minutes, depending on your internet connection). LaTeX packages that are missing at the first PDF render are then installed automatically, which can add a few more minutes to the first run. If the render stops with a cryptic LaTeX error message, it is worth starting it a second time; often only one package was missing the first time.



Word: for co-authors who want to add comments with Word’s review function. You have less control over the layout, but working together is easier.

Several formats at once:
format:
  html: default
  pdf:
    documentclass: article
  docx: default
Quarto renders all three in the next run. With quarto publish you can publish HTML output directly to GitHub Pages, Quarto Pub or Netlify, without setting up a server.
