text:
5.2 Transforming data
A handful of functions from dplyr covers most data transformations:







Function
Effect




mutate()
Create or change variables (SPSS: COMPUTE)


case_when() / recode_values()
Vectorised conditional logic (SPSS: IF)


if_else()
Short form for conditions with two outcomes


summarise()
Summaries per group (SPSS: AGGREGATE)


group_by()
Grouping for the operations that follow


distinct()
Unique values of a variable


rename()
Rename variables




5.2.1 New variables with mutate() and across()
mutate() is the R counterpart of COMPUTE in SPSS. You pass mutate() one or more assignments of the form “new column name = expression”, and dplyr adds the new column(s) to the tibble. Note that mutate() returns the whole tibble, so you need to assign the result (allbus <- allbus |> mutate(...)) if the new column is to be kept. Without an assignment, the change is printed once and then disappears.

allbus |>
  select(age) |>
  mutate(birth_year = 2023 - age) |>
  head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  age       birth_year
  <dbl+lbl>      <dbl>
1 50              1973
2 51              1972
3 69              1954


mutate() computes the new column row by row: for the first respondent 2023 − 50 = 1973, for the second 2023 − 51 = 1972 (Figure 5.1). The new tower birth_year is a number without value labels (<dbl>).






Figure 5.1: mutate() computes the new tower birth_year from age, separately for each row. The first three rows are shown.



The chunk above has no allbus <-. R prints the result with birth_year, but allbus itself keeps its 579 columns (Figure 5.2). Only allbus <- allbus |> mutate(...) saves the new tower in allbus; the dataset then has 580 columns.






Figure 5.2: Without an assignment, R only shows the new tower (grey), and allbus stays at 579 columns. With allbus <-, the tower is saved in allbus.



Stop and think. You write allbus_new <- allbus |> mutate(birth_year = 2023 - age). How many columns do allbus and allbus_new have afterwards?






TipAnswer






allbus_new <- allbus |> mutate(birth_year = 2023 - age)
ncol(allbus)

[1] 579

ncol(allbus_new)

[1] 580


R saves the result under the name to the left of the arrow. allbus_new has the new tower and therefore 580 columns; allbus stays at 579. This way you keep an intermediate result without overwriting the original.



To apply the same transformation to several variables, use across():

allbus |>
  mutate(across(c(mm01, mm02, mm03), as.numeric))



5.2.2 Conditional logic with case_when(), if_else() and recode_values()
case_when() is the R equivalent of IF in SPSS. You list conditions in the form condition ~ value; the first one that applies wins.

allbus |>
  select(educ) |>
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      educ %in% 1:2 ~ "low",
      educ == 3 ~ "medium",
      educ %in% 4:5 ~ "high",
      .default = NA
    )
  ) |>
  count(education)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  education     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 high       2472
2 low         982
3 medium     1639
4 <NA>        153








Warning



Caution: Order matters. case_when() checks the conditions from top to bottom and takes the first one that applies; all later ones are ignored for that case. If you put a general condition before a specific one, the general one hides the specific one:

# WRONG: the first line catches everyone aged 18 and over, "senior" is never reached
case_when(
  age >= 18 ~ "adult",
  age >= 65 ~ "senior",
  .default = "under 18"
)

# RIGHT: more specific first
case_when(
  age >= 65 ~ "senior",
  age >= 18 ~ "adult",
  .default = "under 18"
)

When a recoding gives strange results, check the order of the conditions first.


Figure 5.3 runs through both orders from the box with the first five respondents. In the wrong order, all five stop at the first condition, age >= 18, including the respondents aged 69 and 72. In the right order, case_when() checks age >= 65 first; only those who do not stop there move on to the next line.






Figure 5.3: The first five values of age with both orders from the box. Each value stops at the first condition that applies to it.



For only two outcomes, if_else(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) is shorter:

allbus |>
  mutate(young = if_else(age < 30, "young", "30+")) |>
  count(young)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  young     n
  <chr> <int>
1 30+    4529
2 young   694
3 <NA>     23


If you only map individual values to new values (without comparison operators), recode_values() is shorter than case_when(), with the old value on the left and the new one on the right:

allbus |>
  select(eastwest) |>
  mutate(region = recode_values(eastwest, 1 ~ "West", 2 ~ "East")) |>
  count(region)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  region     n
  <chr>  <int>
1 East    1679
2 West    3567








NoteBackground: recode_values() instead of case_match()





In older tutorials you will find case_match() for the same task. Since dplyr 1.2 it is deprecated and gives a warning; recode_values() is its successor and is written the same way. For recoding whole scales, mariposa’s rec() (next section) remains the more convenient tool.





5.2.3 Aggregating with group_by(), summarise() and n()

allbus |>
  group_by(eastwest) |>
  summarise(
    n_cases         = n(),
    n_distinct_educ = n_distinct(educ),
    mean_age        = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  eastwest               n_cases n_distinct_educ mean_age
  <dbl+lbl>                <int>           <int>    <dbl>
1 1 [OLD FEDERAL STATES]    3567               8     51.7
2 2 [NEW FEDERAL STATES]    1679               8     54.3


n() counts all cases in the group, n_distinct() counts the unique values of a variable.
summarise() turns each group into one row (Figure 5.4): the 3567 respondents in the West become one row with a mean age of 51.7 years, the 1679 in the East one row with 54.3 years.






Figure 5.4: The two groups of eastwest, shown with the first three respondents from West and East. summarise() combines all rows of a group into one row with the mean.









NoteBackground: Grouping with .by





Since dplyr 1.1 you can also set the grouping directly in the call to summarise() or mutate(), without group_by() before it:

allbus |>
  summarise(
    mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = eastwest
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  eastwest               mean_age
  <dbl+lbl>                 <dbl>
1 1 [OLD FEDERAL STATES]     51.7
2 2 [NEW FEDERAL STATES]     54.3


This is shorter, and you cannot forget ungroup().





5.2.4 distinct() and rename()
distinct() shows you all unique values of a variable. It is the quickest answer to “which codes are there?”:

allbus |>
  distinct(eastwest)

# A tibble: 2 × 1
  eastwest              
  <dbl+lbl>             
1 1 [OLD FEDERAL STATES]
2 2 [NEW FEDERAL STATES]


rename() renames variables, with the new name on the left and the old name on the right:

allbus |>
  rename(gender = sex, age_years = age) |>
  select(gender, age_years) |>
  head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  gender     age_years
  <dbl+lbl>  <dbl+lbl>
1 1 [MALE]   50       
2 1 [MALE]   51       
3 2 [FEMALE] 69       


Both are small tools that you will use often, especially when you turn cryptic ALLBUS names into meaningful short names for your analysis dataset.
crumbs: 5  Transforming data and building scales

title: 5  Transforming data and building scales
text:
5.3 Recoding with rec()
Imagine you have the school education of 5246 people in the variable educ. The values 1 to 5 stand for school-leaving certificates, from “no certificate” through the lowest level, the intermediary level and the qualification for a university of applied sciences up to the qualification for university; in addition there are 6 (“other school certificate”) and 7 (“still at school”). For a regression, you want coarser categories than these seven: low / medium / high. You recode the variable.
This is the most common data operation in social research, and one of the most error-prone. If you swap one value or forget one category, your whole analysis runs on the wrong scale. SPSS has the RECODE command with its own small syntax for this. mariposa’s rec() function does the same but is built for tidyverse workflows: you use it inside mutate(), it keeps labels, and it understands a compact rule syntax in which you express a whole recoding in a single string.
The syntax:
data |>
  mutate(new = rec(old, rules = "1=1; 2:3=2; else=NA"))
rec() takes the old variable and the rule and returns the recoded values. mutate() stores them under the name to the left of the =.
The rule syntax at a glance:








Pattern
Effect
Example




old=new
Recode a single value
"1=10; 2=20"


lo:hi=new
Recode a range of values
"1:3=1"


a,b=new
Recode a list of values/ranges
"1,2=1; 3,4:5=2"


min:x=new, x:max=new
Dynamic limits
"min:5=1; 6:max=2"


[Label]
Assign an inline value label
"1:2=1 [low]; 3:5=2 [high]"


else=copy
Keep all values not mentioned unchanged
"1:3=1; else=copy"


else=NA
All values not mentioned become NA
"1=1; else=NA"


NA=new
Replace NA with a value
"NA=0; else=copy"


val=NA
Turn specific values into NA
"-9=NA; -8=NA; else=copy"


"rev"
Reverse a scale (hi + lo - x, limits from the value labels)
rules = "rev"


"rev(lo, hi)"
Reverse a scale with explicitly given limits
rules = "rev(1, 5)"


"dicho"
Dichotomise at the median (0/1)
rules = "dicho"


"dicho(x)"
Dichotomise at a fixed cut point (≤ x → 0, > x → 1)
rules = "dicho(3)"


"mean"
Dichotomise at the mean
rules = "mean"


"quart"
Split into four quartile groups
rules = "quart"



Rules are checked in order; the first matching rule wins. Valid values that no rule matches become NA; mariposa then warns you and names the values concerned. With else=copy you keep them; with else=NA you confirm explicitly that they are dropped. Missing values declared on import (the tagged NAs that set_na() created) keep their missing type when you recode, unless an NA= or else= rule covers them. else=NA therefore also turns NO ANSWER or CANNOT BE CODED into a plain NA, and the distinction between the missing types is gone. If you want to keep it, name the codes to drop explicitly (for example 6:7=NA) and leave out the else rule or write else=copy.

5.3.1 Example: categorising education

allbus |>
  mutate(
    educ = rec(educ, rules = "1:2=1 [low]; 3=2 [medium]; 4:5=3 [high]; else=NA",
               as_factor = TRUE)
  ) |>
  count(educ)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  educ       n
  <fct>  <int>
1 low      982
2 medium  1639
3 high    2472
4 <NA>     153


With as_factor = TRUE, the recoded variable becomes a factor straight away; the […] notation in the rules assigns the value labels in the same step. The 153 NA consist of the 44 respondents with code 6 or 7 and the 109 missing values declared on import (DATA ERROR, CANNOT BE CODED, NO ANSWER). In the result, all 153 are plain NA.
Figure 5.5 breaks the rule down into its parts. Each part takes the codes it names: 1:2=1 [low] combines 1 and 2 into the level low, and else=NA takes everything else, including the missing values declared on import.






Figure 5.5: The rule of rec() in its parts. Each part turns one or more codes of educ into a level of the new factor.





5.3.2 Special modes: dichotomising and quartiles
Instead of writing a chain of rules, you can split a variable at the median, at a fixed cut point, at the mean or into quartiles in a single call:

allbus |>
  mutate(age_d = rec(age, rules = "dicho(50)")) |>
  count(age_d)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  age_d                           n
  <dbl+lbl>                   <int>
1     0                        2281
2     1                        2942
3 NA(j) [CANNOT BE GENERATED]    23


Here age_d becomes 0 for everyone aged 50 or under and 1 for everyone over 50, so the cut point itself belongs to the lower group. The name age_d to the left of the = creates a new variable; the original age is kept.
In Figure 5.6 the cut lies between 51 and 50. The 23 respondents without a valid age (CANNOT BE GENERATED) also stay missing in age_d.






Figure 5.6: dicho(50) splits age into two groups. The first five values are shown, sorted by size; the 50 ends up in group 0.




allbus |>
  mutate(age_q = rec(age, rules = "quart")) |>
  count(age_q)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  age_q                           n
  <dbl+lbl>                   <int>
1     1                        1322
2     2                        1344
3     3                        1259
4     4                        1298
5 NA(j) [CANNOT BE GENERATED]    23


age_q is now a categorical variable with the values 1–4 for the age quartiles.


5.3.3 Worked example: reverse coding
What happens if you combine six items into a scale when four of them are worded in the same direction and two in the opposite direction? You get rubbish. The positively worded items pull the mean in one direction, the negative ones in the other, and in the end effects that should add up cancel each other out.
This is exactly the case with the Islamophobia scale of the mini study. The researchers deliberately worded the six items in mixed directions: four negatively (“restrict Islam”), two positively (“Islam fits into society”). It is a way of countering a classic survey bias called acquiescence: the tendency of some respondents to agree with statements across the board, whatever they are about. If all six items pointed in the same direction, this tendency would distort the result. Mixing the directions cancels it out.
For you, this means that before you combine the items into a scale, you need to reverse-code the two positively worded items, that is, recode them so that in the end all six point in the same direction.










Item
Wording
Direction




mm01
Restrict the practice of Islam in Germany
high = Islamophobic


mm02
Islam fits in with German society
high = TOLERANT, reverse-code


mm03
Presence of Muslims leads to conflicts
high = Islamophobic


mm04
State should monitor Muslim communities
high = Islamophobic


mm05
Would not object to a Muslim mayor
high = TOLERANT, reverse-code


mm06
Many religious fanatics among Muslims
high = Islamophobic





Before you form a mean from the six items, you must reverse-code mm02 and mm05; otherwise the effects cancel each other out. mariposa has the special mode "rev" for this:

allbus <- allbus |>
  mutate(
    mm02r = rec(mm02, rules = "rev"),
    mm05r = rec(mm05, rules = "rev")
  )







NoteBackground: What allbus <- allbus |> … overwrites





When you write allbus <-, you add the recoded columns to the tibble in memory. The original file ALLBUS2023.sav on your hard drive stays untouched, so you can restart the pipeline at any time. If you want to keep intermediate results alongside, assign to a new variable (allbus_mm <- allbus |> mutate(...)).



"rev" computes hi + lo - x internally. mariposa takes the scale limits lo and hi from the value labels of the valid codes; for the mm items, these are 1 (COMPLETELY DISAGREE) and 7 (COMPLETELY AGREE). This gives 8 - x, exactly the reversal you want. The value labels are mirrored as well: in mm02r, the 7 now carries the label COMPLETELY DISAGREE. Missing values (-9, -11, …) stay missing and keep their missing type.






Warning



Caution: Scale limits come from the labels. Because "rev" reads the limits from the value labels, it protects you from a subtle trap: if nobody had chosen the extreme value 7 for an item, reversing on the basis of the observed maximum (6) would shift the scale (7 - x instead of 8 - x). If a variable has no value labels (for example after an import from Excel), mariposa falls back on the observed minimum and maximum and tells you so in a message. In that case it is better to give the theoretical limits yourself: rules = "rev(1, 7)".


The mutate() has one line per item. The names mm02r and mm05r to the left of the = create two new variables; the originals mm02 and mm05 stay unchanged. This is the clean approach: you lose nothing and can trace the reversal at any time. If you write the same name on the left (mm02 = rec(mm02, rules = "rev")), you overwrite the original instead. To check the result, cross-tabulate the original and the reversed version. Every 1 must have become a 7, every 2 a 6, and so on:

allbus |> count(mm02, mm02r)

# A tibble: 8 × 3
  mm02                        mm02r                           n
  <dbl+lbl>                   <dbl+lbl>                   <int>
1     1 [COMPLETELY DISAGREE]     7 [COMPLETELY DISAGREE]   954
2     2 [..]                      6 [..]                    515
3     3 [..]                      5 [..]                    494
4     4 [..]                      4 [..]                    629
5     5 [..]                      3 [..]                    350
6     6 [..]                      2 [..]                    235
7     7 [COMPLETELY AGREE]        1 [COMPLETELY AGREE]      227
8 NA(l) [NAP: SPLIT]          NA(l) [NAP: SPLIT]           1842


In Figure 5.7, each row of the cross-tabulation is a pair of old and new value. The tower mm02r is mm02 turned upside down, and the stickers move with the values: COMPLETELY DISAGREE is now on the 7. The last row combines all 1842 missing values; they stay missing.






Figure 5.7: The cross-tabulation from count(mm02, mm02r) as bricks: 1 becomes 7, 2 becomes 6, 4 stays. The value labels move with the values.



Stop and think. The pa items, which you reverse-code in Section 5.7, have the values 1 to 5. What does rules = "rev" turn a 2 into there?






TipAnswer






allbus |>
  mutate(pa29r = rec(pa29, rules = "rev")) |>
  count(pa29, pa29r)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  pa29                        pa29r                           n
  <dbl+lbl>                   <dbl+lbl>                   <int>
1     1 [COMPLETELY AGREE]        5 [COMPLETELY AGREE]     1827
2     2 [TEND TO AGREE]           4 [TEND TO AGREE]        1013
3     3 [A BIT OF BOTH]           3 [A BIT OF BOTH]         608
4     4 [TEND TO DISAGREE]        2 [TEND TO DISAGREE]      115
5     5 [COMPLETELY DISAGREE]     1 [COMPLETELY DISAGREE]    28
6 NA(l) [NAP: SPLIT]          NA(l) [NAP: SPLIT]           1655


The 2 becomes a 4. "rev" computes hi + lo - x; with the limits 1 and 5 this is 6 - x, so 6 − 2 = 4. Here too the value labels move with the values: TEND TO AGREE is now on the 4.





5.3.4 Dummy variables with to_dummy()
For regressions you often need dummy variables: a categorical variable with k values is split into k-1 indicator columns (0/1 per value). mariposa’s to_dummy() does this in one call:

allbus |>
  to_dummy(eastwest, ref = 1)        # West (=1) as reference, dummy for East

The new columns are added automatically; with ref = you set which value is left out as the reference. You only need dummy variables in Chapter 9 for regression, and lm() and linear_regression() from mariposa also create them automatically in the background for factors (Figure 9.1).

title: 5  Transforming data and building scales
section: 5.4 Standardising and centring with std() and center()
text:
5.4 Standardising and centring with std() and center()
Before some analyses it makes sense to put a variable on a uniform scale. There are two related operations:

std() (standardisation) turns each variable into a z-standardised one (mean 0, SD 1). You need it when you want to make variables on different scales comparable, for example so that a standardised beta coefficient in a regression stays interpretable (Chapter 9).
center() (mean centring) only subtracts the mean, without dividing by the SD. The main use is before interaction terms in regressions, because centred variables reduce the multicollinearity between main effects and interactions.


allbus |>
  std(age, suffix = "_z") |>     # new variable age_z (mean 0, SD 1)
  select(age, age_z) |>
  head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  age         age_z
  <dbl+lbl>   <dbl>
1 50        -0.138 
2 51        -0.0828
3 69         0.903 


center() works the same way for mean-centred variables:

allbus |>
  center(age, suffix = "_c")     # new variable age_c (mean 0)

In ALLBUS, age has a mean of 52.51 years and a standard deviation of 18.25. center() subtracts the mean from each value: 50 becomes -2.51, 69 becomes 16.49. std() also divides the result by the standard deviation, so the 69 lies 0.903 standard deviations above the mean (Figure 5.8). The respondents keep their positions relative to each other; only the zero point and the unit of the scale change.






Figure 5.8: center() subtracts the mean of age, and std() also divides by the standard deviation. The first and the third person from the output of std() are shown.



Without the suffix argument, both functions overwrite the original variable, which is rarely what you want. Both also accept a weights = argument if you want a weighted standardisation.

title: 5  Transforming data and building scales
section: 5.5 Joining datasets with left_join(), inner_join() and full_join()
text:
5.5 Joining datasets with left_join(), inner_join() and full_join()
In research practice, your information rarely comes from one file. You have individual data (ALLBUS respondents), but you want to add context information: election results by federal state, economic data, regional migration shares. The two tables are linked through a key variable that occurs in both.
The tool for this is left_join() from dplyr. The name describes what it does: the left table is kept in full, and the right one is attached row by row where the key matches. Where there is no match, the new columns stay NA.
Question: You want to add context information to each ALLBUS respondent, for example an estimated share of the Muslim population and the GDP per capita, separately by region. First the small context table:

region_context <- tibble(
  eastwest       = c(1, 2),
  muslim_share   = c(7.2, 1.4),     # share in percent (synthetic)
  gdp_per_capita = c(45000, 32000)  # euros (synthetic, rounded)
)
region_context

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  eastwest muslim_share gdp_per_capita
     <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
1        1          7.2          45000
2        2          1.4          32000


This table has two rows. Now the join: on the left ALLBUS (5246 cases), on the right region_context (2 rows), key eastwest:

allbus_with_context <- allbus |>
  left_join(region_context, by = "eastwest")

allbus_with_context |>
  select(eastwest, age, muslim_share, gdp_per_capita) |>
  head(6)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  eastwest               age       muslim_share gdp_per_capita
  <dbl+lbl>              <dbl+lbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
1 1 [OLD FEDERAL STATES] 50                 7.2          45000
2 1 [OLD FEDERAL STATES] 51                 7.2          45000
3 1 [OLD FEDERAL STATES] 69                 7.2          45000
4 2 [NEW FEDERAL STATES] 72                 1.4          32000
5 1 [OLD FEDERAL STATES] 18                 7.2          45000
6 1 [OLD FEDERAL STATES] 45                 7.2          45000


Interpretation. Compare the table before and after the join. Before, the context table had only two rows; now the context values are attached to each case. Respondents in western Germany get muslim_share = 7.2 and gdp_per_capita = 45000, respondents in eastern Germany the corresponding other values. The original 5246 ALLBUS rows stay unchanged; only two new columns have been added.
For each row of allbus, left_join() looks for the row in region_context with the same value of eastwest and attaches its other columns (Figure 5.9). The fourth row belongs to the new federal states (eastwest 2) and therefore gets 1.4 and 32000.






Figure 5.9: left_join() attaches to each row of allbus the values from the row of region_context with the same key eastwest. All rows stay, and two towers are added; the first four rows are shown.









Tip



SPSS → R: Merging datasets. In SPSS this is MATCH FILES /TABLE = ... /BY = eastwest.. In R, the equivalent is left_join(). The concept and the arguments translate directly; only the syntax is more compact.


dplyr has four join verbs. They differ only in which rows remain at the end:








Function
Which rows remain?
When useful




left_join(x, y)
all rows from x, matching ones from y
Standard: context data for individual data


inner_join(x, y)
only rows that occur in both
Intersection: only cases with complete information


right_join(x, y)
all from y, matching ones from x
Rare; usually easier to read as left_join(y, x)


full_join(x, y)
all rows from both
Union: typical when consolidating data



For two small tables x (key id 1, 2, 3) and y (id 1, 2, 4), Figure 5.10 shows the results of left_join(), inner_join() and full_join(). If a key occurs in only one table, the columns of the other table stay empty (NA).






Figure 5.10: Three joins with the same tables x and y, linked by id. left_join() keeps all rows of x, inner_join() only the keys that occur in both tables, full_join() all keys.



In 90% of social research, left_join() is what you need: individual data on the left, context data on the right.






Warning



Caution: Keys must be unique in the right table. If the right table has several rows per key, every match is duplicated, and 5246 cases suddenly become 10000. Before every join, check region_context |> count(eastwest): each key value should occur only once.

title: 5  Transforming data and building scales
section: 5.6 Reshaping datasets: wide and long with pivot_*()
text:
5.6 Reshaping datasets: wide and long with pivot_*()
Data can come in two fundamentally different formats, and the choice matters: some operations only work in one format, some only in the other.

Wide format: one row per respondent, one column per variable. This is how ALLBUS comes by default: mm01 to mm06 are six columns side by side.
Long format: one row per observation, that is, per respondent × item. Instead of six columns there are two: one for “which item?” and one for “which value?”. 5246 rows with 6 item columns become 5246 × 6 = 31476 rows with 2 columns.

This matters because ggplot2 usually expects long format (one aesthetic = one column), while statistical functions often need wide format (one variable = one column). Two functions from tidyr do the reshaping:

5.6.1 pivot_longer(): wide → long
Question: You want to show all six mm items together in one ggplot2 plot, for example as a box plot per item. For this you need long format.
First a look at the wide format, the way ALLBUS comes by default, with one column per item and one row per person:

allbus |>
  select(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06) |>
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  mm01               mm02r       mm03        mm04        mm05r       mm06       
  <dbl+lbl>          <dbl+lbl>   <dbl+lbl>   <dbl+lbl>   <dbl+lbl>   <dbl+lbl>  
1     5 [..]             5 [..]      4 [..]      2 [..]      2 [..]      2 [..] 
2 NA(l) [NAP: SPLIT] NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP…
3 NA(l) [NAP: SPLIT] NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP…
4 NA(l) [NAP: SPLIT] NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP… NA(l) [NAP…


Now turn the same data into long format, with one row per person × item, so six rows per person instead of one:

allbus_long <- allbus |>
  select(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06) |>
  unlabel() |>                      # drop value labels (see the caution below)
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = everything(),       # which columns to reshape?
    names_to  = "item",             # new column for the old column names
    values_to = "response"          # new column for the values
  )

allbus_long |> head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  item  response
  <chr>    <dbl>
1 mm01         5
2 mm02r        5
3 mm03         4
4 mm04         2
5 mm05r        2
6 mm06         2
7 mm01        NA
8 mm02r       NA


Interpretation. Before: 6 columns × 5246 rows, a wide table. After: 2 columns × 31476 rows. The column names (mm01, mm02r, …) have moved into the new column item, the original values into the column response. The first six rows above belong to the first person, the next six to the second person.
The column names become values: the six name tags turn into bricks in the tower item, and each person gets six rows (Figure 5.11).






Figure 5.11: pivot_longer() turns the six column names into values in the tower item and the answers into the tower response. Afterwards the first person (orange) takes up six rows.









Warning



Caution: Stacking labelled columns. pivot_longer() writes all items into one column, response, and that column can carry only one set of value labels. The items, however, have different labels: in the reversed mm02r and mm05r, COMPLETELY DISAGREE is on the 7, in the others on the 1, and the labels of the missing values also differ from item to item. Without unlabel(), R therefore gives warnings such as “mm01 and mm02r have conflicting value labels” and silently uses the labels of the first item, which would be wrong for mm02r. With unlabel() (see Section 4.6) you stack the plain numbers; missing values stay NA.


This is exactly what you need to visualise all six items in one ggplot, with aes(x = item, y = response):

allbus_long |>
  filter(!is.na(response)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = item, y = response, fill = item)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Response (1–7)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")










5.6.2 pivot_wider(): long → wide
You need the reverse when aggregated data from a summarise() (which typically comes out in long format) should go into a report as a wide comparison table.
First the intermediate result in long format, the means per region × item:

means_long <- allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(eastwest)) |>
  select(eastwest, mm01, mm03, mm06) |>
  to_label(eastwest) |>                     # region with labels instead of 1/2
  unlabel(mm01, mm03, mm06) |>              # stack items as plain numbers
  pivot_longer(c(mm01, mm03, mm06),
               names_to = "item", values_to = "response") |>
  summarise(m = round(mean(response, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            .by = c(eastwest, item))

means_long

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  eastwest           item      m
  <fct>              <chr> <dbl>
1 OLD FEDERAL STATES mm01   3.19
2 OLD FEDERAL STATES mm03   3.97
3 OLD FEDERAL STATES mm06   4.14
4 NEW FEDERAL STATES mm01   4.01
5 NEW FEDERAL STATES mm03   4.63
6 NEW FEDERAL STATES mm06   4.58


Six rows: three items × two regions. This is readable, but impractical for a direct comparison of East and West. pivot_wider() turns it into a comparison table:

means_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = eastwest, values_from = m)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  item  `OLD FEDERAL STATES` `NEW FEDERAL STATES`
  <chr>                <dbl>                <dbl>
1 mm01                  3.19                 4.01
2 mm03                  3.97                 4.63
3 mm06                  4.14                 4.58


Now each item is in one row and the regions are in two columns, with East and West side by side. This is the format that looks good in an essay or a report.
names_from = eastwest sets where the new column names come from: the two levels of eastwest become name tags. values_from = m supplies the bricks below them (Figure 5.12).






Figure 5.12: pivot_wider() turns the values of eastwest into two column names and distributes the means from m among them.



Which format you need depends on the task:

Plotting? → usually long. ggplot2 maps aesthetics to columns, for example an item variable to the x-axis.
Computing statistics? → usually wide. pearson_cor(mm01, mm02) needs two columns.
A table for the report? → usually wide. It is easier for people to read.

If exactly one step in a pipeline needs the other format, you reshape with pivot_*() in between and, if necessary, back again afterwards. This is completely normal.

title: 5  Transforming data and building scales
section: 5.7 Building scales with row_means(), row_sums() and pick()
text:
5.7 Building scales with row_means(), row_sums() and pick()
Now comes the moment this chapter has been leading up to: six items, now all coded in the same direction, become one scale. Methodologically this is simple, and conceptually it is the most important step towards understanding what social research actually does.
The logic is as follows. If the six items all measure the same construct (which you check with factor analysis in Chapter 8), then the mean across the six items is a better estimate of the underlying attitude than any single item on its own. Individual items are noisy: every person understands a question slightly differently, has a bad day or reacts strongly to a particular word. Across six items the noise averages out, and what remains is the common signal, the underlying attitude.
In SPSS this would be a short COMPUTE statement. In R you use row_means() from mariposa, which is built for exactly this purpose. There are three related functions:







Function
What it does




row_means(data, ..., min_valid = N)
Mean per case across the given variables


row_sums(data, ..., min_valid = N)
Sum per case


row_count(data, ..., count = value)
How often a particular value occurs in the row



The argument min_valid sets how many valid answers there must be at least for the mean to be computed. Otherwise the scale score stays NA. As a rule of thumb, use at least 80% of the items: min_valid = 5 for 6 items, min_valid = 6 for 7 items.
Why this threshold? For someone who answered 3 of 6 items, the scale score would rest half on what they said and half on what is missing, and this shifts the mean systematically. With min_valid = 5 you only lose the cases with many missing answers and gain a more robust measure in return. The trade-off is always the same: too strict a min_valid leaves few cases, and too lenient a threshold gives unreliable values. 80% is the methodological consensus.
Note that row_means() (and its siblings) return a numeric vector, so they belong inside a mutate() call, with pick() to select the variables. This is idiomatic tidyverse code and makes it clear that a new column is created.

5.7.1 Islamophobia scale

allbus <- allbus |>
  mutate(
    islamophobia = row_means(pick(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06),
                             min_valid = 5)
  )

row_means() computes for each person the mean of the items they answered (Figure 5.13). With six valid answers this is all six, with five it is the five available. Anyone with only four valid answers gets no scale score with min_valid = 5.






Figure 5.13: Three respondents from ALLBUS: the first person with six, the first with five and the first with four valid answers. Empty bricks are missing answers.



Stop and think. Which scale score would the person with respid 120 from Figure 5.13 get if you set min_valid = 4?






TipAnswer






allbus |>
  mutate(scale_4 = row_means(pick(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06),
                             min_valid = 4)) |>
  filter(respid == 120) |>
  select(respid, islamophobia, scale_4)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  respid islamophobia scale_4
   <dbl>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1    120           NA       4


With min_valid = 4, their four valid answers are enough: (3 + 4 + 4 + 5) / 4 = 4. With min_valid = 5 the value stays missing. A lower threshold brings more respondents into the scale, but their scores rest on fewer items.



A quick check of whether the scale is plausible:

allbus |> describe(islamophobia)


Descriptive Statistics
----------------------

  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Variable       Mean  Median     SD  Range    IQR  Skewness     N  Missing
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  islamophobia  4.113   4.000  1.549  6.000  2.333     0.147  3345     1901
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------


Values close to 1 mean little agreement with Islamophobic statements, values close to 7 strong agreement. Because the positively worded items (mm02r, mm05r) are reverse-coded, a favourable attitude towards Muslims pulls the scale score down, as it should for a scale of Islamophobia.






NoteBackground: Who measured this?





The six mm items are established in German-language research on group-focused enmity (Decker & Brähler; Pickel and Pickel). They measure a coherent construct; you check this with factor analysis in Section 8.5 and with Cronbach’s α in Section 8.7. The mini study uses the scale under the name islamophobia (short and understood internationally). Its subject is hostility towards Islam and Muslims as a specific facet of group-focused enmity.





5.7.2 Checking response style with row_count()
Before you build the populism scale, here is a small data quality check: how often did someone choose the most extreme answer (7) on the mm items? A high value points to a response style: someone ticks COMPLETELY AGREE throughout, whatever the item.

allbus |>
  mutate(n_extreme = row_count(pick(mm01, mm02, mm03, mm04, mm05, mm06),
                               count = 7)) |>
  count(n_extreme)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  n_extreme     n
      <int> <int>
1         0  3399
2         1   958
3         2   407
4         3   214
5         4   233
6         5    30
7         6     5


row_count() counts in each row how many of the six answers are a 7 (Figure 5.14). The person with respid 95 chose 7 three times, the person with respid 1 not once. The person with respid 2 was not shown the items and also gets 0; row_means() would have given them a missing value.






Figure 5.14: row_count(count = 7) counts the sevens in each row (blue); the other values do not count (grey). A row without answers gives 0.



Most respondents show no such pattern; those who answer all six items with 7 are a small minority. Read the row 0 with care, though. It also contains the roughly 1650 respondents who were not shown the items because of the split design; missing values never count as hits. row_count() is generally useful for data quality checks: how many “don’t know” answers, how many extreme answers, how many answers in the middle? You can count several values at once with count = c(1, 7); both extremes then go into the sum.


5.7.3 Populism scale






NoteBackground: Measuring populism





The seven pa items are based on a scale by Schulz et al. (2017) and cover three classic dimensions of populism: anti-elitism, people-centrism and Manichaeism (the people versus a corrupt elite). High values indicate populist attitude patterns. Such an attitude can occur across the whole party spectrum and is not the same as a preference for populist parties.



Here a second trap with the coding direction is waiting, and it is the reason why you look at the codebook before building any scale. First look at the value labels of a pa item:

val_labels(allbus$pa29)

   COMPLETELY AGREE       TEND TO AGREE       A BIT OF BOTH    TEND TO DISAGREE 
                  1                   2                   3                   4 
COMPLETELY DISAGREE 
                  5 


The pa module uses a 5-point scale on which 1 = COMPLETELY AGREE and 5 = COMPLETELY DISAGREE. This is the reverse of the mm items, where 1 meant disagreement and 7 agreement. For pa29 (“MPs are bound only to the will of the people”), a low value therefore means populist.






Warning



Caution: Check the labels first, then build the scale. The items of an item battery are not always coded in the same direction, not even within the same wave of the same dataset. So before building any scale, look at the value labels (val_labels()) and the wording (var_label()) of the items, even for items you have seen a hundred times. A forgotten reversal shows up later when the item correlates negatively with the others and Cronbach’s α (Section 8.7) drops sharply.


So that populism works like islamophobia in the end (high = more of the measured attitude), you reverse-code all seven pa items. They are all coded in the same (inverse) direction, so the reversal is identical for all of them (6 - x; the limits 1 and 5 again come from the value labels):

allbus <- allbus |>
  mutate(
    pa29r = rec(pa29, rules = "rev"),
    pa30r = rec(pa30, rules = "rev"),
    pa31r = rec(pa31, rules = "rev"),
    pa32r = rec(pa32, rules = "rev"),
    pa33r = rec(pa33, rules = "rev"),
    pa34r = rec(pa34, rules = "rev"),
    pa35r = rec(pa35, rules = "rev")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    populism = row_means(pick(pa29r, pa30r, pa31r, pa32r, pa33r, pa34r, pa35r),
                         min_valid = 6)
  )

allbus |> describe(populism)


Descriptive Statistics
----------------------

  ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  Variable   Mean  Median     SD  Range    IQR  Skewness     N  Missing
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  populism  3.398   3.429  0.767  4.000  1.143     0.041  3563     1683
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------


Figure 5.15 shows the value labels side by side. For mm01, agreement is at the highest value; for pa29, it is at the lowest. After reverse coding, agreement is at the highest value for pa29r as well. Without this step, populism would measure the opposite: high values would stand for rejecting populist statements.






Figure 5.15: The value labels of mm01, pa29 and pa29r. For pa29, agreement is at the lowest value; rec() with "rev" turns the scale round.









Importantmariposa tip: Reverse-coding several variables with across()





The seven reversals are written out one below the other here on purpose, so that each step of the pipeline is visible. It is more compact with across(), which you met with mutate(). ~ rec(.x, rules = "rev") applies rec() to each variable from pa29 to pa35; .x stands for the variable in question. .names = "{.col}r" sets the new names: {.col} is the old name, followed by an r. This one line is equivalent to the seven rec() lines above and also creates pa29r to pa35r:

allbus |> mutate(across(pa29:pa35, ~ rec(.x, rules = "rev"), .names = "{.col}r"))

title: 5  Transforming data and building scales
text:
5.8 Making scales comparable with pomps()
Imagine you are asked to judge which attitude is more pronounced among the respondents: their Islamophobia or their populism. With the original scale scores, this is a trap. Islamophobia runs from 1 to 7, populism from 1 to 5. A mean of 4 means “around the middle” on the first scale and “upper half” on the second. A direct comparison of the means is therefore misleading; you would be comparing apples with oranges.
The solution is a methodological classic: both scales are converted to a common range, typically 0 to 100. A person with the minimum value of their original scale ends up at 0, one with the maximum value at 100, and everything in between is converted linearly. This makes the values directly comparable, much like converting school marks from two different grading systems to the same percentage scale.
The method is called POMPS (percent of maximum possible scores). It has been established in the methods literature since Cohen et al. (1999) and is a standard tool for comparing scales.
The formula itself is simple. All values are converted into a proportion of the theoretical range:
\[
\text{POMPS} = \frac{x - \text{min}}{\text{max} - \text{min}} \times 100
\]
mariposa has this built in as pomps():

allbus <- allbus |>
  mutate(
    islamophobia_p = pomps(islamophobia, scale_min = 1, scale_max = 7),
    populism_p     = pomps(populism,     scale_min = 1, scale_max = 5)
  )

allbus |>
  summarise(
    islam_orig = round(mean(islamophobia,   na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    islam_p    = round(mean(islamophobia_p, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    pop_orig   = round(mean(populism,       na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    pop_p      = round(mean(populism_p,     na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  islam_orig islam_p pop_orig pop_p
       <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1       4.11    51.9      3.4  60.0


Now you can read the comparison directly: if the POMPS mean for Islamophobia is higher than the one for populism, the average respondent is more Islamophobic than populist in relative intensity, and vice versa.
On their own scales, the means are 4.11 out of 7 and 3.4 out of 5; on the common scale from 0 to 100 they are 51.9 and 60.0 (Figure 5.16).






Figure 5.16: The means of both scales on their own rulers and, after pomps(), on a common ruler from 0 to 100.



POMPS is a linear transformation: the distribution of the values does not change, only the scale. Correlations, effect sizes and all linear models give exactly the same results on the POMPS variables as on the originals. You lose nothing, and scales with different ranges become comparable.






Warning



Caution: Always give scale_min and scale_max. Without these arguments, pomps() uses the observed range (min(x), max(x)). On a 1–7 scale on which nobody ticked the value 1, the value 2 would become the “new zero”, which distorts the scale and makes results incomparable across samples. For Likert items, always give the theoretical range.

title: 5  Transforming data and building scales
text:
5.9 The complete data preparation pipeline
Everything you have built step by step in this chapter can be combined into a single clean pipeline. This pipeline is the anchor for Chapters 6–9: you will find it as a setup block at the start of each of the following chapters, read in with source().
In your own project, save the pipeline below as R/prep.R and read it in with source("R/prep.R"). In this book’s repository, the English version is R/prep_en.R.

1allbus <- read_spss("ALLBUS2023.sav") |>
  set_na(-56, -55, -54, -53, -51, -50, -42, -41,
         -33, -32, -15, -11, -10, -9, -8, -7, -6) |>
  mutate(
2    mm02r = rec(mm02, rules = "rev"),
    mm05r = rec(mm05, rules = "rev"),
3    pa29r = rec(pa29, rules = "rev"),
    pa30r = rec(pa30, rules = "rev"),
    pa31r = rec(pa31, rules = "rev"),
    pa32r = rec(pa32, rules = "rev"),
    pa33r = rec(pa33, rules = "rev"),
    pa34r = rec(pa34, rules = "rev"),
    pa35r = rec(pa35, rules = "rev")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    islamophobia   = row_means(pick(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06),
4                               min_valid = 5),
    populism       = row_means(pick(pa29r, pa30r, pa31r, pa32r, pa33r, pa34r, pa35r),
5                               min_valid = 6),
6    islamophobia_p = pomps(islamophobia, scale_min = 1, scale_max = 7),
    populism_p     = pomps(populism,     scale_min = 1, scale_max = 5)
  )


1

Read ALLBUS 2023. set_na() turns the negative missing-value codes into missing values (tagged NAs).

2

Reverse-code the inverse mm items (mm02, mm05) into mm02r/mm05r; 7-point scale.

3

Reverse-code all pa items, because they are coded in the inverse direction on a 5-point scale (1 = agree, 5 = disagree). After reverse coding, high = populist.

4

Islamophobia scale as the mean of the six items (now all in the same direction); at least 5 of 6 must be valid.

5

Populism scale as the mean of the seven reverse-coded pa items; at least 6 of 7 must be valid.

6

POMPS versions of both scales on 0–100 for direct comparison (optional; the original scales are kept).




With this pipeline, the dataset is ready for analysis. Figure 5.17 assigns the six steps to the sections in which you learned them. Saved together as R/prep.R, they form the script that the setup chunks of the following chapters read with source().






Figure 5.17: The six steps of the pipeline with the sections in which they are introduced. Saved as R/prep.R, they form the script that the setup chunks of Chapters 6 to 9 read.









NoteBackground: What belongs in the methods report?





In a methods report you would document exactly these steps: Which items? Which were reverse-coded, and why? What minimum number of valid answers? Which direction does the scale run in? If you make this transparent, you give reviewers the means to assess the operationalisation. Reporting only Cronbach's α = 0.87 is not enough.

title: 5  Transforming data and building scales
text:
Exercises






NoteExercise 1 · Political efficacy scale · Reproduction



The pe items (pe01, pe04, pe05, pe06, pe07, pe08) measure political efficacy (cognitive component). First check the variable labels with var_label(), identify whether any items need to be reverse-coded, and build a scale pol_efficacy in the same way, with min_valid = 5. Tip: look closely at the wording.








TipSolution






allbus |>
  select(pe01, pe04, pe05, pe06, pe07, pe08) |>
  var_label()
# Items pe05 and pe07 point in the positive direction and need to be reverse-coded.
allbus <- allbus |>
  mutate(
    pe05r = rec(pe05, rules = "rev"),
    pe07r = rec(pe07, rules = "rev")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    pol_efficacy = row_means(pick(pe01, pe04, pe05r, pe06, pe07r, pe08),
                             min_valid = 5)
  )










NoteExercise 2 · Categorising ISCED education · Reproduction



Instead of educ, you can also use the internationally comparable ISCED variable isced97 (1–6) as a measure of education. Create three categories from it: ISCED 1–2 = “low”, 3–4 = “medium”, 5–6 = “high”.








TipSolution






allbus |>
  mutate(
    isced97 = rec(isced97, rules = "1:2=1 [low]; 3:4=2 [medium]; 5:6=3 [high]",
                  as_factor = TRUE)
  ) |>
  count(isced97)










NoteExercise 3 · Making scales comparable · Transfer



In the mini study, do respondents in Germany in 2023 score higher on the populism scale or on the Islamophobia scale? Convert both scales to POMPS and compare the weighted means (hint: w_mean() from mariposa for weighted means, argument weights = wghtpew).








TipSolution






allbus |>
  summarise(
    islam = w_mean(islamophobia_p, weights = wghtpew),
    pop   = w_mean(populism_p,     weights = wghtpew)
  )










NoteExercise 4 · Building your own scale · Mini research question



Choose a political science or sociological construct that interests you (satisfaction with democracy, trust in institutions, attitudes to gender roles, …). Use find_var() to find at least three suitable items in ALLBUS 2023, check their direction, build a scale with row_means(min_valid = ...) and describe in 3–4 sentences how you operationalised the construct and which items you included or excluded, and why.
There is no model solution here. The exercise trains operationalisation, the core skill of empirical social research.








Note



Research journal: Where your mini study stands. You have two scales that you built yourself: islamophobia (1–7) and populism (1–5), both with a controlled minimum number of valid answers and with POMPS versions for direct comparison. Building the scales is your methodological step; everything from Chapter 7 onwards builds on it. What comes next: before you test the scales statistically, you learn the grammar of ggplot2 in Chapter 6, the tools you use to make distributions and relationships visible.

title: 5  Transforming data and building scales
text:
What you know now

You transform variables with mutate(), case_when(), recode_values() and if_else().
You aggregate subgroups with summarise(.by = ...) and use n()/n_distinct().
You recode variables with rec() inside mutate(), from simple recoding through "dicho"/"quart" to clean reverse coding.
You create dummy variables with to_dummy().
You standardise and centre variables with std() and center().
You join datasets by a key with left_join() (and know the family of joins).
You reshape data between wide and long format with pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().
You build mean scales with row_means() and a controlled min_valid.
You check response styles and data quality with row_count().
You make scales with different ranges directly comparable with pomps().
You know the complete data preparation pipeline for the mini study; you can save it as R/prep.R and read it in with source(), as the following chapters do.

In the next chapter (Chapter 6) you get to know the ggplot2 graphics system. You need it from the chapter after that onwards to visualise distributions, group comparisons and relationships.

Schulz, A., Müller, P., Schemer, C., Wirz, D. S., Wettstein, M., & Wirth, W. (2017). Measuring populist attitudes on three dimensions. International Journal of Public Opinion Research, 30(2), 316–326. The source of the populism scale.
Decker, O., & Brähler, E. (Eds.) (2020). Autoritäre Dynamiken. Neue Radikalität – alte Ressentiments. Leipziger Autoritarismus-Studie [Authoritarian dynamics: New radicalism, old resentments. Leipzig Authoritarianism Study]. In German. Research background on group-focused enmity.

title: 6  Visualisation basics
text:
6.1 What this chapter is about
In this chapter you learn to make your findings visible. The methods chapters that follow (univariate and bivariate analysis, latent structures, explanatory models) make extensive use of what you learn here. You lay the foundation for visualising distributions, group comparisons and relationships.
A good plot answers a research question in two seconds. A good paragraph of text needs two minutes. And a table? Nobody reads it unless they have to. When your analysis is finished, only half of your work is done. The other half is communicating it so that readers understand what you have found.
In SPSS you build what you need by clicking through the Graphs menu: bars, lines, points. Each chart type has its own sequence of clicks. If you want something more complex, such as a box plot with facets by education, it quickly becomes tedious. And the result looks as if it had been designed in 1998.
ggplot2 works differently. Imagine you are describing over the phone a graphic that a designer will make for you. You would have to tell them exactly three things:
That is all you need. From these three pieces of information, ggplot2 builds the plot automatically. The official names of the three components are data, aesthetic mapping and layer (geom). Hadley Wickham derived the system from a 2005 book in which Leland Wilkinson described statistical graphics systematically as a “grammar”, hence the name grammar of graphics. Just as you can build any sentence from nouns, verbs and adjectives, you can build any graphic from these three components.
This has a big practical advantage: once you have understood how one chart is built, you understand all of them. If you can make a box plot, the step to a histogram or a scatter plot is just a different geom_*(); the basic structure stays the same.
This chapter takes you through these three steps and the most important geom variants. You learn which plot suits which data type, how to split the data into subgroups with facets, and how to adjust colours, themes and labels. The more advanced visualisation topics (coefficient plots, combining several plots, saving in publication quality) follow in Chapter 9 at the end of the methods chapters, where you present concrete model results.

title: 6  Visualisation basics
text:
Which data do you want to show? Which dataset?
What goes where? Which variable goes on the x-axis, which on the y-axis, which determines the colour, which the grouping?
What should the data points look like? Bars? Points? A line? A box plot?









NoteBackground: Who invented the grammar?





In The Grammar of Graphics (2005), Leland Wilkinson proposed building every statistical graphic from a small number of orthogonal components. Hadley Wickham implemented this in R in 2007 as ggplot (later ggplot2). Today the grammar is also standard in Python (plotnine), JavaScript (Observable Plot) and many commercial tools. Once you have learned in one system which layers a graphic is made of, you can read graphics in all of them.

title: 6  Visualisation basics
section: What you will be able to do after this chapter
text:
What you will be able to do after this chapter

Explain the grammar of graphics approach of ggplot2.
Visualise frequencies, distributions and relationships with the appropriate geom_*() layers.
Split the data into subgroups with facet_wrap() and facet_grid().
Adjust colours, themes and labels, including readable axis labels with to_label().
Explain the role of the book-wide theme theme_rworkshop().

title: 6  Visualisation basics
text:
6.2 The grammar of graphics
As explained in the introduction, every ggplot2 plot consists of exactly three components: data, aesthetic mapping and layers. In code it looks like this:
allbus |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ..., y = ...)) +    # data + aesthetic mapping
  geom_...(...)                      # layer
The function aes() (short for aesthetics) does the translation: “take this column and map it to this visual property”, for example education variable → x-axis, scale score → y-axis, sex → colour. Then the geom_*() functions add a visible layer on top: bars, points, boxes, whatever you need.
Here is what this looks like for four respondents. The chunk takes the first four rows in which educ_cat, islamophobia and sex have a value and draws them as points:

four <- allbus |>
  select(respid, educ_cat, islamophobia, sex) |>
  drop_na() |>
  head(4)
four

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  respid educ_cat islamophobia sex   
   <dbl> <fct>           <dbl> <fct> 
1      1 medium           3.33 MALE  
2      5 high             4    FEMALE
3      6 high             3.83 FEMALE
4      9 high             1.5  MALE  

four |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ_cat, y = islamophobia, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)







aes() sets which tower determines which property of the plot, and geom_point() draws each row as a point (Figure 6.1). The x-axis shows only medium and high, because none of the four rows has low education.





Figure 6.1: aes() assigns the towers of four to the x-axis, the y-axis and the colour. geom_point() turns each row into a point; the numbers next to the points are the respid values.


Notice that the layers are joined with + instead of the pipe |>. The reason is historical: ggplot2 is older than the native pipe and has kept its own operator. You can remember it like this: everything before ggplot(...) is joined with |>, everything after ggplot(...) with +.






Warning



Caution: + vs. |>. If you accidentally put |> between ggplot(...) and a geom_*() layer, you get a cryptic error message such as:
Error in geom_bar(): could not find function "geom_bar"
or
Error: `mapping` must be created by `aes()`
The fix is a + instead of |> between the ggplot2 layers; nothing else changes.



6.2.1 First plot: frequency distribution of an item
Question: How are the answers to the item mm03 (“Presence of Muslims leads to conflicts”) distributed?

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(mm03)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mm03, weight = wghtpew)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2563eb") +
  labs(x = "mm03: Presence of Muslims leads to conflicts",
       y = "Count (weighted)",
       caption = "ALLBUS 2023, weighted with wghtpew") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7)







Interpretation. The scale runs from 1 (COMPLETELY DISAGREE) to 7 (COMPLETELY AGREE). The distribution shows in which direction the respondents lean.






Warning



Caution: weight = (ggplot2) vs. weights = (mariposa). Both apply weights, but they are spelled differently. ggplot2 uses weight (singular, without s) as an aesthetic inside aes(); mariposa functions such as frequency() or t_test() use weights (plural, with s) as a function argument. If you write both in the same script, you will occasionally mistype one. An unweighted result produces no error message, so the mistake easily goes unnoticed.



6.2.2 Second plot: comparing subgroups
Question: How does Islamophobia differ by level of education?

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(educ_cat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ_cat, y = islamophobia, fill = educ_cat)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Education group", y = "Islamophobia (1–7)",
       caption = "ALLBUS 2023") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Both plots follow the same three-step structure. The next section goes through it in detail.

title: 6  Visualisation basics
text:
6.3 How a plot is built

6.3.1 Creating the plot object with ggplot()

You create the plot object with ggplot(). The first argument is the dataset:

g <- allbus |> ggplot()

On its own, g is an “empty” plot object: it knows nothing yet about axes or content.

6.3.2 Aesthetic mapping with aes()

With aes() you map columns of the dataset to visual properties of the plot. The most important properties are:


Argument
Purpose




x =, y =

axes


weight =
survey weighting


fill =
fill colour (areas: bars, boxes)


colour =
line or point colour


shape =
point shape


linetype =
line style



size =, alpha =

size / transparency


group =
invisible grouping



If aes() is inside ggplot(), the mapping applies to all layers of the plot. You can also set mappings for a single layer; then they apply only there.
Whether a setting is inside or outside aes() makes a big difference. This is the beginner’s trap in ggplot2. The rule is simple, but the two cases have opposite consequences:

Inside aes(): a data column is mapped to a visual property. The colour then varies with the values of the variable, and ggplot2 adds a legend automatically.
Outside aes(): a constant property for all points or bars. No legend, everything in the same colour.


ggplot(allbus, aes(x = age, fill = sex)) + geom_bar()         # one bar per age, stacked by sex
ggplot(allbus, aes(x = age)) + geom_bar(fill = "steelblue")   # all bars the same blue

In the first call, the tower sex determines the colour of each segment of a bar; in the second, the single value "steelblue" applies to all bars (Figure 6.2).





Figure 6.2: At the top, the tower sex determines the fill colour: each bar is stacked by sex, and the legend shows the colours. At the bottom, the single value "steelblue" applies to all bars, and there is no legend. The bars for ages 18 to 24 are shown.


Stop and think. What does R draw if the constant is inside aes(): ggplot(allbus, aes(x = age, fill = "steelblue")) + geom_bar()? What colour are the bars, and is there a legend?






TipAnswer






ggplot(allbus, aes(x = age, fill = "steelblue")) + geom_bar()







Inside aes(), ggplot2 treats "steelblue" like a tower that holds the same value in every row. That is a single level, and it gets the first colour of the default palette, a salmon red (#F8766D). The legend has exactly one entry, “steelblue”. A legend like this is a clear sign that a constant is inside aes().



For colours, ggplot2 distinguishes two aesthetics, fill and color:


fill is the fill colour, for areas: bars, boxes, polygons, densities.

color is the stroke colour, for lines, points and outlines.

If you want to colour a bar and write color = sex, you see only thin outlines around an otherwise empty area. For points and lines color is right, for bars fill. Some geoms (e.g. geom_boxplot()) need both: fill for the box, color for the outline.

g <- allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(eastwest)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = eastwest, y = islamophobia, weight = wghtpew, fill = eastwest))

g is now a plot object with axis mappings, but you do not see anything yet because there is no layer.

6.3.3 Adding layers with geom_jitter(), geom_boxplot() and geom_violin()

You add layers with +. The layer functions all start with the prefix geom_.
A point plot with geom_jitter():

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(populism)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = populism, y = islamophobia)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0.08, alpha = 0.2, color = "#1f77b4") +
  labs(x = "Populism (1–5, reverse-coded)",
       y = "Islamophobia (1–7)",
       caption = "ALLBUS 2023")







geom_jitter() moves overlapping points apart slightly. With two discrete axes (scales with few values) this is essential; otherwise all respondents with the same values look like one point.
The box plot and the violin plot build on the same base, g_base:

g_base <- allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(educ_cat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ_cat, y = islamophobia, fill = educ_cat))

g_base + geom_boxplot()







Box plots show the median (line in the box), the middle 50% (box) and the whiskers (1.5 × IQR). Violin plots show the density instead:

g_base + geom_violin()







A common trick is to combine both layers, with the violin as the background and a thin box plot on top:

g_base +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







g_base contains the data and the mapping, but no layer yet. Up to ggplot(), the baseplate passes through |>; after that, each + adds a layer, and whatever comes later lies on top (Figure 6.3). theme() is also added with +, but it does not create a layer: it changes the appearance and here hides the legend.





Figure 6.3: Up to ggplot(), the baseplate passes through |>; the result g_base has axes but no layer. With +, violins and boxes are added as separate layers, and the boxes lie on top.

title: 6  Visualisation basics
text:
6.4 Geoms for different data types
Which geom_* makes sense depends on the data type of the variables. A quick overview:






Data type
Recommended geoms



One categorical variable
geom_bar()


One continuous variable

geom_histogram(), geom_density()



Two categorical variables

geom_bar(position = "dodge") or position = "fill"



One categorical + one continuous

geom_boxplot(), geom_violin()



Two continuous variables

geom_point(), geom_jitter(), geom_smooth()



Time series
geom_line()




6.4.1 One categorical variable with geom_bar() and after_stat()

A classic bar chart with geom_bar():

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(educ_cat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ_cat, weight = wghtpew)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Education group", y = "Count (weighted)")







For relative frequencies, modern ggplot2 (version 3.4 and later) uses after_stat() instead of the old ..count../..prop.. syntax:

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(educ_cat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ_cat, weight = wghtpew)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = after_stat(prop), group = 1), fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Education group", y = "Share")







Before geom_bar() draws anything, it counts: for each level of educ_cat it sums the weights from wghtpew into count (1049.6, 1524.7 and 2510.5) and calculates the share prop from these (0.206, 0.300 and 0.494). Without further instructions, count goes on the y-axis, as in the previous chunk; after_stat(prop) takes the shares instead (Figure 6.4). group = 1 puts all levels into one group; without it, ggplot2 calculates the share of each level relative to itself, and every bar would be 100% high.





Figure 6.4: geom_bar() sums the weights for each level of educ_cat into count and calculates the share prop from these; after_stat(prop) puts the shares on the y-axis. On the left are the first two respondents of each level.


With fill = as a second grouping variable you get stacked bars, and with position = "dodge" bars side by side:

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(educ_cat), !is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ_cat, weight = wghtpew, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Education group", y = "Count (weighted)", fill = "Sex")








6.4.2 One continuous variable with geom_histogram() and geom_density()

A histogram with geom_histogram(). The most important setting is binwidth:

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = islamophobia, weight = wghtpew)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Islamophobia (1–7)", y = "Count (weighted)")







With geom_density() you get a smoothed density estimate instead:

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = islamophobia, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Islamophobia (1–7)", y = "Density", fill = "Sex")








6.4.3 Two continuous variables with geom_smooth()

The classic is a scatter plot with a regression line:

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(populism), !is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = populism, y = islamophobia, color = sex)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, width = 0.05, height = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Populism", y = "Islamophobia",
       color = "Sex", caption = "ALLBUS 2023")







geom_smooth(method = "lm") draws a linear regression line for each group. For non-linear trends you use method = "loess". You learn what a regression line is mathematically in Section 9.4; here it only serves as a visual aid for the trend.

title: 6  Visualisation basics
section: 6.5 Splitting data into subgroups with facets: facet_wrap() and facet_grid()
text:
6.5 Splitting data into subgroups with facets: facet_wrap() and facet_grid()

Imagine you want to show the relationship between populism and Islamophobia, but separately for each education group. You could overlay the three groups in a single plot in three different colours. With two groups this still works; with three or more it becomes chaotic: points overlap, trend lines cross, and the plot becomes hard to read.
The solution is facets: ggplot2 turns one plot into several, one per subgroup, arranged side by side with identical axes. This lets you compare the subgroups directly without them overlapping. It is one of the most powerful features of ggplot2, and it is extremely useful in social research, because almost every question there is worth looking at group by group.
There are two variants: facet_wrap() for one grouping variable, facet_grid() for two. Both are built the same way: you give the grouping variable as a formula with ~.

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(populism), !is.na(educ_cat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = populism, y = islamophobia)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, color = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ educ_cat) +
  labs(x = "Populism", y = "Islamophobia")







With two grouping variables, use facet_grid(), which arranges the panels in rows and columns:

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(populism),
         !is.na(educ_cat), !is.na(eastwest)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = populism, y = islamophobia)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, color = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black") +
  facet_grid(eastwest ~ educ_cat) +
  labs(x = "Populism", y = "Islamophobia")







In publications, facets say more than tables of subgroup statistics. If you want to show in the discussion that a relationship is stronger in one subgroup than in another, facet_wrap() or facet_grid() makes this visible at a glance.

title: 6  Visualisation basics
text:
6.6 Colours and themes

6.6.1 Colour palettes with scale_color_*() and scale_fill_*()

The default colours of ggplot2 are not accessible. A small collection of standard solutions:

# Discrete categorical variables: Brewer palettes
scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")     # for lines/points
scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues")     # for areas

# Continuous: viridis (accessible)
scale_color_viridis_c()
scale_fill_viridis_c()

# Your own palette
color_values <- c("#2563eb", "#16a34a", "#dc2626")
scale_color_manual(values = color_values)

About 8% of men (and 0.5% of women) have some form of red-green colour vision deficiency. Default colour palettes often use red and green as the main contrast, so for readers with this deficiency the information disappears. Viridis (the default palette in matplotlib, now also in ggplot2) stays distinguishable for all forms of colour vision deficiency and is also readable when printed in black and white. As a rule of thumb, use viridis for continuous scales and a ColorBrewer palette for categorical variables (Set1, Set2, Blues, RdYlBu).

6.6.2 Themes with theme_*() and theme()

Complete themes replace the default appearance with a single line:

p <- allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(educ_cat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ_cat, y = islamophobia, fill = educ_cat)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Education", y = "Islamophobia") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p + theme_minimal()







theme_bw(), theme_classic(), theme_dark() and theme_void() are further options.
The two function families theme_*() and theme() sound alike but do different things:


theme_minimal(), theme_bw(), theme_classic() …: complete themes. They set the overall style (background, grid, font sizes).

theme(legend.position = "none", …): adjusts individual elements. This function accepts dozens of elements (axis.text, plot.title, panel.grid …).

In practice you combine both: first a complete theme as the base, then individual adjustments with theme().
All plots in this book automatically use the theme theme_rworkshop(), which is defined in R/_common.R and set globally with theme_set(). This gives all plots in the Quarto project the same look without you having to specify the theme in every chunk. For your own project, you define a suitable theme once and load it with source("R/_common.R") in the setup chunk of each chapter.






Tip



SPSS → R: Clicking vs. code. In SPSS you click colours in a dialog box, and the next chart starts from scratch again. In ggplot2 you store the theme and the colour palette as code and can apply them to every new plot without repeating yourself.

title: 6  Visualisation basics
text:
6.7 Labels with labs() and to_label()

labs() sets all titles and labels of a plot in one function call:

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(populism)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = populism, y = islamophobia)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, color = "#1f77b4", width = 0.05, height = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title    = "Islamophobia and populism in Germany, 2023",
    subtitle = "Bivariate relationship, unweighted",
    x        = "Populism (1–5, reverse-coded)",
    y        = "Islamophobia (1–7)",
    caption  = "Source: ALLBUS 2023, GESIS Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences"
  )







to_label() makes axes readable. For <haven_labelled> variables from SPSS, you usually want to see the value labels in the plot, not the numeric codes. The setup chunk of this chapter did exactly that: to_label(eastwest, sex) turned the two variables into factors:

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = eastwest, y = islamophobia, fill = eastwest)) +
  geom_boxplot()






# The axis now shows 'OLD FEDERAL STATES' / 'NEW FEDERAL STATES'
# instead of 1 / 2, because eastwest was converted with to_label() in the setup chunk.

If you need another labelled variable in a plot, apply to_label() in the pipeline before you call ggplot().

title: 6  Visualisation basics
section: 6.8 Outlook: saving plots with ggsave() and combining them
text:
6.8 Outlook: saving plots with ggsave() and combining them
Two more tools that you will need in the next chapters:

Saving with ggsave(): you get a plot into your paper or onto your slides with ggsave("plot.png", width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300). Section 9.9.3 covers this in full.
Combining several plots with patchwork: if you need two plots side by side or one above the other, combine them with p1 + p2 (side by side) or p1 / p2 (one above the other). Section 9.9.2 covers this in full.

text:
Exercises






NoteExercise 1 · Your own distribution · Reproduction



Create a histogram of the populism scale (populism) with a binwidth of 0.25, weighted, with your own title and axis labels.








TipSolution






allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(populism)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = populism, weight = wghtpew)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#7c3aed", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Populism (reverse-coded)", y = "Count (weighted)",
       title = "Distribution of populist attitudes",
       caption = "ALLBUS 2023")










NoteExercise 2 · Subgroup box plot with facets · Reproduction



Create a box plot of Islamophobia by eastwest, split by the education groups educ_cat (with facet_wrap).








TipSolution






allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(eastwest), !is.na(educ_cat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = eastwest, y = islamophobia, fill = eastwest)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ educ_cat) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Islamophobia") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")










NoteExercise 3 · Density plot with two groupings · Transfer



Create a density plot (geom_density) of Islamophobia, coloured by eastwest, and split it by educ_cat with facet_wrap. Where are the largest differences between East and West?








TipSolution






allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(eastwest), !is.na(educ_cat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = islamophobia, fill = eastwest)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ educ_cat) +
  labs(x = "Islamophobia", y = "Density", fill = NULL,
       title = "Distributions by education and region")










NoteExercise 4 · Your own visualisation · Mini research question



Choose an interesting political or social science question from ALLBUS 2023 and visualise it. Examples: How is satisfaction with democracy (ps03) distributed? Is life satisfaction (ls01) related to age? Pay attention to a suitable geom type, weighting if your statement refers to Germany as a whole (weight = wghtpew), readable axes and an informative caption.
No model solution. Judge your plot by whether it answers a specific question in 10 seconds or less.








Note



Research journal: Where your mini study stands. You now know the vocabulary of visualisation: histogram, box plot, scatter plot, facets, themes. From the next chapter on, every statistical analysis comes with a matching plot. In Chapter 7 you then describe the scale (univariate and bivariate), illustrate it with a histogram and a box plot, and test the first hypotheses, weighted and with effect sizes.

title: 6  Visualisation basics
text:
What you know now

You build ggplot2 plots in three steps: data, aesthetic mapping, layers.
You choose suitable geom_* layers by data type (categorical/continuous, one/two variables).
You split the data into subgroups with facet_wrap() and facet_grid().
You use Brewer and viridis palettes for accessible colours.
You know theme_rworkshop() as the default theme of this book and can use it in your own projects.
You use to_label() to put readable labels on the axes.

In the following methods chapters you use these basics straight away: in Chapter 7 to visualise distributions and groups, in Chapter 9 for coefficient plots and combined plots.
