Further reading

mariposa vignettes “Descriptive Statistics”, “Hypothesis Testing” and “Correlation Analysis”; on weighting, the vignette “Working with Survey Weights”.
Andy Field et al., Discovering Statistics Using R: the chapters on comparing means and on correlation.
Jacob Cohen, Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed., 1988): the original source of the rules of thumb for effect sizes.
ALLBUS 2023 methods report (GESIS; see the documentation of ZA8833): explanation of the weighting variables and the sample design.

title: 8  Latent structures
text:
8.1 What this chapter is about
In Chapter 5 you combined several items into a scale. But is that actually legitimate? Does each item load evenly on the construct, or do some items stand apart? Does the scale measure one thing or several? And how consistent are the items with each other?
Most of the constructs that social researchers are interested in cannot be measured directly; you can only infer them indirectly. Nobody can read “intelligence” off a thermometer, measure “satisfaction with democracy” with a ruler or record “Islamophobia” as a single value with a sensor. These are all latent (hidden) quantities. They only become visible when you ask people several concrete questions and combine the answers, like a detective who does not see the offender but works out who it is from the clues.
When you do this, a follow-up question arises: how do you actually know that the six items really measure one construct together? Perhaps they measure two different things that you are wrongly lumping together. Or one of the items is out of line and measures something else entirely. Or the items are related so unreliably that your scale score is nothing but noise.
This validation is the task of this chapter. Three tools are available for it, and they build on each other:
At the end you take a brief look at confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with lavaan, the next step when you want to test a specific structural hypothesis instead of only exploring the data. EFA asks: “Which structure fits best?” CFA asks: “Does this specific structure, which I derive from theory, fit the data?”
Figure 8.1 shows what a latent variable is, using Islamophobia as the example. The six item towers hold the respondents’ answers. Nobody has measured Islamophobia itself; it is a factor without values of its own. The scale score islamophobia from Chapter 5 is calculated from the items.
The arrows run from the invisible factor to the observed items. The assumption is that the factor produces the answers. A person with a high level of Islamophobia therefore tends to choose high values on all six items. You will see the same direction of the arrows again in CFA path diagrams.

title: 8  Latent structures
text:
Correlation matrix: the simplest preliminary check. If the items do not even correlate strongly in pairs, there is nothing for them to measure together. Factor analysis is only worthwhile when the inter-item correlations are at least of medium strength.

Exploratory factor analysis (EFA): the statistical answer to the question “How many invisible factors explain the pattern of the observed correlations?” With EFA you check whether your items really measure one dimension or whether they split into several sub-dimensions.

Reliability (Cronbach’s α): the answer to “Are the items that together form a factor internally consistent enough to serve as a common measure?” Cronbach’s α has been the standard index for this since the 1950s.








Figure 8.1: The six items are measured, shown here with the answers of the first three respondents who answered all six. The factor Islamophobia has no values; an arrow leads from it to each item.

title: 8  Latent structures
section: What you will be able to do after this chapter
text:
What you will be able to do after this chapter

Set up and read an inter-item correlation matrix and visualise it as a heatmap with ggplot2.
Understand the KMO measure and Bartlett’s test as assumption checks and find them in the efa() output.
Decide on the number of factors with the eigenvalue criterion and a scree plot drawn by hand.
Run an exploratory factor analysis, read factor loadings and visualise them as a sorted bar chart.
Explain the difference between PCA, EFA and CFA, and know when each method is appropriate.
Choose a rotation (varimax, oblimin) deliberately.
Calculate Cronbach’s α, read item statistics, identify problematic items, check α-if-deleted as a bar chart and compare α with McDonald’s ω.
Set up a simple CFA model with lavaan and interpret fit indices.

title: 8  Latent structures
text:
8.2 Inter-item correlations

8.2.1 The preliminary check before any factor analysis
Imagine six reporters sending in their reports on the same situation. If five of them paint a similar picture and one describes something completely different, you know before any analysis that five probably measure the same thing and one measures something else. Inter-item correlations give you this preliminary diagnosis for your scale.
They are the basic requirement for any meaningful factor analysis: if the items do not correlate with each other in pairs, there is nothing for them to measure together, and an EFA would find no factors because there are none.






NoteBackground: What does a correlation measure mathematically?





The Pearson correlation \(r\) is the standardised covariance. It measures how strongly two variables deviate together from their respective means, relative to their individual spread:
\[r = \frac{\text{Cov}(x, y)}{\text{SD}(x) \cdot \text{SD}(y)}\]
Read it as: “how strongly x and y vary together, in units of each variable’s own typical variation.” Because of the division, \(r\) always lies between \(-1\) (perfectly opposed) and \(+1\) (perfectly in step). This is the number you get in the pearson_cor() output for each pair of items.




8.2.2 Computing the matrix with pearson_cor()

Question: How strongly are the six Islamophobia items related to each other?

allbus |>
  pearson_cor(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06, weights = wghtpew)

Pearson Correlation: 6 variables [Weighted]
  mm01 x mm02r:  r = 0.459, p < 0.001 ***
  mm01 x mm03:   r = 0.520, p < 0.001 ***
  mm01 x mm04:   r = 0.548, p < 0.001 ***
  mm01 x mm05r:  r = 0.488, p < 0.001 ***
  mm01 x mm06:   r = 0.536, p < 0.001 ***
  mm02r x mm03:  r = 0.368, p < 0.001 ***
  mm02r x mm04:  r = 0.361, p < 0.001 ***
  mm02r x mm05r: r = 0.450, p < 0.001 ***
  mm02r x mm06:  r = 0.381, p < 0.001 ***
  mm03 x mm04:   r = 0.548, p < 0.001 ***
  mm03 x mm05r:  r = 0.348, p < 0.001 ***
  mm03 x mm06:   r = 0.524, p < 0.001 ***
  mm04 x mm05r:  r = 0.341, p < 0.001 ***
  mm04 x mm06:   r = 0.564, p < 0.001 ***
  mm05r x mm06:  r = 0.363, p < 0.001 ***
  15/15 pairs significant (p < .05), N = 3224-3366
Use summary() for detailed output.



8.2.3 Reading the thresholds
The compact output lists all fifteen item pairs with Pearson’s r and the p-value. summary() gives you the classic square matrix, together with p-values, confidence intervals and N per cell. All pairs lie between 0.34 and 0.56. Three thresholds help you to classify such values straight away:






Inter-item r

Interpretation



< 0.20
item does not belong: probably measures something else


0.30 – 0.70
healthy range: items are related, but not redundant


> 0.85
redundancy: two items measure almost the same thing; one is almost superfluous









NoteBackground: The correlation matrix in the appendix





An inter-item correlation matrix belongs in the appendix of an empirical paper that uses a scale of its own. It is the quickest sanity check for the operationalisation: anyone who sees a value close to 0 or above 0.85 there starts to worry.




8.2.4 Heatmap with ggplot2
A table of fifteen numbers is tedious to read. The same information as a heatmap can be read at a glance: dark cells mean a strong relationship. You build it by hand from the pearson_cor() output:

cor_obj <- allbus |>
  pearson_cor(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06, weights = wghtpew)

cor_obj$matrices[[1]]$correlations |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "Item1") |>
  pivot_longer(-Item1, names_to = "Item2", values_to = "r") |>
  ggplot(aes(Item1, Item2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), color = "white", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r",
       title = "Inter-item correlations of the six Islamophobia items",
       caption = "ALLBUS 2023, weighted with wghtpew") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))







Interpretation. The diagonal is trivially 1.0 (each item correlates perfectly with itself). The off-diagonal cells are the interesting ones: all six items show values well above 0.3. The reporter from the example above who describes something else does not appear here; all items clearly point in the same direction. The preliminary check is passed, and the EFA can start.






Importantmariposa tip: The full matrix from the pearson_cor() object





pearson_cor() returns more than the printed view: underneath is a structured list object. cor_obj$matrices[[1]]$correlations is the square correlation matrix (rownames = colnames = variable names). In the same way you get $p_values, $ci_lower, $ci_upper and $n_obs as parallel matrices. That is everything you need for your own visualisations, without calling cor() from base R separately. If you want to process the list of pairs as a table instead, as_tibble(cor_obj) returns it as a tibble; this works for every analysis result since mariposa 0.7.4.



The inter-item correlations give the green light: all items are related, and none of them is out of place. Now comes the actual factor analysis. It works like an X-ray of the correlations: it tries to infer how many invisible dimensions must lie behind the observed correlations to produce this pattern.
Imagine that all six items are driven by a single underlying attitude. Then all items must correlate clearly with each other, since a person with high Islamophobia ticks high values everywhere. That would be a one-factor model. If two underlying attitudes are at work (such as “cognitive stereotypes” and a “politically restrictive stance”), some item pairs correlate more strongly than others, and the result is a two-factor model. The EFA checks which one fits.
You take this step by step: first the assumptions (KMO, Bartlett), then the decision on the number of factors (eigenvalues, scree plot), then the final models (one factor or two factors) including rotation.

title: 8  Latent structures
section: 8.3 Checking the assumptions: KMO and Bartlett
text:
8.3 Checking the assumptions: KMO and Bartlett
Before you start the EFA at all, two tests check whether it makes sense technically. Both appear automatically at the top of every efa() output. You do not have to compute them separately, but you need to be able to read them.

8.3.1 KMO: how much shared variance is there at all?
Imagine you want to distil one editorial from six newspaper articles. If the articles overlap in content, that is no problem. But if each of them deals with a completely different topic, there is nothing common to extract. The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure (KMO) quantifies this: what share of the item variance is still left as partial variance (that is, after controlling for all other items), and how much is shared?
The core of the formula: \[\text{KMO} = \frac{\sum r_{ij}^2}{\sum r_{ij}^2 + \sum a_{ij}^2}\] with \(r_{ij}\) = pairwise correlations and \(a_{ij}\) = partial correlations (correlations after the influence of all other items has been removed).
Read it as: “what share of the relationships between the items cannot be explained away by other items, and can therefore really be traced back to a common underlying factor.”
Conceptually, KMO is the average over all items: for each item, the shared part (good for factor analysis) is weighed against the partial part, and KMO itself is the aggregate of these parts. You will see the per-item values (officially MSA, measure of sampling adequacy) shortly in the diagnostic block, with actual values from our model and as a plot. The table of thresholds for practical use:


KMO
Sampling adequacy



≥ 0.90
marvelous


≥ 0.80
meritorious


≥ 0.70
middling


≥ 0.60
mediocre (lower limit)


< 0.60
factor analysis not recommended



8.3.2 Bartlett’s test: are the correlations different from zero at all?
Bartlett’s test of sphericity asks a basic minimum question: is the correlation matrix significantly different from an identity matrix at all (a matrix in which only the diagonal is 1 and all off-diagonal values are 0, that is, no correlation whatsoever)?
If the test is significant (\(p < .05\)), this means: “at least one correlation in the matrix is different from zero, so there is something to factor-analyse.” With N > 1000, Bartlett’s test is almost always significant; it is more of a technical minimum check than a substantive argument. KMO is the far more informative measure.

8.3.3 Three diagnostic levels from one call to efa()

You call efa() once with n_factors = 1 and store the result. The number of factors does not matter here; you are only interested in the values for the assumption checks. From the returned object you read three diagnostic levels.
Level 1 is the overall KMO. The compact print shows it as the central number:

efa_check <- allbus |>
  efa(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06,
      weights = wghtpew, n_factors = 1)
efa_check

Exploratory Factor Analysis: 6 items, 1 component (PCA/Unrotated) [Weighted]
  KMO = 0.862 (Meritorious), Variance explained: 54.7%, N = 3224 (smallest pairwise)
  Only one component was extracted. The solution cannot be rotated.
Use summary() for detailed output.


Overall KMO ≈ 0.86: as a whole, the sample is “meritorious” (see the table of thresholds above).
efa_check is a list with 34 elements; the print shows only a few numbers from it. Like the list result in Figure 3.13, it is a box with compartments (Figure 8.2): with $ you take out one compartment, and because $kmo is itself a list, efa_check$kmo$per_item leads to the per-item values in two steps.





Figure 8.2: Four of the 34 elements of efa_check in their order in the list; the values come from the outputs in this section and from summary() in Section 8.5. The compartment that efa_check$kmo$per_item takes out is outlined in green.


Level 2 is Bartlett’s test. You read it from the object slot $bartlett:

efa_check$bartlett

$chi_sq
[1] 6532.633

$df
[1] 15

$p_value
[1] 0


χ² ≈ 6533 with df = 15 and p < .001: the correlation matrix is clearly different from an identity matrix. The minimum requirement is met.
Level 3 is the per-item KMO (MSA). This is the really interesting diagnostic step, because it shows whether each individual item fits into the common factor model. In the output object it is stored as a named numeric vector in $kmo$per_item; you put it into a tibble:

tibble(item = names(efa_check$kmo$per_item),
       MSA  = round(efa_check$kmo$per_item, 3))

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  item    MSA
  <chr> <dbl>
1 mm01  0.857
2 mm02r 0.876
3 mm03  0.874
4 mm04  0.849
5 mm05r 0.851
6 mm06  0.867


Rule of thumb per item: an MSA ≥ 0.5 is acceptable, and a value below 0.5 suggests removing this item from the factor analysis. Here all six items lie between 0.85 and 0.88. These are clean values throughout, and no item needs to be removed.
As a plot, with shared (blue) and partial (grey) variance per item and the MSA threshold of 0.5 as a dashed line:

tibble(item   = names(efa_check$kmo$per_item),
       shared = efa_check$kmo$per_item) |>
  mutate(partial = 1 - shared) |>
  pivot_longer(c(shared, partial),
               names_to = "share", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(share = fct_relevel(share, "shared")) |>   # shared part at the bottom
  ggplot(aes(x = item, y = value, fill = share)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 6.4, y = 0.52,
           label = "MSA threshold 0.5",
           color = "grey30", size = 3, hjust = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(shared = "#1f77b4", partial = "grey80"),
    labels = c("shared variance (MSA)", "partial variance"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share per item",
       title = "How much shared variance does each item have?",
       caption = "Actual values from efa_check$kmo$per_item · ALLBUS 2023, weighted")







In every bar the blue part reaches far above the 0.5 threshold. The plot confirms what the table above shows in numbers.
Overall interpretation. All three levels give the green light: overall KMO 0.86, Bartlett’s test significant, an MSA ≥ 0.85 for every single item. In the next section you decide on the number of factors.

title: 8  Latent structures
text:
8.4 Determining the number of factors

8.4.1 Eigenvalue: how much information does a factor capture?
Imagine you squeeze the information from six items into one common underlying factor. How much of the total variation in the items fits into this one dimension? This is what the eigenvalue \(\lambda\) measures.
The intuitive rule of thumb is surprisingly simple: each item has a standardised variance of 1. So you can read eigenvalues “in item units”:


\(\lambda = 1\) → the factor captures as much information as a single item and adds nothing.

\(\lambda = 3\) → the factor captures as much as three items, a substantial gain.

\(\lambda = 0.3\) → the factor captures less than one item and picks up only noise.

This gives the Kaiser criterion: keep all factors with \(\lambda > 1\). It is simple and robust and has been the standard since the 1960s, even though newer methods (see below) refine it.

8.4.2 Three criteria for deciding on the number of factors







Criterion
Decision rule
Strength / weakness



Kaiser
all factors with \(\lambda > 1\)

simple; tends to overestimate



Scree test
number of factors at the “elbow” in the eigenvalue plot
visually intuitive; subjective


Parallel analysis
comparison with eigenvalues of randomly generated data of the same size
methodological gold standard; more effort



Most methods textbooks now recommend parallel analysis (via psych::fa.parallel()). For this workshop, the combination of the Kaiser criterion and a visual scree plot is enough; you see both in the next step.

8.4.3 Scree plot: finding the elbow
The scree plot (scree is the loose rock that collects on a mountain slope) shows the eigenvalues as a descending line. Imagine a mountain with large boulders at the top and fine scree at the bottom: the “real” factors are at the top, the noise factors at the bottom. You are looking for the point that separates them.
You read the eigenvalues from the efa() object with $eigenvalues and plot them by hand:

efa_obj <- allbus |>
  efa(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06,
      weights = wghtpew, n_factors = 1)

tibble(
  factor     = seq_along(efa_obj$eigenvalues),
  eigenvalue = efa_obj$eigenvalues
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor, y = eigenvalue)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#1f77b4", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 5.5, y = 1.08, label = "Kaiser threshold (λ = 1)",
           color = "grey40", size = 3, hjust = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_along(efa_obj$eigenvalues)) +
  labs(x = "Factor", y = "Eigenvalue (λ)",
       title = "Scree plot of the six Islamophobia items",
       caption = "ALLBUS 2023, weighted with wghtpew")







Interpretation. You are looking for two signals: (a) How many factors lie above the Kaiser line (\(\lambda > 1\))? (b) Where is the clearest “elbow” in the line? A first eigenvalue that clearly stands out, followed by a flat rest, is the classic picture of a one-dimensional scale. Two clearly raised values point to a two-dimensional structure.

title: 8  Latent structures
text:
8.5 Extracting a one-factor solution
You have checked the assumptions and decided on the number of factors. Now comes the actual model, with the focus on the factor loadings.

8.5.1 What is a factor loading?
Think of an invisible factor as a dial. When the dial is turned up, people tick strongly agreeing answers on some items: the loading is high. On other items the answer hardly responds: the loading is low. The factor loading is the strength of the relationship between item and factor.
Mathematically, in the one-factor solution the loading equals the correlation between item and factor. It ranges from \(-1\) to \(+1\), with the usual thresholds:


|Loading|
Interpretation



< 0.30
irrelevant


0.30 – 0.50
moderate


0.50 – 0.70
usable


≥ 0.70
high (item is a core indicator)



In the plot the factor sits in the middle and the items radiate outwards; the thickness of a line shows the strength of the loading. Items with a thick line are strongly tied to the factor, items with a thin line less strongly. The loadings already come from the actual one-factor solution (the efa_obj from the scree plot chunk); in the next section you look them up in the output table:

factor_radial <- efa_obj$loadings |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "item") |>
  rename(loading = PC1) |>
  mutate(angle = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 7)[1:6],
         x = cos(angle), y = sin(angle))

factor_radial |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y,
                   linewidth = loading),
               color = "#1f77b4", lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(aes(x = x, y = y), size = 5, color = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_label(aes(x = x * 1.20, y = y * 1.20,
                 label = sprintf("%s\nλ = %.2f", item, loading)),
             size = 3.2, linewidth = 0, fill = "white") +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, size = 16,
           color = "black", fill = "#fbbf24", shape = 21) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "Factor",
           fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  scale_linewidth_continuous(range = c(0.5, 3.5)) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.5, 1.5), ylim = c(-1.5, 1.5)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "Factor loading as strength of connection",
       caption = "Line thickness = how strongly the item is tied to the factor.")







Interpretation. mm01 (λ = 0.81) is the strongest core indicator; it responds most clearly when the factor “turns”. mm03, mm04 and mm06 follow close behind (each about 0.75–0.77). The two reverse-coded items mm02r and mm05r are tied somewhat less strongly to the factor at around 0.66, but still lie clearly in the usable range. There is no real peripheral indicator (λ < 0.5).

8.5.2 Running the model with efa() and reading the loadings
You already know the compact output from Section 8.3: KMO, explained variance, N. For the loadings you need the detailed version with summary(), which is structured like the SPSS output of FACTOR:

allbus |>
  efa(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06,
      weights = wghtpew, n_factors = 1) |>
  summary()

8.5.3 Visualising the loadings
A table with six loadings is still easy to read. A sorted bar chart, however, shows at a glance which items are most strongly tied to the construct and which are more peripheral indicators. You build this by hand from the efa() object as well:

efa_1 <- allbus |>
  efa(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06,
      weights = wghtpew, n_factors = 1)

efa_1$loadings |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "item") |>
  rename(loading = PC1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loading, y = fct_reorder(item, loading))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.5, 0.7), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Factor loading", y = NULL,
       title = "How strongly is each item tied to the latent factor?",
       caption = "Vertical lines: thresholds for usable (0.5) and high (0.7)")







Interpretation. Items above 0.7 are core indicators of the construct; anything between 0.5 and 0.7 is usable; anything below 0.5 you would keep on theoretical grounds or remove on empirical grounds. The bar chart also serves as a quick check of the items: if an item is clearly out of line (for example < 0.3 or with the opposite sign), this points to a reverse-coding error or an item on a different topic.

title: 8  Latent structures
text:
8.6 Two-factor solution with rotation
What if the scale is not one-dimensional? The research debate on Islamophobia sometimes distinguishes between a cognitive, stereotyping component (for example mm06, “fanatics”) and a politically restrictive component (for example mm04, “monitor”). You can try this out with two factors and rotation.
When you extract more than one factor, the way the loadings are divided among the factors is mathematically not unique: many solutions are statistically equivalent. A rotation turns the factor axes geometrically and so enforces one interpretable solution: each item should load as highly as possible on one factor and low on the others.
Three families of rotation:


"varimax": orthogonal, the factors stay uncorrelated. The standard choice if you later interpret the factors as independent constructs.

"oblimin" / "promax": oblique, the factors may be correlated. More realistic in the social sciences, where constructs are rarely completely independent.

"none": no rotation. Rare, only for pure data reduction.

Rule of thumb: if theory makes it clear that the constructs are correlated (Islamophobia and populism are related), use oblimin; otherwise use varimax. mariposa computes all rotations itself with the algorithms of SPSS FACTOR. You need no additional package for this, and the rotated loadings match SPSS.
What does a rotation do visually? The plot shows six items in a two-dimensional factor space, before and after a varimax rotation. Before the rotation the items load diffusely on both axes; after the rotation each of them is neatly aligned with one axis:

items_unrot <- tibble(
  item = paste0("mm0", 1:6),
  F1 = c(0.65, 0.55, 0.50, 0.40, 0.45, 0.35),
  F2 = c(-0.40, -0.50, 0.60, 0.55, -0.45, 0.50)
)

items_rot <- tibble(
  item = paste0("mm0", 1:6),
  F1 = c(0.80, 0.85, 0.10, 0.05, 0.75, 0.10),
  F2 = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.85, 0.80, 0.10, 0.80)
)

baseplot <- function(d, ttl, sub) {
  d |>
    ggplot(aes(F1, F2, label = item)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
    geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = F1, yend = F2),
                 color = "#1f77b4", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1f77b4") +
    geom_text(nudge_y = 0.08, size = 3) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1)) +
    labs(x = "Factor 1", y = "Factor 2",
         title = ttl, subtitle = sub)
}

baseplot(items_unrot, "Before rotation",
         "Loadings are spread across both axes") +
baseplot(items_rot, "After varimax rotation",
         "Each item loads clearly on one axis")







Interpretation. On the left, no axis clearly describes a factor; the items lie between the axes. On the right, the rotation has attached the items either almost only to factor 1 or almost only to factor 2 (at the top). This is what makes the interpretation readable: “F1 = this group of items, F2 = that group of items.”

allbus |>
  efa(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06,
      weights = wghtpew, n_factors = 2, rotation = "varimax") |>
  summary()

Interpretation. The Rotated Component Matrix now has two columns, PC1 and PC2; loadings below 0.4 are hidden. Look at each row: does the item load clearly on one factor or evenly on both? The result is revealing, though it differs from what the research debate would suggest:


mm04, mm03 and mm06 load on PC1 (loadings 0.78–0.83): monitoring, conflict, fanatics.

PC2 contains exactly the two reverse-coded items, mm05r (0.84) and mm02r (0.79).

mm01 loads on both factors (0.63 and 0.51) and cannot be clearly assigned to either.

So the second factor separates the two positively worded items from the four negatively worded ones, and the distinction between “cognitive, stereotyping” and “politically restrictive” does not appear. This is the typical picture of a method factor: it reflects the direction of the wording rather than a second substantive dimension (more on method effects in Section 8.8). The Total Variance Explained fits this: at 0.83, the eigenvalue of the second factor lies below the Kaiser threshold of 1. Both point to the one-factor solution, which is more parsimonious and clearer in content. The principle of parsimony (Occam’s razor) is a strong anchor when you choose a model.
The loading columns are called PC1 and PC2 because by default efa() runs a principal component analysis (PCA). PCA, EFA and CFA differ in their aims:

PCA (extraction = "pca") looks for components that explain as much variance as possible; good for data reduction.
EFA (extraction = "ml") models latent factors behind the items; good for building theory.
CFA (with lavaan, see Section 8.8) tests a factor model specified in advance; good for testing theory.

Rule of thumb: PCA for reduction, EFA for exploration, CFA for confirmation.

title: 8  Latent structures
text:
8.7 Reliability: Cronbach’s α

8.7.1 The idea: six friends and a walk
Imagine you ask six friends whether today is a good day for a walk. If all six say “yes, of course”, you know the judgement is consistent: they probably measure the same thing (weather, free time, mood). If three say “yes” and three say “no”, the scale probably measures different things; perhaps three of them looked out of the window and three at their calendar. Cronbach’s α puts this idea into a number.
While EFA tells you how many dimensions the items contain, reliability analysis answers a different question: “If the items measure one dimension, how consistently do they measure it?” It is the second pillar of validity alongside the factor structure.

8.7.2 The formula and why it looks like this
Cronbach’s α has existed since 1951 (named after Lee J. Cronbach). The formula looks unwieldy at first, but it is straightforward:
\[\alpha = \frac{k \cdot \bar{r}}{1 + (k-1) \cdot \bar{r}}\]
with \(k\) = number of items and \(\bar{r}\) = average inter-item correlation.
Read it as: “the more items there are, and the more strongly they are related on average, the higher α.” Two worked examples make this concrete:


\(k = 6\) items with \(\bar{r} = 0.5\) → \(\alpha = (6 \cdot 0.5) / (1 + 5 \cdot 0.5) = 3 / 3.5 ≈ 0.86\).

\(k = 2\) items with the same \(\bar{r} = 0.5\) → \(\alpha = (2 \cdot 0.5) / (1 + 1 \cdot 0.5) = 1 / 1.5 ≈ 0.67\).

This gives the central rule of thumb: more items buy reliability, even if no single item measures any better. This is also why established scales often have 8–12 items instead of only 3–4.

8.7.3 Calculating α with reliability()


rel_obj <- allbus |>
  reliability(mm01, mm02r, mm03, mm04, mm05r, mm06, weights = wghtpew)
rel_obj

Reliability Analysis: 6 items [Weighted]
  Cronbach's Alpha = 0.833 (Good), McDonald's Omega = 0.835, N = 3071
Use summary() for detailed output.


Interpretation. The compact output gives Cronbach’s α with a classification, McDonald’s ω next to it (more on this shortly) and the N of cases that answered all six items. With α = 0.83 the scale has good reliability. Rules of thumb:


α
Rating



≥ 0.90
excellent

good

acceptable


≥ 0.60
questionable


< 0.60
unacceptable

For the diagnosis, two columns of the Item-Total Statistics table matter most:


Corrected Item-Total (corrected item-total correlation): how strongly is the single item related to the sum of the other items (with its own value left out)? Thresholds: ≥ 0.30 usable, ≥ 0.50 strong.

Alpha if Deleted: how would α change if this item were removed?

From these you can see straight away which item supports the scale and which tends to weaken it:

α rises when the item is removed → the item does not fit the scale and is a candidate for deletion.
α falls when the item is removed → the item contributes to reliability; keep it.

In this scale, all corrected item-total correlations lie between 0.52 (mm05r) and 0.70 (mm01), which is strong throughout. And deleting any one item would not raise α above 0.83: all six support the scale.
For mm05r, reliability() adds up the other five items in each row and correlates this sum with mm05r (Figure 8.3).





Figure 8.3: The corrected item-total correlation of mm05r: the other five items are added up per row, and mm05r does not count. Shown are the first three respondents who answered all six items; the correlation of 0.520 is weighted and calculated over all respondents with six answers.



8.7.5 Visualising α-if-deleted
Here too a bar chart lets you see the diagnosis at a glance. You extract $item_total$alpha_if_deleted from the mariposa object rel_obj above and add the overall α as a vertical reference line:

rel_obj$item_total |>
  ggplot(aes(x = alpha_if_deleted, y = fct_reorder(item, alpha_if_deleted))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rel_obj$alpha, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = rel_obj$alpha, y = 0.6,
           label = sprintf("Overall α = %.2f", rel_obj$alpha),
           color = "grey30", size = 3, hjust = -0.05) +
  expand_limits(x = 1) +
  labs(x = "α if this item is deleted", y = NULL,
       title = "Which item supports the scale, and which weakens it?",
       caption = "Dashed line: Cronbach's α of the full scale")







Interpretation. A bar to the left of the dashed line means “α would fall if I deleted this item” → the item contributes to the scale; keep it. A bar to the right of the line means “α would rise” → a candidate for deletion. In a well-functioning scale, ideally all bars lie close together (and to the left of the line), with no item standing out.






Warning



Caution: Cronbach’s α is a lower bound. α assumes that all items are tied equally strongly to the factor (τ-equivalence). If this is not the case, α underestimates the true reliability. In the current methods literature, McDonald’s ω is therefore considered the cleaner choice: ω is estimated from a one-factor model and lets each item have its own loading. reliability() reports ω as well: in the compact output, in the Reliability Statistics block and as the column Omega if Deleted. Here ω = 0.835 is almost exactly equal to α = 0.833, because the loadings do not differ enough to push α down noticeably. It is best to report both values in your methods section. Unlike α, ω has not yet been checked against SPSS output; the mariposa vignette “SPSS Compatibility” documents the current state.


Besides α and ω, the methods report should include the item-total correlations and the α-if-deleted values of all items, as a table or as a bar chart like the one above. Readers can then judge for themselves whether your scale construction is methodologically consistent.

title: 8  Latent structures
section: 8.8 Outlook: confirmatory factor analysis with cfa() and semPaths()
text:
8.8 Outlook: confirmatory factor analysis with cfa() and semPaths()

So far you have explored the factor structure. If you have a specific hypothesis, such as “the six items measure one latent factor”, and want to test it, you need a confirmatory factor analysis. mariposa is not designed for this. You use lavaan, the standard package for CFA and structural equation models, and you draw the path diagrams with semPlot.
Install them once:

install.packages(c("lavaan", "semPlot"))







Warning



Caution: lavaan masks mariposa’s efa(). lavaan also contains a function called efa(). If you load the package with library(lavaan), R reports “The following object is masked from ‘package:mariposa’: efa”. From then on, efa() calls the lavaan version, and the calls from this chapter stop with a cryptic error message. This is why the code below calls lavaan with the package prefix (lavaan::cfa()) without loading it. If you have already run library(lavaan), write mariposa::efa() explicitly for the mariposa function.


Before you set up the model, here is the lavaan model syntax in three operators:







Operator
Meaning
Example



=~

“is measured by”: factor → items
islam =~ mm01 + mm02r + mm03


~~

covariance: two variables may correlate
mm02r ~~ mm05r


~

regression: a variable is predicted by one or more others
islam ~ educ + age



Set up and estimate the model:

model_cfa <- "islam =~ mm01 + mm02r + mm03 + mm04 + mm05r + mm06"

fit <- lavaan::cfa(model_cfa, data = allbus,
                   sampling.weights = "wghtpew", estimator = "MLR")

summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

A CFA tests whether your specified model fits the data. Fit indices measure how well it fits. Instead of a single figure, there are four standard measures that compare the model from different angles:

CFI / TLI (Comparative Fit Index / Tucker-Lewis Index): compare your model with a null model without any structure. Values close to 1 indicate good fit; higher = better.
RMSEA (Root Mean Square Error of Approximation): absolute fit, corrected for model complexity. Values close to 0 indicate good fit; lower = better.
SRMR (Standardized Root Mean Square Residual): the average of the standardised residuals. Lower = better.

fit.measures = TRUE gives you all four at once. Rules of thumb: CFI/TLI ≥ 0.95, RMSEA ≤ 0.06, SRMR ≤ 0.08. A good model meets several of these thresholds; a single figure never decides on its own.
A “traffic light” plot of the fit shows four indices at a glance, green = threshold met, red = missed (schematic example values for a well-fitting model):

tibble(
  index     = c("CFI", "TLI", "RMSEA", "SRMR"),
  value     = c(0.96, 0.95, 0.055, 0.06),
  threshold = c(0.95, 0.95, 0.06, 0.08),
  direction = c("higher = better", "higher = better",
                "lower = better", "lower = better")
) |>
  mutate(
    met   = if_else(direction == "higher = better",
                    value >= threshold, value <= threshold),
    label = sprintf("%.3f", value)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = fct_rev(index), fill = met)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = threshold),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(`TRUE` = "#16a34a", `FALSE` = "#d62728"),
    labels = c(`FALSE` = "missed", `TRUE` = "threshold met"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.2))) +
  facet_wrap(~ direction, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Value", y = NULL,
       title = "Fit indices as a traffic-light check",
       caption = "green = threshold met · dashed line = rule-of-thumb threshold")







Interpretation. All four bars green → the model fits well. If one index just misses its threshold, that is no disaster; two or more missed indices are a warning sign.
With estimator = "MLR" (maximum likelihood with robust standard errors) you are on the safe side if the items are not ideally normally distributed. For purely ordinal items, "WLSMV" would be the cleaner choice, but it is computationally more demanding.
A path diagram:

semPlot::semPaths(fit, whatLabels = "std", layout = "tree", edge.color = "black")

With scales that have positively and negatively worded items (such as our Islamophobia scale), a strict one-factor CFA model often fits poorly, because the reverse-coded items correlate with each other even after controlling for the main factor. This is a method effect (acquiescence) and not a substantive sub-factor. In the two-factor solution in Section 8.6 it appeared as a factor of its own. In CFA you deal with this by allowing residual covariances between the reverse-coded items (mm02r ~~ mm05r). This specification is methodologically sound and established in the literature.






NoteBackground: When to use CFA and when not





A CFA makes sense if:

You have a specific theoretical hypothesis about the factor structure.
Your sample is large enough (rule of thumb: N ≥ 200).
You accept strict assumptions about distribution and estimation (MLR, WLSMV for ordinal items).

If you simply want to combine items into a scale and are not testing a structural hypothesis, EFA and α are the more pragmatic route.

Exercises






NoteExercise 1 · EFA of the pa items · Reproduction



The research debate on populism discusses whether it is a one-dimensional attitude or consists of three components (anti-elitism, people-centrism, Manichaean worldview). Run an EFA of the seven reverse-coded pa items, first with n_factors = 1, then with n_factors = 3 and varimax rotation. Which solution fits better?

allbus |>

      n_factors = 3, rotation = "varimax")










NoteExercise 2 · Reliability of the populism scale · Reproduction



Calculate Cronbach’s α for the seven reverse-coded pa items. Which item has the weakest item-total correlation? Would deleting it improve reliability?








TipSolution

              weights = wghtpew)










NoteExercise 3 · Checking your own scale · Transfer



Go back to the scale you built in the exercise at the end of Chapter 5 (your own construct). Check it: (a) correlation matrix, (b) EFA with one factor, (c) Cronbach’s α. Write two or three sentences on whether the operationalisation is methodologically sound.
No model solution: this exercise practises the complete validation workflow.








NoteExercise 4 · CFA with lavaan · Mini research question



If you have installed lavaan: specify a one-factor CFA model for the six Islamophobia items, allow a residual covariance between mm02r and mm05r (see the note on method effects above), and check the fit indices. Does the model meet CFI ≥ 0.95, RMSEA ≤ 0.08, SRMR ≤ 0.08?








TipSolution sketch






model <- '
  islam =~ mm01 + mm02r + mm03 + mm04 + mm05r + mm06
  mm02r ~~ mm05r
'
fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, data = allbus,
                   sampling.weights = "wghtpew", estimator = "MLR")
lavaan::fitMeasures(fit, c("cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr"))










Note



Research journal: Where your mini study stands. Your scales are methodologically validated: the Islamophobia scale has good reliability with α = .83 and ω = .84, the EFA confirms a parsimonious one-factor structure (the second factor would only be a method factor of the reverse-coded items), and the CFA (see Exercise 4) shows that a one-factor model fits well once the method effect of the reversed wording is allowed for. What comes next: in Chapter 9 you take these scales and model them as dependent and independent variables in multivariate models.

title: 8  Latent structures
text:
What you know now

You create weighted inter-item correlation matrices with pearson_cor() and visualise them by hand as a heatmap in ggplot2 (source: cor_obj$matrices[[1]]$correlations).
You read KMO and Bartlett’s test as assumption checks and understand what lies behind the formulas.
You extract eigenvalues from the efa() object and decide on the number of factors with the Kaiser criterion and a scree plot drawn by hand.
You run an EFA with efa(), read factor loadings and visualise them as a sorted bar chart.
You choose a rotation (varimax, oblimin) deliberately, based on theoretical expectations.
You know the difference between PCA (data reduction), EFA (exploratory) and CFA (confirmatory).
You calculate Cronbach’s α and McDonald’s ω with reliability(), read the item statistics from summary(), identify problematic items and show α-if-deleted as a bar chart.
You recognise a method factor of reverse-coded items in a two-factor solution and know why library(lavaan) masks mariposa’s efa().
You know when CFA with lavaan makes sense and what a minimal specification including a method effect looks like.

The next chapter (Chapter 9) moves from structure to explanation: you model Islamophobia as a dependent variable and test which sociostructural and political predictors explain it best.

title: 8  Latent structures
section: Mini glossary: terms for latent structures
text:
Mini glossary: terms for latent structures






Term
Meaning in one sentence



latent
unobserved underlying variable that is measured indirectly through several items


manifest
directly observed item (one column in the dataset)


loading
strength of the item–factor relationship; in a one-factor solution = correlation; ≥ 0.5 usable, ≥ 0.7 high


eigenvalue (λ)
how much standardised item variance a factor accounts for; λ > 1 = more than a single item (Kaiser criterion)


KMO
proportion of shared (not partial) item variance; ≥ 0.6 acceptable, ≥ 0.7 good, ≥ 0.8 very good


Bartlett’s test
test of whether the correlation matrix differs significantly from the identity matrix; minimum condition for any EFA


scree plot
eigenvalues as a descending line; read off the number of factors at the “elbow” or at the Kaiser threshold


rotation
geometric turn of the factor axes for an interpretable solution (orthogonal: varimax; oblique: oblimin)


Cronbach’s α
reliability measure: \(\alpha = k\bar{r} / (1 + (k-1)\bar{r})\); ≥ 0.7 acceptable


McDonald’s ω
reliability measure from a one-factor model that lets each item have its own loading; usually ≥ α


item-total correlation
relationship of an item with the sum of the remaining items; ≥ 0.3 usable


α-if-deleted
how α changes if an item is deleted; diagnosis for items that do not belong to the scale


fit index
measure of agreement between a CFA model and the data (CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR)


method effect
systematic response tendency (e.g. acquiescence), not a substantive sub-dimension

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
9.1 What this chapter is about
In Chapter 7 you described variables one at a time and compared them in pairs. In Chapter 8 you validated the scales empirically. Now you bring the methods of the previous chapters together in one explanatory model: several predictors at the same time, each controlled for the influence of the others.
The real strength of quantitative social research only shows when you look at more than two variables at the same time. In Chapter 7 you showed that Islamophobia correlates positively with populism and negatively with education, and that it is higher in the East than in the West. But this immediately raises the next question: Are these all independent effects, or are they related?
Perhaps the East–West difference is not “real” at all. Perhaps it exists only because the average level of education is somewhat lower in the East, and the actual driver is education. Perhaps populism works quite differently for people with low education than for people with high education. Bivariate tests cannot answer such multicausal questions. You need a model that takes several predictors into account at the same time and shows what remains for each variable when the others are controlled for.
This is the core of multivariate methods: they isolate the effect of one variable by “partialling out” all the others at the same time. If the effect of region becomes smaller as soon as education is in the model, you know that part of the apparent East–West difference was really an education effect. If it stays the same, you know that region is a predictor in its own right.
This chapter takes you through the four most important tools of this kind:
At the end we communicate the findings graphically: coefficient plots make model results readable at a glance, patchwork combines several plots into a publication-ready composition, and ggsave() exports the result in any format.

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
Factorial ANOVA: when two categorical factors act at the same time, possibly with an interaction (the question “Is the effect of A stronger or weaker in different subgroups of B?”).
ANCOVA: an ANOVA with a continuous covariate whose influence you want to remove as a confounder.
Multiple linear regression: the all-rounder when your dependent variable is interval-scaled (like our Islamophobia scale). With it you can model any number of predictors and compare their relative strength.
Logistic regression: when your dependent variable has only two values (yes/no, high/low). It is the standard method for modelling the probability of a binary outcome.

title: 9  Explanatory models
section: What you will be able to do after this chapter
text:
What you will be able to do after this chapter

Run a simple linear regression with one predictor, draw the regression line by hand from the model coefficients in a scatter plot (geom_abline()) and follow the OLS logic (“least squares”).
Run, weight and interpret a multiple linear regression: coefficients, Beta, R², model F.
Compare two regression models formally with anova().
Check multicollinearity with VIF and tolerance, both recalculated by hand and taken directly from summary().
Build the four standard residual plots (Residuals vs Fitted, Normal Q-Q, Scale-Location, Residuals vs Leverage) by hand with ggplot2 from broom::augment() and combine them into a diagnostic composition with patchwork.

Run a logistic regression for a dichotomous outcome, including odds ratios and average marginal effects in percentage points (marginal_effects()).
Visualise regression results as a coefficient plot with broom::tidy().
Combine several plots into one composition with patchwork.
Export plots at publication-quality resolution with ggsave().

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
9.2 Simple linear regression
We start with the simplest case: one predictor, one dependent variable. Once you understand this case, you understand the mechanics of the whole regression family. Multiple regression, ANOVA and logistic regression are all variants of the same basic principle.

9.2.1 The rubber band idea
Imagine the regression line as a rubber band that you stretch through a cloud of points. Each data point pulls the line towards itself. The method looks for the position in which the sum of all (squared) pulling forces is smallest, hence the name ordinary least squares (OLS).
Why squared? There are two reasons. The signs disappear (otherwise deviations above and below the line cancel each other out), and large deviations are penalised more heavily (a point 4 units off pulls 16 times as hard as a point 1 unit off).
The plot shows the cloud of points and the line; the red lines show exactly what OLS minimises: the vertical residuals between observation and prediction.

set.seed(2)
rubber_demo <- tibble(
  x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
  y = c(2.5, 2.8, 4.5, 4.0, 5.8, 6.5, 7.2)
)
m_rubber <- lm(y ~ x, data = rubber_demo)
rubber_demo$y_hat <- predict(m_rubber)

rubber_demo |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = y_hat),
               color = "#d62728", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(m_rubber)[[1]],
              slope     = coef(m_rubber)[[2]],
              color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "#1f77b4") +
  labs(x = "Predictor x", y = "Outcome y",
       title = "OLS: what exactly is minimised?",
       caption = "Black line = regression line · red lines = residuals.\nOLS looks for the line for which the sum of the SQUARED red lines is smallest.")







Interpretation. Each blue point pulls the line a little towards itself, like a rubber band. The line is the unique position in which the sum of the squared red lines is as small as possible. If you turned or shifted the line even slightly, this sum would immediately become larger.
The closed-form solution for the slope looks like this:
\[\hat{\beta} = \frac{\text{Cov}(x, y)}{\text{Var}(x)}\]
Read it as: “how strongly x and y vary together, relative to how strongly x varies on its own.” R calculates this in microseconds; the value in the column B of the output is exactly this number.

9.2.2 Fitting the model with linear_regression()

Question: How much of Islamophobia can be explained by populism alone?

m_simple <- allbus |>
  linear_regression(islamophobia ~ populism, weights = wghtpew)

m_simple

Linear Regression: islamophobia ~ populism [Weighted]
  R2 = 0.165, adj.R2 = 0.165, F(1, 1901) = 375.73, p < 0.001 ***, N = 1903
Use summary() for detailed output.


Interpretation of the compact output. Three numbers summarise the model:

R²: the share of the variance in Islamophobia that populism alone explains. With one explanatory variable, \(R^2 = r^2\), the square of the Pearson correlation from Chapter 7.
F (model): tests whether \(R^2\) differs significantly from 0.
N: how many cases entered the model.

summary() gives you the full table with intercept and slope:

  --------------------------
  VIF > 10 (Tolerance < 0.1) indicates problematic collinearity.

Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05


The Coefficients table contains the two key numbers:


(Intercept): the value of Islamophobia that the model predicts when populism = 0. Mathematically, this is where the line crosses the y-axis.

populism: the slope, “by how much does Islamophobia change when populism increases by one unit?” This is exactly \(\hat{\beta}\) from the formula above.

9.2.3 Drawing the regression line by hand with coef() and geom_abline()

Unlike the quick-and-dirty geom_smooth(method = "lm"), we extract the coefficients directly from the model and draw the line with geom_abline(). This makes the link between model and visualisation visible:

intercept <- coef(m_simple)[["(Intercept)"]]
slope     <- coef(m_simple)[["populism"]]

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(populism)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = populism, y = islamophobia)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.15, color = "#1f77b4",
              width = 0.05, height = 0.05) +
  geom_abline(intercept = intercept, slope = slope,
              color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Populism (1–5, reverse-coded)",
       y = "Islamophobia (1–7)",
       title = "Simple regression: Islamophobia ~ populism",
       caption = sprintf("Line from the model: y = %.2f + %.2f · x · ALLBUS 2023, weighted",
                         intercept, slope))







Interpretation. The black line is exactly the OLS solution of the lm model above, not a new fit by ggplot2. The slope in the plot equals the coefficient in the output table, and the point where the line crosses the y-axis equals the intercept. The caption gives you the equation of the line in one sentence: “Islamophobia = intercept + slope · populism.”
geom_smooth(method = "lm") also fits an lm model internally and draws its line, but the model itself stays invisible. In publications you will find both approaches, depending on the context.

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
9.3 Categorical predictors: dummy coding
The simple regression had a continuous predictor: populism on a 1–5 scale. As soon as you move on to multiple regression in the next section, categorical predictors also enter the model: education with three levels, region as East/West, sex as male/female/non-binary. Regression models, however, calculate with numbers. How does that work?
R solves this with a technique called dummy coding, and you need to understand it to read the output table correctly.

9.3.1 The idea: k levels become k − 1 dummies
For a factor with k levels, R internally creates k − 1 new 0/1 variables (the dummies). One original level becomes the reference category: it does not appear as a separate row in the output but is absorbed into the intercept.
For educ_cat with three levels, the internal coding looks like this:


Original value
educ_catmedium
educ_cathigh



low (reference)
0
0


medium
1
0


high
0
1



Figure 9.1 shows this for rows 1, 2 and 8 of allbus: the tower educ_cat becomes two 0/1 towers, and there is none for low.





Figure 9.1: From the factor educ_cat, R internally builds one 0/1 tower each for medium and for high. The first level, low, is the reference and gets no tower of its own.


Each respondent gets a pair of 0/1 values. “Low education” means that both dummies are 0: the person is the reference. The model then estimates two coefficients:


educ_catmedium = “difference between medium and low education”


educ_cathigh = “difference between high and low education”


The reference itself has no coefficient; by definition it would be 0. This matters for the interpretation: each dummy row in the output means “difference from the reference group”, not “absolute value”.
Stop and think. Which dummies does R create for sex with the levels MALE, FEMALE and NON-BINARY?






TipAnswer






levels(allbus$sex)

[1] "MALE"       "FEMALE"     "NON-BINARY"


MALE is the first level and therefore the reference. R creates two dummies, sexFEMALE and sexNON-BINARY; exactly these two rows appear in the coefficient table in Section 9.4.




9.3.2 Which level becomes the reference? Changing it with fct_relevel()

R takes the first level of the factor. For educ_cat this is low (this is how the factor was defined in the setup: 1:2=1 [low]; 3=2 [medium]; 4:5=3 [high]). If you want a different basis for comparison, for example because you want to treat medium education as “normal” and “high/low” as deviations from it, change the order with fct_relevel():

allbus <- allbus |>
  mutate(educ_cat = fct_relevel(educ_cat, "medium"))

The output would then show educ_catlow and educ_cathigh, both now compared with medium.
Important: R², the model F and all predictions stay the same. Only the interpretation of the individual coefficients shifts. So the choice of reference is a matter of interpretation.






Importantmariposa tip: The factors argument





Since version 0.6.2 you can control how linear_regression() and logistic_regression() treat factor predictors:


factors = "dummy" (default): as described above, k − 1 dummy contrasts. Consistent with base R lm().

factors = "numeric": the factor is converted into its integer codes (1, 2, 3, …) and treated as numeric; you get one slope instead of k − 1 contrasts. This reproduces SPSS REGRESSION with ordinally coded variables.

The choice between the two is an assumption about the level of measurement. Do you treat education as ordinal with equal distances (the step from level 2 to level 3 is the same as from level 1 to level 2 → numeric)? Or as purely categorical with unknown distances between the levels (dummy)? In this book we use the dummy default because it is methodologically more conservative: it does not impose the assumption of equal distances.

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
9.4 Multiple linear regression with linear_regression()

The simple regression had one predictor: populism. But Islamophobia probably does not depend only on populism. Education, age, region and sex also play a role, and they are related to each other. Multiple linear regression puts all of them into the model at the same time and shows what remains for each predictor when the others are controlled for. It is the most important method in quantitative social research.
Instead of a line in two dimensions, you now look for a plane (two predictors) or a higher-dimensional surface (more predictors) that fits the cloud of points. Each predictor gets its own coefficient, and this coefficient reads: “If this variable increases by one unit while all other variables are held constant, y changes by this value.” “Held constant” is the decisive point: this is how multiple regression isolates independent effects.






NoteBackground: What does “controlled for” mean?





Take a numerical example. You first calculate a bivariate regression (islamophobia ~ education) and get a coefficient of, say, −0.20: higher education → lower Islamophobia. Then you add populism to the model (islamophobia ~ education + populism), and the education coefficient shrinks to, say, −0.13.
As an arrow diagram:
                          indirect (−0.07)
                ┌─────► Populism ───────┐
                │                       ▼
   Education ───┤                     Islamophobia
                │                       ▲
                └──── direct (−0.13) ───┘

   Total effect of education: −0.20 = direct (−0.13) + indirect (−0.07)
The difference of −0.07 is the part of the education effect that actually runs through populism: people with higher education are on average less populist, and populism explains Islamophobia better than education alone. What remains after controlling for populism (−0.13) is the direct education effect, which is not mediated by populism. This breakdown into direct and mediated effects is what multivariate modelling adds.
Note: the numbers here are illustrative. The exact breakdown depends on the model specification (for example, on whether education enters as a continuous variable or as a dummy-coded categorical one, see Section 9.3). The principle of splitting the effect into a direct and an indirect part stays the same.



The most important number for the overall quality of the model is R²: the share of the variance in the dependent variable that the model explains. An R² of 0.30 means that your predictors explain 30% of the variation in the dependent variable; 70% remain unexplained (by variables that are not in your model, by measurement error, by chance). In social research, an R² above 0.30 is already a clear finding; near-perfect explanation with an R² close to 1 exists only in the natural sciences. Attitudes depend on very many influences, from personality and experience to social contexts, and no model can capture them all.
Question: Which variables explain Islamophobia best: education, age, region, sex, populism?

model <- allbus |>
  linear_regression(
    formula = islamophobia ~ educ_cat + age + eastwest + sex + populism,
    weights = wghtpew
  )

model

Use summary() for detailed output.


The compact output shows R², adjusted R², the F-test of the overall model and N. This is good for a quick overview: “Does the model fit at all?” summary() gives you the full SPSS-style table with all coefficients; you need it as soon as you look at individual predictors:

Interpretation. The Coefficients table is the core of the output:

B: unstandardised coefficients. For continuous predictors: “If x increases by one unit, y changes by B units.” For dummy variables (e.g. educ_cathigh): “difference from the reference group.”
Std. Error and t: the precision of the estimate.
Beta: standardised coefficients. They do not depend on the scale of the variables and can therefore be compared directly between predictors. They are the best guide to which predictor has the strongest relative effect.
Sig.: p-values.
95% CI Lower / Upper: the confidence interval for B (SPSS: /STATISTICS CI). If it excludes 0, the coefficient is significant at the 5% level.

Below it is the Collinearity Statistics table with tolerance and VIF for each predictor; more on this in Section 9.5. In the header at the top there is a note about age: because the variable still carries value labels from SPSS, it enters the model with its numeric values as a continuous predictor, as in SPSS REGRESSION. This is what we want for age. Only if you want to model a labelled variable as categories do you convert it to a factor with to_label() first.
Note also N = 1881: only cases with valid values on all variables enter the model (listwise deletion). Because islamophobia and populism come from different split modules (see Chapter 7), just over a third of the sample remains.
In our model, populism is the strongest predictor with a Beta of 0.32: people with more populist attitudes are also more Islamophobic.
For education, the dummy coding now shows something interesting that the old reading “education has a negative effect” had hidden. Medium education hardly differs from low education (educ_catmedium: Beta ≈ 0.00, p = .88, not significant). Only high education clearly lowers Islamophobia (educ_cathigh: Beta = −0.15, p < .001). So there is no even gradient across the three levels; the education effect comes from high education. This is an important substantive distinction, and only dummy coding makes it visible.
The other categorical predictors are read in the same way:


eastwestNEW FEDERAL STATES (Beta = 0.09, p < .001): respondents from the new federal states are more Islamophobic than respondents from the old federal states (= reference).

sexFEMALE (Beta = 0.04, p = .03): a weak positive effect for women compared with men (= reference).

sexNON-BINARY (Beta = −0.02, p = .43): not significant; but be careful, this is a very small group in the ALLBUS, and the estimate is unstable.

Continuous predictors keep the familiar interpretation: age (Beta = 0.30, p < .001) has a positive effect; older respondents have higher values.
The model explains a share of the variance in Islamophobia. How large is this share, and how large is the unexplained remainder? Here is the R² from the output, made visible:

library(broom)
r2 <- broom::glance(model)$r.squared

tibble(
  share = factor(c("explained by model (R²)", "unexplained (residuals)"),
                 levels = c("unexplained (residuals)", "explained by model (R²)")),
  value = c(r2, 1 - r2)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = "", fill = share)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", value * 100)),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`explained by model (R²)` = "#1f77b4",
                               `unexplained (residuals)` = "grey60"),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = sprintf("How much variance does the model explain? R² = %.2f", r2),
       caption = "Typical for the social sciences: an R² of about 0.20–0.30 is a clear finding.")







Interpretation. The blue share is the finding: “this much of the variation in Islamophobia can be explained by our five predictors.” The grey remainder is due to all variables that are not in the model, plus measurement error and chance.






NoteBackground: B or Beta?





The two coefficients answer different questions:

B (unstandardised) answers “by how many scale points does y change?” It can be interpreted in the original units of measurement: “One education level higher → 0.17 scale points less Islamophobia.” This is easy to grasp, but it cannot be compared between predictors measured on different scales.
Beta (standardised) answers “which predictor has the strongest relative effect?” All variables are brought to the same scale (mean 0, SD 1). Beta can be compared within one model, but not between models or samples (the standardisation depends on the sample SD).

Rule of thumb: use B for the substantive interpretation and Beta for ranking the predictors.



A complete regression table in a report contains B, SE, β, 95% CI, p-value, R², adjusted R², the model F, df and N. If someone asks about multicollinearity, you should have VIF and tolerance to hand; summary(model) gives you both in the table Collinearity Statistics. These values belong in the methods section or the appendix.

9.4.1 Comparing models with anova()

If you want to test whether an additional predictor improves the model significantly, you fit both models and compare them with anova().
mariposa’s linear_regression() returns an object that inherits directly from lm (class = c("linear_regression", "lm")). You do not need to extract anything: standard R functions such as anova(), predict(), coef(), confint() and vcov() work directly with the model:

# Both models must use the same set of cases, otherwise anova() refuses.
allbus_model <- allbus |>
  drop_na(islamophobia, educ_cat, age, eastwest, sex, populism)

m_base <- allbus_model |>
  linear_regression(islamophobia ~ educ_cat + age + eastwest + sex,
                    weights = wghtpew)
m_full <- allbus_model |>
  linear_regression(islamophobia ~ educ_cat + age + eastwest + sex + populism,
                    weights = wghtpew)

anova(m_base, m_full)   # F-test of the incremental explained variance

SPSS → R: Hierarchical regression. In SPSS you click through several Block steps in Linear Regression and get the model comparison statistics for free. In R you fit each model separately and compare them explicitly. This takes more code, but every step is visible.

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
9.5 Checking multicollinearity: VIF
Imagine a jury in which two members always vote the same way. From their votes you can no longer tell who holds which opinion; the information is redundant. The same happens in a regression with two strongly correlated predictors: both contribute almost the same information, and the model can no longer separate their individual contributions. Coefficients become unstable, standard errors inflate and confidence intervals become wider. Your estimates become less precise, without this showing in the model R².

9.5.1 The formula is surprisingly simple
The VIF (variance inflation factor) puts a number on multicollinearity:
\[\text{VIF}_i = \frac{1}{1 - R^2_i}\]
where \(R^2_i\) comes from an auxiliary regression in which exactly this predictor \(x_i\) is predicted by all the others.
Read it as: “by what factor is the variance of this coefficient higher because the predictor is partly explained by the others?” Two examples:


\(R^2_i = 0\) (the predictor cannot be explained by any of the others) → VIF = \(1 / (1-0) = 1\): no inflation.

\(R^2_i = 0.9\) (90% of the predictor can be explained by the others) → VIF = \(1 / (1-0.9) = 10\): the standard error is \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\) times larger than ideal.

The tolerance is the reciprocal: \(\text{Tolerance} = 1/\text{VIF} = 1 - R^2_i\).

9.5.2 Rules of thumb


VIF
Tolerance
Assessment



≈ 1
≈ 1
no multicollinearity


2 – 5
0.20 – 0.50
not critical


5 – 10
0.10 – 0.20
warning threshold: check


> 10
< 0.10
problematic: take action



9.5.3 Calculating the VIF by hand in three steps
mariposa gives you VIF and tolerance ready-made in summary(model). To see where this number comes from, you calculate the VIF once yourself, exactly according to the formula above, for one predictor in three visible steps. Example: the VIF for populism.
Step 1: auxiliary regression. We make populism the dependent variable and let all other predictors of the main model predict it. Important: this must be done on the same set of cases as the main model, so we use allbus_model from the model comparison above. With the full allbus, respondents without any value for Islamophobia would also enter, and the VIF would refer to a different sample from the model.

aux_model <- lm(populism ~ educ_cat + age + eastwest + sex,
                data = allbus_model, weights = wghtpew)

Step 2: read the R² of the auxiliary regression. How well do the other variables predict populism?

r2 <- summary(aux_model)$r.squared
r2

[1] 0.1703667


About 17% of the variance of populism can be explained by the other predictors.
Step 3: apply the VIF formula.

vif_populism <- 1 / (1 - r2)
vif_populism

[1] 1.205352


Result: VIF ≈ 1.21, far below the warning threshold of 5. So populism has no multicollinearity problem with the other predictors. To cross-check, look at the table Collinearity Statistics of summary(model) above: it shows exactly the same value for populism (VIF = 1.205, tolerance = 0.830). The calculation by hand and mariposa arrive at the same number because both apply the same definition to the same set of cases.






Importantmariposa tip: Collinearity without an extra package





summary() of a linear_regression() model contains VIF and tolerance for each predictor, the SPSS equivalent of /STATISTICS COLLIN. If you do not need the table, hide it with summary(model, collinearity = FALSE). As a tibble, the values are in the columns Tolerance and VIF of model$coef_table.



For the other predictors you repeat the same three steps, each with an adjusted auxiliary formula: age ~ populism + educ_cat + eastwest + sex for the VIF of age, eastwest ~ populism + educ_cat + age + sex for region, and so on. In Exercise 2 at the end of the chapter you work through this for another predictor.






NoteBackground: Categorical predictors and VIF





For a factor such as educ_cat (three levels → two dummy variables, see Section 9.3), each dummy variable gets its own VIF; this is also how summary(model) reports it (educ_catmedium 1.79, educ_cathigh 2.12). It is normal that the two education dummies have somewhat higher values: anyone who is not “medium” is very likely to be “high”. Specialised functions such as car::vif() (from the package car) calculate the generalised VIF (GVIF) for factors instead. This is a single statistic per original variable, and its column GVIF^(1/(2·Df)) can be compared directly with the VIF rules of thumb. For models like ours (all VIFs well below 2.5) the difference hardly matters; for models close to the warning threshold it is worth checking the GVIF.

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
9.6 Residual diagnostics by hand
A linear regression makes four key assumptions about what remains after fitting the model: the residuals (observed minus predicted y). With large samples the model is usually robust to violations of these assumptions, but every methods report should check them visually. The standard diagnostics consist of four plots. We build them by hand from the mariposa model with ggplot2 and combine them with patchwork.

9.6.1 Why not plot(model)?
Base R offers plot() for every lm object, and because mariposa models inherit from lm, plot(model) works directly: four diagnostic plots in one line. It is quick, but the plots look like 1995 and hardly fit the style of the book. With broom::augment() you instead extract the model residuals as a clean tibble; from then on it is ordinary ggplot2.

9.6.2 The four assumptions and their diagnostic plots







Plot
checks
what you want to see



Residuals vs Fitted
linearity
points scattered randomly around the zero line


Normal Q-Q
normality of the residuals
points lie on the diagonal


Scale-Location
homoscedasticity
constant spread across all fitted values


Residuals vs Leverage
outliers / leverage points
no isolated points with high leverage



9.6.3 Extracting the model residuals with augment()


# install once: install.packages("broom")
library(broom)

diag_df <- model |> augment()
glimpse(diag_df)

For each observation, the tibble contains, among other things:


.fitted: the model prediction

.resid: the residuals (observed − predicted)

.std.resid: standardised residuals

.hat: leverage (how unusual a case’s predictor values are)

.cooksd: Cook’s distance (the overall influence of a case)

Figure 9.3 shows the first two rows of diag_df; they are the respondents from rows 1 and 6 of Figure 9.2. augment() places the new columns next to the model data: .fitted is the calculation with the coefficients B from summary(model), and .resid is the observed value minus this prediction.





Figure 9.3: The first two rows of diag_df, rounded to three decimal places; eastwest and sex as well as .sigma, .cooksd and .std.resid are not shown. In row 1 the dummies of eastwest and sex are all 0: the respondent is a man from the old federal states, and both are reference levels.



9.6.4 Building the four plots

p_rf <- diag_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "black", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals",
       title = "Residuals vs Fitted",
       subtitle = "Linearity")

p_qq <- diag_df |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = .std.resid)) +
  geom_qq(alpha = 0.2, color = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_qq_line(color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles (normal distribution)",
       y = "Standardised residuals",
       title = "Normal Q-Q",
       subtitle = "Distribution of the residuals")

p_sl <- diag_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = sqrt(abs(.std.resid)))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "black", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = expression(sqrt("|Standardised residuals|")),
       title = "Scale-Location",
       subtitle = "Homoscedasticity")

p_rl <- diag_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .hat, y = .std.resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "black", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Leverage", y = "Standardised residuals",
       title = "Residuals vs Leverage",
       subtitle = "Outliers / leverage points")

(p_rf + p_qq) / (p_sl + p_rl)







Interpretation. With N ≈ 1900 (as here), visible deviations are the exception; the LOESS lines should run largely flat around 0 (or horizontally in the Scale-Location plot). If the Q-Q plot deviates clearly from the diagonal at the ends, the assumption of normally distributed residuals is violated. With large samples this is usually unproblematic thanks to the central limit theorem. To check individual points with high leverage, use diag_df |> filter(.cooksd > 4/n()); Cook’s distance values above 1 clearly call for a closer look.
