title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
9.7 ANOVA with several factors
The one-way ANOVA from Chapter 7 tests one grouping factor. In practice you often want to test several factors at the same time and, above all, whether a factor has a different effect in different subgroups (interaction). Methodologically, ANOVA is a special case of regression with categorical predictors. The logic is the same as in Section 9.4; only the presentation is more compact and tailored to comparisons of group means.

9.7.1 Two-way ANOVA with factorial_anova()

Question: Is the education effect on Islamophobia the same in East and West, or does it differ?

allbus |>
  factorial_anova(islamophobia,
                  between = c(educ_cat, eastwest),
                  weights = wghtpew)

Factorial ANOVA (2-Way): islamophobia by educ_cat, eastwest [Weighted], N = 3274
  educ_cat:          F(2, 3268) = 136.964, p < 0.001 ***, eta2p = 0.077
  eastwest:          F(1, 3268) = 74.259, p < 0.001 ***, eta2p = 0.022
  educ_cat:eastwest: F(2, 3268) = 1.686, p = 0.185, eta2p = 0.001
Use summary() for detailed output.


Interpretation. You get three F-tests: one for each main effect (education, region) and one for the interaction (education × region), each with the partial η² (eta2p), the share of variance that the effect explains when the other effects are partialled out. A significant interaction means that the education effect on Islamophobia differs between East and West. This is also called a moderating relationship: region moderates the education effect. If the interaction is not significant, the two effects are additive: each works in a similar way in both regions.
Here both main effects are highly significant, education with a partial η² of .077 and region with .022. The interaction, by contrast, is not significant with F(2, 3268) = 1.69, p = .19 and a partial η² of .001: the education effect is similar in East and West. summary() gives you the full SPSS table Tests of Between-Subjects Effects with sums of squares, weighted cell means and Levene’s test.
An interaction is easiest to understand visually. Imagine two line charts with education on the x-axis, Islamophobia on the y-axis and one line per region:

Parallel lines → no interaction effect. The education effect is equally strong in East and West; the lines are only at different heights (main effect of region).
Non-parallel lines (crossing or with different slopes) → interaction effect. The education effect is stronger or weaker in the East than in the West.

If you want to communicate a finding after a significant interaction, such a line chart (factor 1 on x, factor 2 as colour or line type) is the established format.

9.7.2 Making the interaction visible
You calculate this plot for the ANOVA model above yourself, with the tools from Chapters 5 and 6:

allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(educ_cat), !is.na(eastwest)) |>
  summarise(
    m  = w_mean(islamophobia, weights = wghtpew),
    se = w_se(islamophobia, weights = wghtpew),
    .by = c(educ_cat, eastwest)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = educ_cat, y = m, color = eastwest, group = eastwest)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = m - 1.96 * se, ymax = m + 1.96 * se),
                  linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Education group", y = "Islamophobia (mean)",
       color = "Region",
       title = "Interaction: education × region",
       caption = "ALLBUS 2023, weighted with wghtpew (95% CI)")







Interpretation. The lines for East and West run almost parallel. The East is higher at all three education levels (main effect of region), and in both regions Islamophobia drops markedly, above all from medium to high education (main effect of education). Between “medium” and “high” the line for the East falls slightly more steeply, but this small deviation from parallel is within the range of chance: the interaction term of the ANOVA above is not significant (p = .19). So region and education act additively.
Lines from sample data are never exactly parallel. The interaction term only becomes significant when the deviation is larger than chance can plausibly explain, and the F-test makes exactly this judgement for you. The plot and the test therefore belong together: the plot shows you what a possible difference looks like, and the test shows whether it holds up.

9.7.3 ANCOVA with ancova()

Analysis of covariance combines ANOVA and regression. You have a categorical grouping factor (e.g. education) and a continuous covariate (e.g. age). ANCOVA tests the group difference after the influence of the covariate has been removed.
Question: Do education groups differ in Islamophobia when age is held constant?

allbus |>
  ancova(islamophobia,
         between = educ_cat, covariate = age,
         weights = wghtpew)

ANCOVA: islamophobia by educ_cat, covariate: age [Weighted], N = 3268
  age (covariate): F(1, 3264) = 275.550, p < 0.001 ***, eta2p = 0.078
  educ_cat:        F(2, 3264) = 136.643, p < 0.001 ***, eta2p = 0.077
Use summary() for detailed output.


Interpretation. The group effect of education is reported adjusted for the age effect. Both are highly significant, and each explains a similar share of variance (partial η² just under .08 each). ANCOVA is useful when a known confounder varies between the groups and you want to isolate its influence. It links pure ANOVA (categorical predictors) and regression (continuous predictors).
You can see how much the adjustment changes the picture in the estimated marginal means from summary(): the group means that would result if all groups had the same average age.

allbus |>
  ancova(islamophobia,
         between = educ_cat, covariate = age,
         weights = wghtpew) |>
  summary()

So part of the apparent education effect was an age effect: respondents with a low school-leaving certificate are older on average, and older people are more Islamophobic. This matches the educ_catmedium coefficient of the multiple regression above.
Figure 9.4 puts both sets of means on the same scale: low moves from 4.68 to 4.41 and is then almost level with medium, while high rises from 3.48 to 3.60.

In the table Parameter Estimates, ancova(), like SPSS UNIANOVA, uses the last category as the reference (here “high”, marked “0 (a)”). linear_regression(), like lm(), uses the first category (“low”). title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
9.8 Logistic regression with logistic_regression()

Linear regression is only suitable for interval-scaled dependent variables, that is, quantities with an ordered, continuous range of values. What do you do if your outcome has only two values? For example “votes Green / does not vote Green”, “has a university degree / does not have one”, “has high Islamophobia / has low Islamophobia”?
Here linear regression fails. It might predict that a person votes Green with a probability of 1.3, which obviously makes no sense (probabilities lie between 0 and 1). The solution is logistic regression. Instead of the value of the dependent variable itself, it models the probability that the event occurs, and a clever transformation (the logistic function) makes sure that the predictions always stay between 0 and 1.
The coefficients can be interpreted as odds ratios: the factor by which the odds (the ratio of occurrence to non-occurrence) change when the predictor increases by one unit.
Three related quantities appear in logistic regression:

Probability (p): the familiar quantity between 0 and 1. “p = 0.25 → 25% probability.”


Odds = p / (1 − p): the ratio of occurrence to non-occurrence. “p = 0.25 → odds = 0.25 / 0.75 = 1/3.” This reads as “the odds are 1 to 3”.

Logit = log(odds): the logarithm of the odds. It ranges from −∞ to +∞ and makes it possible to model the dependent variable linearly with predictors.

Logistic regression estimates the coefficients in logit space: a predictor that is one unit higher changes the logit linearly. To make this interpretable, mariposa transforms the coefficients into odds ratios (= exp(logit coefficient)). An odds ratio > 1 means: higher values of the predictor → higher probability. An odds ratio < 1 means: higher values → lower probability.
Why the logit transformation is the central trick of logistic regression is easiest to see in a plot. The function that translates the logit back into a probability is an S-curve (sigmoid):

tibble(
  logit = seq(-6, 6, length.out = 200),
  probability = exp(logit) / (1 + exp(logit))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = logit, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1f77b4", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Logit (modelled linearly by the predictors)",
       y = "Probability p",
       title = "From logit to probability: the sigmoid curve")







Interpretation. In logit space (x-axis), any value is possible, from −∞ to +∞. The sigmoid function always squeezes the result (y-axis) between 0 and 1. At logit = 0, p = 0.5 (where the dotted reference lines cross). Logit = +2 corresponds to p ≈ 0.88, logit = −2 to p ≈ 0.12. At the ends the curve flattens out: the same increase in the logit changes the probability by different amounts, depending on where you start on the curve. This is why interpreting odds ratios (see below) requires care.
For our mini study we construct a dummy variable: “high Islamophobia” (scale value ≥ 4).






Warning



Caution: Dichotomising continuous variables. Shrinking a 1–7 scale to 0/1 is a methodological decision; nothing technical requires it. You lose information (loss of power), and the choice of threshold (median? a cut-off based on theory?) is always open to criticism. Dichotomise only if the research question suggests it (“who falls into the upper half?”), and not because a logistic regression seems simpler. A linear regression on the original scale is usually the methodologically cleaner choice.


Question: Which characteristics distinguish respondents with high Islamophobia from the others?

allbus_dummy <- allbus |>
  mutate(islamophobia_high = as.integer(islamophobia >= 4))

model_log <- allbus_dummy |>
  logistic_regression(
    formula = islamophobia_high ~ educ_cat + age + eastwest + sex,
    weights = wghtpew
  )

model_log

Logistic Regression: islamophobia_high ~ educ_cat + age + eastwest + sex [P(islamophobia_high = 1)] [Weighted]
  Nagelkerke R2 = 0.206, chi2(6) = 549.01, p < 0.001 ***, Accuracy = 68.4%, N = 3265
Use summary() for detailed output.


Interpretation. The compact output shows:


[P(islamophobia_high = 1)] in the title: which probability is modelled, namely that of the value 1, i.e. high Islamophobia.
Nagelkerke R²: a pseudo-R², roughly comparable with the R² of a linear regression.
χ² of the model: the likelihood ratio test against the null model.
Accuracy: the share of correctly classified cases.







NoteBackground: Accuracy is only one classification measure





Accuracy = (true positives + true negatives) / total. But it does not tell you where the model fails. With unbalanced classes (e.g. 90% “low”, 10% “high”), a model that predicts every case as “low” already reaches an accuracy of 90% without recognising a single “high” case. Two complementary measures are:

Sensitivity (recall): the share of actual “high” cases that are correctly recognised.
Specificity: the share of actual “low” cases that are correctly recognised.

Both are already in the Classification Table of summary(): the column % Correct in row 1 is the sensitivity (here 67.4%), and in row 0 it is the specificity (69.3%). So our model recognises both groups about equally well.



You again get the full table with coefficients, odds ratios and confidence intervals with summary():

summary(model_log)

Interpretation. The table Variables in the Equation is the core of the output; the odds ratios are in the column Exp(B). Odds ratios > 1 increase the odds of the outcome, odds ratios < 1 decrease them. Compared with low education, high education reduces the odds of high Islamophobia to about a third (OR = 0.33). Respondents from the new federal states have almost twice the odds (OR = 1.89), and each year of age increases the odds by just under 3% (OR = 1.028). As in the linear regression, medium and low education do not differ (p = .86). At the very top, Dependent Variable Encoding documents how the dependent variable is coded internally. This matters if your outcome is not coded 0/1: logistic_regression() accepts any variable with exactly two values (such as 1/2 codes, labelled, factor or logical) and, like SPSS, models the probability of the higher value (for factors the second level, for logical variables TRUE).






Warning



Caution: An odds ratio is not a probability factor. A common misunderstanding is that an OR of 2 doubles the probability. It does not. A concrete example with a 2 × 2 table shows why:



Outcome = 1
Outcome = 0
Total
Probability



Men
25
75
100
25/100 = 0.25


Women
40
60
100
40/100 = 0.40




Odds for men = 25/75 = 1/3
Odds for women = 40/60 = 2/3
Odds ratio (women vs. men) = (2/3) / (1/3) = 2.0

The OR of 2.0 says: “Women have twice the odds.” But the probability only rises from 0.25 to 0.40, that is by 60%, not by 100%. For small probabilities (≤ 0.10), OR ≈ probability factor; for large ones the discrepancy becomes noticeable.
If you show the same 2×2 table as stacked bars, you see the probabilities directly:

tibble(
  group   = factor(rep(c("men", "women"), each = 2),
                   levels = c("men", "women")),
  outcome = factor(rep(c("Outcome = 1", "Outcome = 0"), 2),
                   levels = c("Outcome = 0", "Outcome = 1")),
  n       = c(25, 75, 40, 60)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = n, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill", width = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", n, n)),
            position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5),
            color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Outcome = 1` = "#d62728",
                               `Outcome = 0` = "grey60"),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share",
       title = "OR = 2.0 in pictures: the probability rises from 25% to 40%",
       caption = "Increase in probability = 15 percentage points (= 60% relative), not 100%.")







Interpretation. The red share is the probability, and it rises from 25% for men to 40% for women. This is an increase in probability of 60%, although the odds double. If you want to say in your discussion that “factor X increases the probability by Y percentage points”, calculate concrete probabilities rather than paraphrasing ORs: with predict(model, type = "response") or, for the average effect of each predictor, with marginal_effects() (see below).



9.8.1 Translating odds ratios into probabilities: marginal_effects()

Odds ratios are hard to communicate (see the Caution box above). If you want to say by how many percentage points the probability changes, you need average marginal effects (AME). An AME is the average change in the predicted probability: for a factor compared with the reference category, for a continuous variable per unit. In Stata this is margins, dydx(*); mariposa calculates it directly from the model with marginal_effects():

model_log |> marginal_effects()

Average Marginal Effects: islamophobia_high ~ educ_cat + age + eastwest + sex [Weighted]
  educ_cat: medium vs. low: AME = -0.004, p = 0.861
  educ_cat: high vs. low: AME = -0.252, p < 0.001 ***
  age: AME = 0.006, p < 0.001 ***
  eastwest: NEW FEDERAL STATES vs. OLD FEDERAL STATES: AME = 0.134, p < 0.001 ***
  sex: FEMALE vs. MALE: AME = 0.028, p = 0.086
  sex: NON-BINARY vs. MALE: AME = -0.297, p = 0.139
AME = average change in predicted probability. Use summary() for detailed output.


Interpretation. Now the numbers are on the probability scale:

High vs. low education: −0.25. High education lowers the probability of high Islamophobia by 25 percentage points on average.
New vs. old federal states: +0.13. In the East the probability is 13 percentage points higher.
Age: +0.006 per year. Ten years of age therefore add about 6 percentage points.

Figure 9.5 shows how marginal_effects() arrives at −0.252. For each person in the model, R predicts the probability twice, once with low and once with high education; age, region and sex stay as they are. The weighted mean of these differences is the AME.





Figure 9.5: The first three people in the model: educ_cat is set once to low and once to high for each of them, and predict() calculates the probabilities with type = "response". The mean of the differences is taken over all people in the model, weighted with wghtpew. The differences are rounded to two decimal places.


You can write exactly these sentences in a term paper without misinterpretation. Statements about odds (“high education reduces the odds to a third”) are different: many readers instinctively read them as probabilities. summary() shows standard errors, z values and confidence intervals of the AMEs (via the delta method). For a linear model you do not need marginal_effects(): there, the coefficient B already is the marginal effect.

9.8.2 The sigmoid curve with real data
Here is the abstract sigmoid curve from above, now with data. We plot the probability of islamophobia_high = 1 as a function of populism. The 0/1 points (made visible with jitter) are real respondents; the black curve is a logistic regression with populism as the only predictor:

allbus_dummy |>
  filter(!is.na(populism), !is.na(islamophobia_high)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = populism, y = islamophobia_high)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.08, color = "#1f77b4",
              width = 0.05, height = 0.06) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm",
              method.args = list(family = "binomial"),
              color = "black", linewidth = 1.2, se = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1),
                     labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Populism (1–5, reverse-coded)",
       y = "Probability (Islamophobia ≥ 4)",
       title = "The sigmoid curve with real data",
       caption = "Points (jittered) = individual respondents (top = islamophobia_high = 1) · curve = logistic regression")







Interpretation. At low populism (left), the probability of high Islamophobia is below 30%. At high populism (right) it rises to over 80%. The shape (flat, then steep, then flat again) is exactly the sigmoid curve from the abstract plot above, now filled with real ALLBUS data. This is what logistic regression models.

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
9.9 Communicating findings graphically
The models are fitted and the coefficients interpreted; what remains is communicating the results. In a term paper, an article or a presentation, a regression table is the standard; a plot makes the result readable at a glance.

9.9.1 Coefficient plots: visualising regression results with tidy()

The most effective format is a coefficient plot: a point for the estimate, a line for the confidence interval and a vertical zero line as a reference. Coefficient plots have become standard in empirical political science and social science (see Gelman & Hill 2007; King et al. 2000). They do not replace the full table in the appendix, but they also make the result accessible to readers without statistical training. This is the plot for our main model, taken directly from the lm object via broom::tidy():

library(broom)

model |>
  tidy(conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>           # the constant is not of interest here
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = fct_reorder(term, estimate),
             xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Coefficient with 95% CI", y = NULL,
       title = "What explains Islamophobia in Germany in 2023?",
       caption = "Multiple linear regression · ALLBUS 2023, weighted\nValues from broom::tidy(model)")







Interpretation. At a glance you see how strong the effect of each predictor is: populism has the largest positive effect, education the largest negative one. Confidence intervals that cross the dashed zero line are statistically uncertain: the effect does not differ clearly from 0.






NoteBackground: What does broom::tidy() do?





tidy() takes the lm object and puts the coefficients table into an ordinary tibble with the columns term, estimate, std.error, statistic and p.value, plus conf.low/conf.high with conf.int = TRUE. This makes every model output ready for ggplot2 without you typing in any values. broom belongs to the tidymodels family and is the de facto standard link between statistical models and tidyverse workflows.




9.9.2 Combining several plots with patchwork: +, / and |

patchwork is the modern replacement for gridExtra::grid.arrange(). You save plots as objects and combine them with +, / and |:

p1 <- allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = islamophobia, weight = wghtpew)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#2563eb", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution", x = "Islamophobia", y = "Frequency")

p2 <- allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(eastwest)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = eastwest, y = islamophobia, fill = eastwest)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "East vs. West", x = NULL, y = "Islamophobia") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p3 <- allbus |>
  filter(!is.na(islamophobia), !is.na(populism)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = populism, y = islamophobia)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, color = "#1f77b4", width = 0.05, height = 0.05) +
  geom_abline(intercept = intercept, slope = slope,
              color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "With populism", x = "Populism", y = NULL)

(p1 | p2) / p3







p1 | p2 places plots side by side, / places them one below the other. Brackets group them, much as in an arithmetic expression. The tasks are divided: mariposa provides the statistical results (coefficients, χ², r, F), ggplot2 draws the individual plots, and patchwork arranges them.

9.9.3 Saving plots with ggsave()

ggsave() exports the last plot (or a named object) in any format:

ggsave(
  filename = "mini_study_findings.png",
  plot     = (p1 | p2) / p3,
  width    = 10,
  height   = 7,
  dpi      = 300
)

In practice: PDF for LaTeX reports (filename = "....pdf"), PNG with dpi ≥ 300 for Word and slides, SVG for the web (scalable).

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
Exercises






NoteExercise 1 · Model with interaction · Reproduction



Extend the main model with an interaction term between education and populism. Is the education effect stronger or weaker depending on the level of populism?








TipSolution






allbus |>
  linear_regression(
    formula = islamophobia ~ educ_cat * populism + age + eastwest + sex,
    weights = wghtpew
  ) |>
  summary()










NoteExercise 2 · Checking multicollinearity · Reproduction



Calculate the VIF for the predictor age by hand, following the three-step pattern from Section 9.5 (auxiliary regression → R² → 1 / (1 − R²)). Is the VIF below the warning threshold of 5, and does it match the value in summary(model)? And what would the auxiliary formula for the VIF of eastwest look like? You do not need to calculate it, just write it down.








TipSolution






# Step 1: auxiliary regression (explain age by all other predictors)
# (on the same set of cases as the main model: allbus_model)
aux_age <- lm(age ~ populism + educ_cat + eastwest + sex,
              data = allbus_model, weights = wghtpew)

# Step 2: read the R²
r2_age <- summary(aux_age)$r.squared

# Step 3: VIF formula; gives about 1.14, as in summary(model)
1 / (1 - r2_age)

# Auxiliary formula for the VIF of eastwest (not calculated):
# eastwest ~ populism + educ_cat + age + sex
# (to calculate it, use eastwest as a 0/1 dummy, because lm() does not take a factor as the DV)










NoteExercise 3 · Logistic regression with a dichotomous outcome · Transfer



Create a dummy variable for “high satisfaction with democracy” (ps03 ≤ 2, because low values mean satisfaction here) and test which characteristics are related to it.








TipSolution






allbus |>
  mutate(demo_satisfied = as.integer(ps03 <= 2)) |>
  logistic_regression(
    formula = demo_satisfied ~ educ_cat + age + eastwest + sex + islamophobia + populism,
    weights = wghtpew
  ) |>
  summary()










NoteExercise 4 · Mini project: your own regression with a composition of findings · Mini research question



Choose your own dependent variable (e.g. satisfaction with democracy, life satisfaction, a scale you built yourself). Specify a linear regression model with at least three predictors, check multicollinearity, build a coefficient plot and use patchwork to combine it with a plot of the distribution of the dependent variable. Export the result as a PNG with ggsave(). Write 3–5 sentences on what you found and how you interpret it.
No model solution: the exercise is a mini research project that takes you all the way from the model to a publication-ready finding.








Note



Research journal: Your mini study is complete. You have gone all the way: data import (Chapter 4) → building scales (Chapter 5) → visualisation (Chapter 6) → bivariate tests (Chapter 7) → validating the structure (Chapter 8) → multivariate modelling (here). You now know that populism, with Beta ≈ 0.32, is the strongest predictor of Islamophobia, that above all high education has a negative effect, that the education effect is similar in East and West, and that East–West differences remain even after controlling for socio-structural variables.
What comes next: transfer the approach to a question of your own. If you have followed the mini research question exercises in the previous chapters as a separate track, you now have a complete mini project at hand, from the codebook and the scale to the coefficient plot.

title: 9  Explanatory models
text:
What you know now

You run a simple linear regression (y ~ x) with linear_regression(), read the intercept, slope, R² and F, and draw the regression line by hand from the model coefficients with geom_abline().
You understand the OLS logic (“least squares”) through the image of the rubber band and know the formula for \(\hat{\beta}\) as the covariance of x and y divided by the variance of x.
You run a multiple linear regression with linear_regression() and interpret Beta coefficients, R², adjusted R² and the model F.
You compare models with anova(). Since version 0.6.3, mariposa models inherit directly from lm, and all standard R functions dispatch without extracting $model.
You check multicollinearity with VIF and tolerance, know the formula \(\text{VIF}_i = 1 / (1 - R^2_i)\) and the rule of thumb VIF > 10, and find both values in the table Collinearity Statistics of summary().
You build the four standard residual plots by hand with broom::augment() + ggplot2 + patchwork and use them instead of the plain plot(model).
You run a factorial ANOVA (factorial_anova()) and an ANCOVA (ancova()), read estimated marginal means and visualise interactions with your own line plots.
You run a logistic regression with logistic_regression(), read odds ratios, translate them into percentage points with marginal_effects() and know accuracy, sensitivity and specificity as complementary classification measures.
You visualise regression results as a coefficient plot with broom::tidy() + geom_pointrange().
You combine several plots into compositions with patchwork and export them with ggsave().

You now have the complete toolkit of this book: SPSS data → data import → data transformation → visualisation → univariate and bivariate analysis → latent structures → explanatory models → publication-ready figure. What next? Apply it to your own research question, with your own data.

title: 9  Explanatory models
section: Mini glossary: terms for explanatory models
text:
Mini glossary: terms for explanatory models






Term
Meaning in one sentence



OLS

ordinary least squares: the standard method that determines the regression line by minimising the squared residuals


coefficient (B)
unstandardised effect: change in y per unit of x, in the original units


Beta (β)
standardised effect: relative strength of the predictors within one model


standard error
precision of the coefficient estimate; smaller = more precise


residual
observed y minus predicted y: the part that the model does not explain


dummy variable
0/1 auxiliary variable that contrasts one factor level with the reference


reference category
the factor level without its own dummy; all other dummies are comparisons with it


treatment contrast
R’s default coding scheme: the first level is the reference, the remaining levels become dummies


R²
share of explained variance in the dependent variable; in the social sciences usually 0.05–0.30


adjusted R²
R² corrected for the number of predictors; fair for model comparisons


VIF

variance inflation factor: \(\text{VIF}_i = 1/(1-R^2_i)\); > 10 problematic


tolerance

\(1/\text{VIF} = 1 - R^2_i\); low (< 0.1) = problematic


leverage
how far a case lies from the others in the space of the predictors; high values = potentially influential case


Cook’s distance
overall influence of a single case on the model; values > 1 call for a closer look


interaction
the effect of one variable depends on the value of another


odds ratio (OR)

\(\exp(\text{logit coefficient})\): the factor by which the odds change


AME

average marginal effect: average change in the predicted probability (in percentage points)


marginal mean
group mean adjusted for covariates (estimated marginal means in the ANCOVA)


pseudo-R² (Nagelkerke)
R² analogue for logistic regression; not directly comparable with the linear R²


accuracy
share of correctly classified cases; misleading with unbalanced classes

Andrew Gelman & Jennifer Hill, Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models: a classic for modern, applied regression.

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
text:
10.1 What this chapter is about
When you get stuck while programming, you probably ask an AI assistant first: a program that answers questions asked in everyday language with text and code. For R, this is often helpful. An assistant finds typos, explains error messages and suggests code for steps you do not know yet. But it knows neither your data nor every package, and it does not tell you on its own when it does not know something. This chapter covers how to give an assistant enough context, how to check its answers and which data you must not give it.
An AI assistant is based on a language model, a program that has learned from a very large amount of text how a text is likely to continue. If you ask for R code, it writes code that resembles the code in its training texts. This works well for common tasks, because it has seen many examples of them. It has seen few or no examples of rare packages such as mariposa. In that case the code often looks correct even though it is not.
Assistants come in different forms. Some run as a chat in the browser, some complete code directly in the development environment. Others work as an agent: they read files in your project folder on their own, run commands and change code. These programs change quickly. The way of working in this chapter is therefore not tied to any particular program and works with any assistant.
An assistant writes code faster than you. Whether the code does the right thing is for you to check, and for that you need the basics from the previous chapters: you have to be able to read what a pipeline does and to recognise whether a result is plausible. You remain responsible for every line of code and every number in your work.

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
section: What you will be able to do after this chapter
text:
What you will be able to do after this chapter

Explain why an AI assistant may invent functions and arguments for mariposa.
Write a request that gives context: goal, package versions, documentation, variables and error message.
Check suggested code with the R help and your own plausibility checks.
Reproduce a problem with made-up example data instead of passing on real data.
Decide what you may show an assistant under the GESIS terms of use.
Declare the use of an assistant in coursework or a thesis.

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
section: 10.2 What an assistant knows about R
text:
10.2 What an assistant knows about R
A language model learns from texts that were collected up to a certain cut-off date. It does not know what appeared after that date, unless the program also searches the web. It knows little about what rarely occurs in those texts. For R, this means:

It knows base R, dplyr and ggplot2 well, because the web has a great deal of code and many answered questions about them.
Older ways of writing code are more common than new ones. You therefore often get %>% instead of |> (Section 3.7) or case_match() instead of recode_values() (Chapter 5).
Many answers follow the logic of SPSS or of other packages that solve similar tasks.
mariposa is young and used by comparatively few people. An assistant therefore often does not know its function names, or knows only those of an older version.

What it does not know, it fills in with whatever sounds plausible. If you ask for a weighted mean with mariposa, the answer may look like this:

allbus |>
  mariposa::weighted_mean(ls01, weights = wghtpew)

Error:
! 'weighted_mean' is not an exported object from 'namespace:mariposa'


A function with a similar name does exist, but as weighted.mean() in base R. In mariposa it is called w_mean(). With an invented name, R stops at once, before it even touches the dataset.






NoteBackground: Why assistants invent functions





A language model produces its answer piece by piece. At each step it chooses a continuation that is likely according to its training texts. It does not look up whether a function really exists, and it has no access to the packages on your computer. If the conversation so far has been about R and weighted means, weighted_mean is a very likely continuation. Whether mariposa has a function with this name plays no part in this choice. This is why invented functions sound just as convincing as real ones, and why it helps to give the assistant the real documentation.



You notice at once when an error stops the code. Harder to spot are suggestions that run without an error message and still calculate something other than what you want. Section 10.5 shows how to find such cases.

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
text:
10.3 Giving context

10.3.1 What belongs in a request
An assistant sees only what you write to it. The more precisely it knows what you are working with, the less often it has to guess. This information is called context. For a question about R code, it includes:

What you want to do, in one or two sentences and with the names of the variables.
What you are working with: the versions of R and mariposa.
The mariposa documentation. At https://yannickdiehl.github.io/mariposa/llms.txt there is an overview of all functions as a plain text file intended for language models. If your assistant can read web pages, the link is enough. Otherwise, copy the help page of the function in question into your request (for example ?w_mean).
The variables with names, labels and values. This information is in the ALLBUS questionnaire and codebook, which are available on the GESIS study page.
If there is an error, the code that causes it and the full text of the error message.

R prints the versions itself:

R.version.string

[1] "R version 4.6.2 (2026-10-29)"

packageVersion("mariposa")

[1] '0.7.4'








Importantmariposa tip: Names and labels as a table





Instead of typing out this information, you can print it as a table with codebook() (Chapter 4) and keep only the columns that describe the variables:

allbus |>
  codebook(mm01:mm06, eastwest, wghtpew, show_freq = FALSE, view = FALSE) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(name, label, value_labels, missing_values)

For each variable, the table contains the name, the label, the value labels and the missing-value codes, which is the same information as in the GESIS codebook. Frequencies and case numbers are left out.




10.3.2 An example with made-up data
A problem often depends on the structure of the data, for example on missing values, labels or weights. A small reproducible example helps here: a few rows of made-up values that have the same structure as your data and show the same problem. The example runs without your data, and no answer from a real respondent leaves your computer.

example_data <- tibble(
  eastwest = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2),            # 1 = West, 2 = East
  ls01     = c(8, 7, NA, 6, 9, 5),           # life satisfaction, 0 to 10
  wghtpew  = c(1.2, 1.2, 1.2, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) # weight
)
example_data

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  eastwest  ls01 wghtpew
     <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1        1     8     1.2
2        1     7     1.2
3        1    NA     1.2
4        2     6     0.5
5        2     9     0.5
6        2     5     0.5


The values are invented. All that matters is that the example shows the problem: here a missing value in ls01 and a weight that differs between East and West. The reprex package copies such examples together with their output as text that you can paste into a request (see Further reading).

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
text:
10.4 A template for your request
The following template brings the context together and lists the rules that apply in this book. Save it as a text file in your project and fill it in for each request. With these rules, the assistant writes code in the style of this book, and you can check that code with what you have learned in the chapters.
I am working in R (version: …) with the tidyverse and the mariposa package (version: …).
Documentation for mariposa: https://yannickdiehl.github.io/mariposa/llms.txt

Please follow these rules:
- Native pipe |> instead of %>%.
- Statistics and tests with mariposa functions, for example describe(),
  frequency(), t_test() or linear_regression().
- Weighting through the argument weights = wghtpew.
- Recoding with rec() inside mutate().
- The English-language ALLBUS file (ZA8833) does not declare missing values.
  I set them to NA with set_na() when I read the data with read_spss(),
  so they are already NA in my data.
- Use only functions and arguments that exist in the packages named above.
  If you are unsure about a function, say so.
- Explain each line in a short comment.

My variables (name, label, values):
…

What I want to do:
…

My code so far and the error message (if any):
…
The template contains no data, and what you fill in at the places marked … should not contain any either. Section 10.6 sets out what you may pass on.






Tip



SPSS → R: Translating old syntax. If you have SPSS syntax from earlier projects, an assistant can translate it into R. Syntax usually contains only commands and no data. Include the rules from the template in your request, because many mariposa functions correspond to an SPSS procedure: FREQUENCIES becomes frequency(), DESCRIPTIVES becomes describe(). Afterwards, check whether R prints the same numbers as SPSS did.

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
text:
10.5 Checking answers
Read an answer before you run it. If you do not understand a line, ask until you do. Then check whether the suggested functions exist and whether the result is correct.

10.5.1 Does the function exist?
Look up every function you do not know with ? (Section 3.3). If RStudio finds no help page, the function probably does not exist in the loaded packages. help(package = "mariposa") lists all functions in the package. For a quick test, this is enough:

c("w_mean", "weighted_mean") %in% ls("package:mariposa")

[1]  TRUE FALSE


w_mean() exists, weighted_mean() does not. Check the arguments as well. Under Usage, the help page shows which arguments a function accepts. If an argument is misspelled, mariposa tells you:

example_data |>
  describe(ls01, weight = wghtpew)

Error in `describe()`:
! Unknown argument `weight` of `describe()`.
ℹ Did you mean `weights` instead of `weight`?



10.5.2 Does the code run, and is the result correct?
Run the code in a chunk of your Quarto document (Section 1.5.2). Then it is part of your report, and later you can trace where a number comes from.
Code that runs without an error message does not necessarily calculate the right thing. A common case is a mean without weights.
Question: What is the mean life satisfaction in the example, unweighted and weighted?

example_data |>
  summarise(mean = mean(ls01, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
   mean
  <dbl>
1     7

example_data |>
  w_mean(ls01, weights = wghtpew)


Weighted Mean Statistics
------------------------
Weights: wghtpew

  ---------------------------
  Variable   Mean  N  Missing
  ---------------------------
  ls01      7.179  4        1
  ---------------------------


Interpretation. Both calls run without a warning. The unweighted mean is 7.0, the weighted mean 7.179. In ALLBUS, the new federal states are deliberately over-represented (Chapter 7, section “Weighting”). An unweighted mean for Germany as a whole therefore gives the East too much weight. An assistant that does not know your data knows this only if you tell it.
Further checks take little time:

Number of cases: Does the N match what you expect? If many cases are missing, this is often due to missing values or a filter.
Range of values: The mean of a scale from 0 to 10 must lie between 0 and 10. Negative values point to missing-value codes that were counted as valid values (Section 4.8).
Weights: mariposa states in the header of the output whether the analysis is weighted, for example Weighted Mean Statistics.
Comparison with a known result: First reproduce a result you know from this book, such as a frequency from Chapter 4. If it matches, the pipeline works up to that point.

Always take the numbers for your report from your own R output. An assistant that has not seen your data cannot know any results. If it gives numbers anyway, they are made up.

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
text:
10.6 Protecting data
What you write to an assistant is sent to the provider, processed there and often stored as well. Research data have their own rules for this.






Warning



Caution: ALLBUS data do not belong in an AI assistant. Section 4 of the GESIS terms of use (valid from 4 February 2026) prohibits using AI systems to process the data GESIS provides. GESIS may grant exceptions only on request in individual cases, and only if you alone have control over, and responsibility for, the AI system and use it exclusively for scientific purposes. Anyone who culpably breaches the terms loses the right of use and pays a contractual penalty of €10,000.


For working with this book, this means:

You can pass on code, error messages, variable names and labels from the public documentation, and examples with made-up values.
Keep the file ALLBUS2023.sav, data rows and any output that shows individual respondents (such as the output of head(), glimpse() or View()) to yourself.
The terms do not explicitly address aggregated results such as a frequency table. The safest approach is to ask for code and interpret the numbers yourself.
An agent that reads files in your project folder and runs R processes the data itself. Use such tools only in a folder without ALLBUS data.

Other datasets have their own terms of use. If you collect data yourself, for example in a survey for your thesis, you also have data protection obligations to your respondents. In both cases, check with your supervisor beforehand which tools you may use. Terms of use change; read the current version before you start a new project.

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
text:
10.7 Assistants in coursework and theses
Your university decides whether and how you may use an assistant in assessed work. Many universities have their own guidance on this, often as part of the declaration of authorship. Read it before you start, and if in doubt, ask your supervisor.
If you use an assistant, state what you used it for, for example writing or correcting code or explaining error messages. To do this, keep a record of which requests you made and what you used from the answers. The simplest place for this is your Quarto document, in a note next to the code that came out of the request. Your report shows the code anyway (Chapter 2); with these notes, readers can also trace how it came about. In any case, you are responsible for the code, the results and their interpretation.






Note



Research journal: Where your mini study stands. Your mini study is complete and reproducible. If you extend it with the help of an assistant, record the requests in your research journal: which question you asked, what the answer suggested and what you checked and used.

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
text:
Exercises






NoteExercise 1 · Request with context · Reproduction



You want to know how school leaving certificates (educ) are distributed in the West and in the East, weighted with wghtpew. Codes 6 (“OTHER SCHOOL CERTIF.”) and 7 (“STILL AT SCHOOL”) should count as missing. Fill in the template from Section 10.4 for this question. Include the variables with names, labels and values, but no data.








TipSolution





I am working in R (version: 4.6.2) with the tidyverse and the mariposa package (version: 0.7.4).
Documentation for mariposa: https://yannickdiehl.github.io/mariposa/llms.txt

[rules as in the template]

My variables (name, label, values):
- educ: RESP: GENERAL SCHOOL LEAVING CERTIFICATE; 1 = NO CERTIFICATE,
  2 = LOWEST LEVEL, 3 = INTERMEDIARY LEVEL, 4 = QUALI.UNIV.APPL.SCI.,
  5 = QUALI.FOR UNIVERSITY, 6 = OTHER SCHOOL CERTIF., 7 = STILL AT SCHOOL
- eastwest: REGION OF INTERVIEW: WEST - EAST; 1 = OLD FEDERAL STATES,
  2 = NEW FEDERAL STATES
- wghtpew: WEIGHT: EAST-WEST, PERSON-LEVEL

What I want to do:
A weighted frequency table of educ, separately for West and East.
Codes 6 and 7 should count as missing.

My code so far:
allbus <- read_spss("ALLBUS2023.sav") |>
  set_na(-56, -55, -54, -53, -51, -50, -42, -41,
         -33, -32, -15, -11, -10, -9, -8, -7, -6)
A suitable answer uses, for example, set_na(educ = c(6, 7)) from Section 4.8, then group_by(eastwest) and frequency(educ, weights = wghtpew). Check it with the steps from Section 10.5 before you use it.









NoteExercise 2 · Checking an answer · Reproduction



An assistant suggested this code for the question “How satisfied are people in the West and in the East with their lives, and how satisfied are they in Germany as a whole?” Find at least three problems, first by reading. Then check your guesses in R.

allbus %>%
  mutate(east = eastwest == "East") %>%
  group_by(east) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(ls01))

mariposa::weighted_mean(allbus$ls01, allbus$wghtpew)









TipSolution







%>% works, but it does not match the style of this book (|>).

eastwest is a number with labels (1 and 2). Comparing it with the text "East" causes an error.

mean() without na.rm = TRUE returns NA as soon as ls01 has missing values (Section 3.6).
The means for West and East are unweighted.

mariposa::weighted_mean() does not exist. In mariposa the function is called w_mean(), and it expects a dataset and variable names instead of allbus$….

In the style of this book:

allbus |>
  group_by(eastwest) |>
  describe(ls01, weights = wghtpew)

allbus |>
  w_mean(ls01, weights = wghtpew)










NoteExercise 3 · Checking functions · Transfer



An assistant suggests four mariposa functions for your analysis: cross_table(), w_sd(), crosstab() and cronbach_alpha(). Check which of them exist. For the others, find the matching function from this book.

w_sd() and crosstab() exist. Instead of cross_table() you use crosstab() from Chapter 7, and instead of cronbach_alpha() the function reliability() from Section 8.7.









NoteExercise 4 · A step for your mini study · Mini research question



Take your own research question from the exercises of the previous chapters and think of a next analysis step that you have not learned yet, for example an additional control variable or a different graph. Write a request for it with the template and check the answer with the steps from Section 10.5. Record in your Quarto document what you asked, what you changed in the answer and why.
There is no model solution for this exercise. What matters is the process from the request to the check.

title: 10  Working with AI assistants
text:
What you know now

A language model writes the code that is most likely given its training texts. For mariposa, it therefore easily invents functions and arguments.
You give an assistant context: goal, versions, the mariposa documentation, variables and error messages.
You reproduce problems with data using made-up example values.
You check suggestions with the R help, with ls("package:mariposa") and with simple checks of the number of cases, the range of values and the weights.
You take numbers only from your own R output.
You do not give ALLBUS data to any AI system, because the GESIS terms of use prohibit it.
In coursework and theses, you state what you used an assistant for.
